last two are education-AI publishers by name and have never been read.

# 🆕 Trends new at `p739` (researched 2026-11-10) — `T337`–`T343`

**Added above `p738`'s `T329`–`T336`.** Two are supply findings, three are instrument findings,
one is a design finding and one records the mandated demand legs and what they did **not** return.
🔴 **`T338` and `T341` are a matched pair and should be read together** — the licence index is
wrong in both directions on the same pass.

## T337 — 🟢 This base's largest asset is its own backlog, and the backlog is institutional

`p739` re-ran `P693-A`'s promotion census with `Gap 248`'s non-address filter applied.
**`42` path fragments removed** — `topics/*` ×38, `orgs/*` ×2, `search/repositories`,
`trending/*` ×3 — leaving **`4,561` distinct trending addresses against `1,145` shelf addresses:
`3,695` repositories discovered, licence-read, written up and never promoted.** p693 put the
region-labelled subset at `825`; the unrestricted figure is `4.5×` that.

🟢 **The composition is the finding, not the count.** The owners with the deepest unpromoted
estates are not hobbyists: `digitalcredentials` (`29`), `openedx` (`20`),
`ed-fi-alliance-oss` (`19`), `openstax` (`14`), `edanalytics` (`14`),
`apereo-learning-analytics-initiative` (`14`), `adlnet` (`13`), `yetanalytics` (`11`),
`bycs-lp` (`11`), `utdanningsdirektoratet` (`10`), `svws-nrw` (`10`), `esupportail` (`10`),
`open-spaced-repetition` (`10`), `project-sunbird` (`7`), `eol-uchile` (`7`). **Consortia,
standards bodies, state ministries and public universities — `278` owners with `≥2` unpromoted
repositories each.**

🔵 **So the standing recommendation inverts the usual one.** A pass that wants a procurement-grade,
region-placed row should **read the backlog, not the search frontier**: `16` of p739's `19`
byte-reads came from it, and they produced a government ministry's BSD-3 SIS, a national
examination directorate's Apache-2.0 code, the US K-12 data standard and India's national content
authoring stack. The frontier, meanwhile, produced `3` single-author tutor skills.

## T338 — 🔴 GitHub's licence index reports `NOASSERTION` on a government ministry's BSD-3 grant

[`SVWS-NRW/SVWS-Server`](https://github.com/SVWS-NRW/SVWS-Server) (`40★`, pushed **2026-11-10**)
indexes as **`NOASSERTION`** via `gh api -X GET search/repositories`. Its `LICENSE` is
**`1,611 B`**, sha256₁₂ `966b53671a2c`, contains `Redistribution and use in source and binary
forms` plus a `Neither the name of` clause → **`BSD-3-Clause`**, holder
**`Copyright (c) Ministerium für Schule und Bildung des Landes NRW`**.

🔴 **The cost of trusting the index here would have been the most procurement-credible platform row
on the shelf** — a German state education ministry's production school-information system, under a
non-reciprocal licence, pushed today. 🔵 The index is not lying; `NOASSERTION` means *"no SPDX
match"*, and a ministry's lightly reworded BSD text does not match. **But `NOASSERTION` is read as
"no licence" by every pipeline that does not open the file,** which is why this base reads bytes.
Extends `p736`'s index-vs-payload census (`3 / 4` index fields wrong) to a fifth case.

## T339 — 🟢 The education agent supply has moved into harness-plugin form, and a third of it carries no usable grant

`topic:ai-tutor created:>2026-10-01` → **`225`** repositories; the top `100` by stars read in full.

| Measure | Count of `100` |
|---|--:|
| MIT | **59** |
| Apache-2.0 | 4 |
| GPL-3.0 / AGPL-3.0 | 6 |
| 🔴 `NONE` (no licence) | **22** |
| 🔴 `NOASSERTION` | 9 |
| **Permissive (MIT / Apache / BSD)** | **63** |
| **Harness plugin or agent skill** (`skill`, `plugin`, `Claude Code`, `Codex`, `MCP`, `harness`, `DSH` in the description) | **28** |

🟢 **Two readings, and both are commercial.** First, **`63 %` permissive** is the healthiest grant
ratio this base has measured on a fresh cohort — the hobbyist education layer defaults to MIT.
🔴 Second, **`31 / 100` carry no usable grant**, so a third of what a keyword leg returns is
unbuyable however good it looks. 🔵 Third, and the structural one: **`28 %` are plugins to someone
else's agent harness.** Those are days of work, not months, because the harness supplies the loop,
the file access and the UI — **which moves the defensible part of an education engagement off the
agent entirely, onto curriculum, rubric, evidence and integration** (`T337`'s institutional
substrate, `P174`'s review step). A studio that sells "an AI tutor" in 2026 is selling a weekend;
one that sells the assessment evidence around it is selling the engagement.

## T340 — 🟢 On deployment artefacts, forks measure adoption and stars measure nothing

| Repo | Stars | Forks | Ratio |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| [project-sunbird/sunbird-collection-editor](https://github.com/project-sunbird/sunbird-collection-editor) | 3 | **45** | **15.0 : 1** |
| [project-sunbird/sunbird-quml-player](https://github.com/project-sunbird/sunbird-quml-player) | 6 | **39** | **6.5 : 1** |

🟢 **The mechanism is specific to this class of software.** You star a framework you admire; you
**fork** an item renderer or an authoring editor because you are branding it, re-pointing it at
your own content service and shipping it. For the Sunbird estate — the stack behind India's
national school content platform — the forks are state education departments and implementation
partners, which is exactly the adoption a star count cannot show.
🔵 **Rule for later passes: on a renderer, editor, theme or installer, read `forks_count` before
`stargazers_count`, and treat a ratio above `3 : 1` as a deployment signal.** 🔴 It does **not**
generalise: on a library or a research repository, a high fork ratio usually means coursework.

## T341 — 🔴 The exact inverse of `T338`: the index asserts `GPL-3.0` and the grant is not in the repository at all

[`1281504089-cell/kaixin-k12-tutor`](https://github.com/1281504089-cell/kaixin-k12-tutor)
(`1★`, created `2026-11-06`, pushed `2026-11-08`, a DeepTutor-derived K-12 desktop app shipping
`136` Chinese textbooks) indexes as **`GPL-3.0`**. `README.md` returns `200`, so the repository is
alive. **`19` probed licence paths all return `404`** — `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, `LICENSE.txt`,
`LICENCE`, `LICENCE.md`, `License`, `License.md`, `license`, `license.md`, `LICENSE-GPL`,
`GPL-license.txt`, `COPYING`, `COPYING.txt`, `COPYING.md`, `NOTICE`, `LICENSE.rst`, `docs/LICENSE`,
`.github/LICENSE`, `src/LICENSE`.

🟢 **The mechanism was found, and it is new to this base.** The README's own licence section says
**`源码归档内附 LICENSE 与 THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`** — *"the source archive ships with a LICENSE"*.
**The grant lives inside a release artefact, not in the default ref.** So the honest verdict is
not *"no grant exists"* (`T302`) and not *"GPL-3.0"* either: it is **"the grant is not readable
from the repository, and a studio cloning `HEAD` receives no licence file."**
🔵 **Actionable rule: when the index asserts a copyleft id and no payload exists on the default
ref, look for a release asset and say so** — and treat the repository as unusable until the
archive is opened, because copyleft asserted-but-unreadable is the worst of both states.
🔴 **Paired with `T338`, the conclusion is symmetrical and should end the question: the index is
wrong in both directions, on the same pass, and only the bytes decide.** `T289` and `P693-H` also
re-confirmed: `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}/git/trees/HEAD` returned `403` for this repository
while the `search/repositories` channel returned full metadata for it.

## T342 — 🟢 Separating deterministic scoring from generative explanation is appearing from the bottom of the market, and it is the Annex III answer

[`prayashcloud/axomiya-study-companion`](https://github.com/prayashcloud/axomiya-study-companion)
(MIT, `3★`, `2026-11-02`) states the split in its own README as step `3` of a four-step loop:
**`Grade: answers are marked in plain Python code (not by the AI), so scores are always exact`.**
The model explains and generates items; **code marks**.

🟢 **This is the architecture that the deferred Annex III duties ask for, arrived at by a hackathon
entry in Guwahati rather than by a compliance team.** Under `Regulation (EU) 2026/1744` the
high-risk education obligations — including AI used in assessment — apply from
**`2 December 2027`** (`T321`), and the hardest of them to retrofit is reproducibility: showing
that the same answer yields the same mark. A deterministic scorer makes that a property of the
code rather than a claim about a model. 🔵 **It is also the cheapest possible version of the
control**, which is why it should be the default recommendation rather than a premium one.
🔵 Converges with `T329`'s reading of [`Khan/perseus`](https://github.com/Khan/perseus), whose
decade-old value is precisely its **deterministic scorer**, and with `P174`'s human-review step.
🔵 **Say it as a rule: the model may write the question and explain the answer; it must not be the
thing that assigns the mark.**

## T343 — 🔴 The four mandated regional demand legs: `0` novel facts, and the nil is now diagnostic rather than disappointing

All four legs ran at `p739` plus the global arm. **Every fact returned was already held**, and the
denominators are recorded under each region in [`market.md`](market.md).

| Leg | Returned | Novel | Notes |
|---|---|--:|---|
| Global (`AI {industry} industry trends {year}`) | Google *AI in Education Report: From potential to practice*, Nov 2026; OECD 2026 chatbot-withdrawal finding; 1EdTech governance shift; credential pathways | **0** | `33rd` consecutive nil. The Google report is held (`p662` mandated-legs evidence) |
| North America | `134` bills / `31` states; Maryland `SB 720`; NY `A 9190`; Illinois `HB2400`; K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act; Khanmigo `$10 M` NC earmark | **0** | `35th` nil |
| EMEA | `Regulation (EU) 2026/1744`; Annex III → `2026-12-02`→`2027-12-02`; Art. 50 since `2026-08-02`; emotion-recognition ban since `2025-02-02`; South Africa draft policy; Rwanda–Anthropic MoU | **0** | Held since `p737`/`p693` |
| APAC | Ipsos Education Monitor 2026 ban-support figures; Japan AI Promotion Act; India labelling from `2026-02-20`; China service-specific rules; TAL / PhysicsWallah pivots | **0** | Held since `p693` |
| LATAM | UNESCO Santiago Observatory; TALIS Brazil `56%` / Chile `55%` vs OECD `36%`; Cetic.br `53%` / `22%`; UNESCO IESALC `87%` / `26%`; Brazil `PL 2338/2023`; Chile `Boletín 16.821-19`; Peru the only enacted law | **0** | `8th` consecutive nil |

🟢 **The diagnosis is `P693-I`, now with a fifth pass of evidence, and it is not that the legs are
badly written.** The aggregator layer this environment can reach has been fully harvested: the
same `~20` facts per region come back in a different order each pass. **The primary instruments
that would move any of these figures are unreadable here** — `unesco.org`, `eur-lex.europa.eu`,
`ipsos.com`, `oecd.org` and `iesalc.unesco.org` all fail at DNS resolution.
🔵 **So the honest allocation, and p739 acted on it: spend the pass on the supply side, where the
GitHub channels still discriminate, and record the demand nil with its denominators** rather than
re-buying the same twenty facts. 🔴 **An informed gap is information; a silent one looks like
coverage.** The single cheapest improvement available to this KB remains a session configuration
that can resolve those five hosts.

# 🆕 Trends new at `p738` (researched 2026-11-10) — `T329`–`T336`

**Added above `p737`'s `T321`–`T328`.** Four are demand findings, two are supply findings and two
are instrument findings. **One corrects a region placement that a secondary source got wrong**
(`T334`), and **one closes a question `T323` and `p737` left half-open** (`T330`).

## T329 — 🟢 The world's most-used open-source assessment engine is MIT, and this base spent dozens of passes declaring the gap it fills

[`Khan/perseus`](https://github.com/Khan/perseus) — **MIT, `1,598★`, pushed 2026-11-10** — is Khan
Academy's exercise and question engine: the renderer, authoring editor and **deterministic scorer**
behind its interactive items. Expression input marked for *mathematical equivalence* rather than
string identity, draggable graphs scored against a target, labelled images, sorting, matching, with
per-widget hint flows. It has run at Khan Academy's scale for a decade.

🔴 **This base has asserted an "assessment component" gap repeatedly while Perseus sat in the open
under the most permissive grant available.** The reason is diagnosable and is the transferable part:
**every leg that would have found it was aimed at the word "AI".** Perseus is not an AI project, does
not carry an AI topic, and does not appear in `topic:ai-education` or `topic:ai-grading`. It is
infrastructure. 🟢 **Standing correction to this base's own search model: the components that make an
education AI product shippable are mostly not AI components**, and they are therefore invisible to
every AI-shaped leg. The publisher leg found it in one request.

🔵 **Why it changes the shape of a grading engagement.** The current pitch — an LLM marks the work —
fails the question a registrar asks: *can you reproduce this mark?* Perseus inverts the architecture:
**the model authors the item, the engine scores it**, and the score is deterministic, reproducible
and explainable without reference to a model version. That is the difference between a pilot and
something that can carry credit (`P200`).

## T330 — 🔴 LATAM's institutions are not missing from the sector, they are missing from GitHub — and that question is now closed

`T323` refuted the discovery-language explanation for LATAM's thin supply on `10` non-English legs.
The one remaining explanation was that this base was querying the wrong publishers. `p738` tested it
directly by naming the obvious ones: **`14` publisher legs at Latin American ministries, agencies and
universities returned `0` fileable rows, and `8 / 14` returned *no such organisation*** —
`SEDUC-SP`, `mec-br`, `inep`, `mineduc-cl`, `educacionar`, `uniandes`, `fundacion-telefonica`,
`lappis-unb`. `org:govbr` has `17` repositories and none is educational; `org:RNP` has `2`, both
inactive since 2014; `org:USPCodeLab` is a student club.

🟢 **Both candidate explanations are now refuted, so the finding is a supply fact with a named
cause: in this region, institutional educational capability is not published as reusable
software.** 🔵 **And it is commercially the better of the two possible worlds.** Where a European
ministry has already open-sourced its school platform, the engagement is integration into someone
else's estate. Where a LATAM ministry has published nothing, **the institutional artefact itself is
unbuilt** — the governance framework, the model-choice record, the teacher-capability programme, the
reusable platform — and that is a larger, earlier and stickier piece of work. 🔵 It also resolves the
apparent paradox that LATAM reads **thin on this base and first in the world on adoption** (`T333`):
adoption is happening in classrooms, not in repositories. ⚠️ Practical consequence: stop spending
publisher legs on LATAM government orgs. Spend them on the named regional programmes that *do*
publish (`Plan Ceibal`, `Fundación Ceibal`, `LATAM-GPT`, `portabilis`, `bncc-dev`) and treat the rest
of LATAM supply as something to be *created* in engagements.

## T331 — 🔴 A manifest licence can be the scaffolding tool's default, which makes `T312`'s rule half a rule

`T312` established that a missing `LICENSE` file is not evidence of a missing grant, because grants
live in manifests — measured `3 / 3`. `p738` measures the inverse failure on
[`cast-org/clusive`](https://github.com/cast-org/clusive): **no licence file at `14` probed paths,
`package.json` declaring `"license": "ISC"`, and a `README.md` §License reading
*"made available under the BSD 3-clause license"*.**

🔴 **`ISC` is the value `npm init` writes when the author does not choose one.** So is `MIT` under
some tooling. A manifest field is therefore evidence of *whatever the scaffold wrote* unless
something corroborates it, and here it contradicted the project's own prose statement.

🟢 **The repaired rule, and it costs one extra fetch:** **licence file → README licence section →
manifest**, and a manifest-only value is recorded as *uncorroborated*. 🔵 Generalisable beyond this
base: when an index says `NOASSERTION` and a manifest says `ISC` or `MIT` with no payload, the
honest record is the README's claim plus a flag — and for a client build, a written confirmation
from the publisher, because **a README sentence is not a licence file and does not grant anything.**

## T332 — 🔴 GitHub repository search matches keywords as substrings, so the obvious education words are unusable — and one of them is farmed

`T326` established that prose legs produce rows and publisher legs do. `p738` names the mechanism
for half of it: **`tutor` matches inside `tutorial`; `grading` matches inside `upgrading`.**

- `tutor created:>2026-09-01 stars:>30` → `47` total, `25` read, **`0` education rows**.
  ⚠️ **`16` of the `25` are a single operator**: `apimart*` throwaway accounts, all `NOASSERTION`,
  all named `*-api-*-tutorial`, all in a uniform **`55`–`87★`** band, all created in one window.
  Organised star inflation on LLM-API-reseller promos, captured by this leg purely on the substring.
- `grading created:>2026-09-01 stars:>20` → `81` total, `25` read, **`0` education rows**, top row
  `2,580★`, all `upgrading` matches in unrelated tooling.
- `student`, `education` and `curriculum` legs: `3` more legs, `29` rows, **`0` education rows**.

🟢 **Five legs, `79` rows, `0` usable — and the rule that follows is cheap to obey: a keyword leg
must not use a word that is a prefix of a common unrelated word.** 🔵 `topic:` and `org:` legs are
immune, because neither matches prose; this is an argument for the structured channels on
mechanism, not just on observed yield. ⚠️ **Star counts in a recency window are not a quality
signal**, because they can be manufactured faster than they can be earned —
`evidence/substring-pollution.2026-11-10-p738.tsv`.

## T333 — 🟢 LATAM higher education now has the sharpest adoption-vs-readiness number in any region: 92% / 79% / 30%

A **Digital Education Council** *AI in Higher Education LATAM Survey 2026*, run with
**Tecnológico de Monterrey** and its **Institute for the Future of Education**, reports
**`92%` of students and `79%` of faculty actively engaging with AI**, and **only `30%` believing
their institution has responded effectively.**

🟢 **This is the `T319`/`T325` "scissors" measured a third time, on a named instrument, with an
institutional co-author a client will recognise — and it is the widest reading yet.** Corroborating
and complicating it: a **UNESCO IESALC** working paper (September 2026) finds adoption *"neither
uniform nor evenly distributed"*, with a significant **public-versus-private university gap**; a
2025 UNESCO regional survey of **200 institutions across 19 countries** finds the
adoption-governance gap especially pronounced in LAC; and the **IDB** has catalogued
**193 AI initiatives** across the region.

🔵 **The commercial reading, and it is the opposite of the usual one.** A `92%` student-adoption
figure is not a reason to sell adoption — adoption already happened without anyone's permission.
**The `30%` is the sellable number**, and the deliverable it names is institutional: a policy that
is actually operative, a model-choice record, an assessment-integrity position, a faculty
capability programme. 🔵 **Faculty at `79%` is the detail to put in a proposal**, because it kills
the "our professors will resist" objection before it is raised; a separate DEC reading characterises
that faculty use as *high adoption, conservative usage*, which is exactly the population a
capability programme converts. ⚠️ All of this is survey self-report on a secondary channel
(`T328` bounds what this base can confirm); the MarketsandMarkets *"Rest of Latin America"*
figure (~USD `18M`, 2024) that appeared alongside is **refused** as a basis for anything.

## T334 — 🔴 The UAE's 25 classroom AI prohibitions are an EMEA fact, and the source that supplied them filed it under APAC

**February 2026: the UAE Ministry of Education issued a set of roughly `25` generative-AI
prohibitions for schools**, covering age suitability, privacy, academic integrity and examination
rules. 🔴 **The secondary source that reported it presented it as an APAC regulatory development,
alongside a UK item it also misplaced.** Both belong to **EMEA** — the `E` in EMEA is Europe, the
`M` is the Middle East, and the Gulf states are the `M`.

🟢 **Recorded as a trend rather than buried as a correction, because the error is systematic and
will recur.** English-language market coverage routinely sorts the Gulf into "Asia-Pacific" or
"Asia", and this base's `region` field is a **closed five-value vocabulary** precisely so that a
source's loose geography cannot silently become a filter bucket. 🔵 **Standing instruction: place
the region from the country, never from the source's section heading.** Country in the prose,
region in the field.

🔵 **The substance matters too, and it cuts against the regional stereotype.** The Gulf is usually
sold as the permissive, build-fast AI market; here it is the **most prescriptive school regulator
of 2026** on this base's reading, more so than any EU member state's national layer. Meanwhile the
**Ipsos Education Monitor 2026** finds *lower* support for banning classroom AI across the Asian
markets it examined. 🔴 **So the restrictive-permissive axis does not run East-West**, and a
proposal that assumes it does will be wrong in both directions.

## T335 — 🟢 North America's binding constraint moved from "is there a policy" to "is the policy legible", and the number is 6%

Adoption and policy have decoupled further. **A June 2026 reading has more than `4` in `5` teens
having used AI tools and over two-thirds using them regularly, with around half of their schools
having no policy at all** — and, from the **Stanford AI Index 2026** reporting,
**only `6%` of teachers say their school's AI policy is clear.**

🟢 **`6%` is the most useful single figure this base holds for North America, and the reason is
that it is not an adoption number or a compliance number — it is a *legibility* number.** The
policy volume is already enormous: the **Public Impact / PIE Network** count of **~`100` state
bills** this year touching students' AI use, **at least `15` states** with enacted or introduced
AI-in-education legislation, **Illinois** statutorily requiring its state board to publish district
guidance **by 1 July 2026**, and the **Education Commission of the States** issuing a set of
**nine recommendations** plus an April 2026 state-guidelines compilation.

🔵 **Which identifies the deliverable exactly, and it is not a policy document.** Districts have
policies; `94%` of teachers cannot read them. The sellable artefact is **translation and
operationalisation** — the role-specific one-page rule, the classroom decision tree, the
training record that evidences it — which is also the artefact the statutes themselves name
(`T324`, `P196`). 🔵 **Funding is attached**: a federal grant priority on AI literacy and educator
training with first competitions in the **2026-27** cycle, and **`$169M` in FIPSE awards** that
include responsible AI use. ⚠️ The teen-usage figures come from vendor and aggregator summaries;
the ECS material is the firmest of the set.

## T336 — 🟡 Europe's teachers are past the adoption question and the AI Act's high-risk rules are two years out, which makes 2026 a soft-law year

**Futuresource reports `67%` of teachers now using AI tools** and expects **AI-enabled devices to
be `15%` of institutional PC shipments in 2026**. An **Epson-commissioned survey of ~`3,360`
respondents across the UK, France, Italy, Germany, Spain and Poland** finds **`80%` of teachers
worried that AI is entering classrooms faster than schools can manage** and **`76%` of students
expecting to be allowed to use AI in their learning**.

🟢 **The regulatory half is now confirmed from a third independent direction and it matches what
this base published**: a **Digital Omnibus deal reached 7 May 2026** means the **high-risk rules,
which include education, apply from 2 December 2027** — the slip from the original August 2026 date
that `T306` closed and `T321` split in two. Two live 2026 items sit under it: the Commission's
consultation on **draft high-risk classification guidelines** (open to **23 June 2026**) and the
Council education ministers' **conclusions on teachers in the AI era, adopted 11 May 2026**.

🟡 **So 2026 in EMEA is a soft-law year with a hard deadline behind it, and that is a specific
selling position rather than a lull.** The binding Annex III duties are 2027; what is live now is
**AI literacy, transparency, and the ministerial expectation about teacher capability** — plus the
standards an auditor will reach for in the absence of applicable regulation, named explicitly in
this pass's sources as **ISO/IEC 42001** alongside **UNESCO's generative-AI guidance** and the
**OECD Digital Education Outlook 2026**. 🔵 **The OECD's framing is the one to quote in a proposal**,
because it is the sentence that justifies the whole engagement rather than the tool: *AI helps
learning only when pedagogy stays in control.* 🔵 **`Eurydice`'s "Digital education at school in
Europe 2026"** is the comparative instrument for a multi-country bid. ⚠️ The `67%` and `15%` figures
are a market-research house's; the Epson survey is vendor-commissioned. Both are reported as
sourced, not adopted as this base's own.

# 🆕 Trends new at `p737` (researched 2026-11-10) — `T321`–`T328`

**Added above `p736`'s `T310`–`T320`.** Three are demand findings, three are supply findings and
two are instrument findings. **Two of the eight correct a claim this base already published**
(`T321` on the EU timeline and on KHDA; `T324` on a North Carolina deadline), and **one refuses a
figure outright** because it could not be confirmed — recorded so no later pass files it.

## T321 — 🔴 The EU AI Act's education obligations split in two, and the half that is live now is the half nobody is planning for

`T318` is right that education sits in Annex III and that the Digital Omnibus
(**Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**, published in the Official Journal **24 July 2026**, in force
**27 July 2026**) moved stand-alone high-risk obligations from `2 August 2026` to
**`2 December 2027`**. `p737` confirms that date from a **third** independent reading and adds the
regulation's citable number, which `T318` did not carry.

🔴 **What `T318` does not say, and what changes a 2026 proposal: Article 50 was not deferred.** The
transparency duties — telling a person they are interacting with an AI system, and marking
AI-generated content — **remain in force on their original schedule**, as does the **AI-literacy
duty, which has applied since February 2025** and was reworded in 2026 to require *measures that
support* AI literacy rather than a guaranteed level per person.

🟢 **So the operative position for a European education engagement today is precise, and it is the
opposite of "the rules were delayed":**

- **Live now** — disclosure to the learner, marking of generated material, and a demonstrable
  AI-literacy measure for staff and students. These are **cheap to build and cheap to omit**, which
  is why they are the ones that get missed.
- **Due `2 December 2027`** — the conformity apparatus for stand-alone high-risk education systems
  (admissions, student evaluation, exam scoring): risk management, data governance, logging, human
  oversight, technical documentation. `2 August 2028` for AI embedded in regulated products.

🔵 **Commercial reading: the delay is a sales window, not a holiday.** Sixteen extra months is
exactly enough to build the conformity artefact properly, and an institution that waits until
mid-2027 will be buying it under time pressure. The disclosure-and-marking layer is the engagement
that gets you in the door this year (`P196`).

⚠️ **Sources disagree on one date and the disagreement is recorded rather than resolved:** the
Article 50 obligations are given as applying from **`2 August 2026`** (general applicability) in one
reading and the **marking/watermarking deadline as `2 December 2026`** in another. Both are 2026 and
both are live; **which clause carries which date must be settled against the Official Journal text**
before it is quoted to a client.

🔴 **And a correction to `T318`'s own Gulf sentence.** `T318` states that *"Dubai's KHDA has issued
explicit responsible-AI guidance to private schools."* That is **overstated as of `2026-11-10`**.
What KHDA has actually issued is: the **nine FutuReady Standards**, one of which covers AI-enabled
career and academic guidance, with a **three-year implementation window** for Dubai private schools;
an **AI-literacy programme announced February 2026** with the DP World Foundation and **MIT RAISE**,
targeting **Grades 6–8**; and, from **term 1 of 2026-27**, **AI-assisted selection of school
inspection visits with no more than 24 hours' notice**. The **classroom AI-use guidelines are
reported as expected in 2027 and are not published**. 🔵 The genuinely notable item is the third:
**the regulator is itself the AI deployer**, which makes "how was this inspection targeted" a
question a Dubai school's leadership will be asked before any classroom AI question.

⚠️ **Secondary sources throughout, and `p737` can now state why that will not improve from this
environment — see `T328`.**

## T322 — 🟢 The APAC classroom-attitude numbers `p736` declared unobtainable exist, and they measure the opposite of what a proposal usually asks

`p736` recorded a declared gap: *"no APAC classroom-adoption percentages obtainable at usable
quality."* `p737` closes it partially, with a caveat that has to travel with the numbers.

**Ipsos Education Monitor 2026** measures **support for banning AI in schools** across its APAC
markets: **`23 %` in Indonesia rising to `31 %` in South Korea**, with **Australia and New Zealand
higher than either**. Support for a ban **rose** over the survey period in **Japan, Australia and
South Korea**.

⚠️ **This is a ban-support series, not an adoption series** — it does not say what share of
classrooms use AI, and it must not be re-stated as if it did. 🟢 **But it answers the question a
regional proposal actually turns on, which adoption rates do not: how much public permission
exists.** A pilot in Indonesia faces roughly a quarter of the public wanting the thing banned
outright; the same pilot in Australia or New Zealand faces more, and **rising**.

🔵 **Two consequences worth carrying into a deck.** First, **APAC is not one market on this axis**,
and the Anglophone APAC markets are the *more* restrictive ones — the reverse of the usual framing.
Second, **where ban-support is rising, the deliverable is the safeguard**, not the capability: the
consent story, the parental surface and the opt-out are the things that make a deployment survivable
(`P196`).

## T324 — 🔴 North America's state mandates are real, but two published specifics do not survive verification

🟢 **The shape holds and is firmer than `T318` states.** Roughly **`134` AI-in-education bills
across `31` states** in the 2026 session on one tracker — but **FutureEd's count is `~71` bills
across `27` states**, a near-twofold spread driven by **what counts as an AI-in-education bill**.
⚠️ **Cite the lower number or cite both**, because the higher one is the easier one to challenge in
a room. Separately and more usefully: **`35+` states had official state-education-agency AI guidance
as of June 2026**, which is a better measure of what a district actually faces than bill counts.

🔴 **Correction to `T318` on North Carolina.** `T318` says Session Law 2026-41 *"mandates AI-literacy
standards, a state model policy by 31 December 2026, district policies by 30 June 2027 and teacher
professional development by June 2028."* On verification: the **model policy (`31 December 2026`)**,

enters the K-12 computer-science standards beginning with the `2028-29` school year**, and the
"mandates AI-literacy standards" phrasing traces to the **2025 draft bills (SB 787, SB 864)**, whose
language may differ from what was enacted. 🔵 Practical effect: the near-term deliverable in North
Carolina is **a policy and a training record**, not curriculum — which is what `T318`'s own
closing paragraph argues, now with the literacy date separated out.

🔴 **And one figure is refused.** A claim that **Illinois requires AI-literacy instruction for grades
6–12 effective `1 August 2026`** appeared in one reading and **could not be confirmed by a targeted
second search**. It is **not published as a fact by this base.** Recorded here so a later pass
treats it as unverified rather than rediscovering it — a specific, quotable, dated mandate is
exactly the kind of claim that reaches a client deck unchecked (`736-J`'s lesson, applied to
regulation instead of to a licence).

## T325 — 🟢 LATAM's adoption–governance scissors, measured a second time at school level, and it is wider than in higher education

`T319` quantified the gap in **higher education** (UNESCO IESALC: `87 %` of institutions using AI,
`26 %` with any formal framework). `p737` finds the same scissors **in schools**, from a different
instrument and a different country, and the school-level gap is **worse**:

- **Brazil — `Cetic.br`: `53 %` of school administrators report using AI, while only `22 %` say
  their school has any guidelines on its use.** A `31`-point gap, and the governed share is
  **lower** than higher education's `26 %`.
- **Uruguay — `75 %` of public-school teachers report using AI tools** (Ceibal, 2026, via UNESCO).
  🟢 **This is the highest teacher-level adoption figure in this base for any country in any
  region**, and it comes from the country with the region's longest-running national device-and-
  connectivity programme — i.e. **the infrastructure precondition is what distinguishes it**.
- **Regional institutions are now standing up the governance layer**: UNESCO launched the
  **Observatory on AI in Education for Latin America and the Caribbean on `14 April 2026`**, with
  **CAF, CENIA, Cetic.br/NIC.br, ECLAC, the Ceibal Foundation, Fundación Santillana, Tecnológico de
  Monterrey, ProFuturo and IRCAI** as partners. **ECLAC/CENIA's ILIA 2026** covers **`20`
  countries** and names the region's largest gaps as **compute capacity, enterprise AI adoption and
  the implementation of national strategies** — implementation, not authorship.

🟢 **The engagement this implies is unchanged from `T319` but now has a second, cheaper entry point:
the school district, not only the university.** A `22 %`-governed school estate with `53 %` usage
needs a usable policy, a teacher training record and a data boundary — the same artefact as the
higher-education engagement, at lower cost and higher volume (`P197`).

⚠️ Figures are secondary readings of UNESCO, Cetic.br, Ceibal and ECLAC publications; the primary
documents are not reachable from this environment (`T328`).

## T327 — 🟢 The permissive-component-over-copyleft-core split is a recurring publisher pattern, not an H5P quirk

`T315` found that **H5P's core is GPL-3.0 while its content types are MIT**, and `T317` found that
**Instructure publishes Canvas's integration surface MIT over an AGPL-3.0 core**. `p737` adds a
third and a fourth instance from unrelated publishers, which makes it a pattern worth naming:

- **Pix (French public operator):** `1024pix/pix` is **AGPL-3.0**; `1024pix/pix-ui`, the accessible
  assessment component library, is **MIT**.
- **openHPI (German university institute):** `codeocean`, the assessment application, is
  **BSD-3-Clause**; `poseidon`, the execution orchestrator beneath it, is **MIT** — the *more*
  reusable component carries the *more* permissive grant.

🟢 **The generalisable rule, and it is a search instruction: when a platform's core is copyleft, go
look for the publisher's component repositories before concluding the estate is unusable.** The
layer a studio actually wants to reuse — design system, API client, renderer, scheduler, content
type — is frequently published separately and permissively, because the publisher wants it adopted.
🔵 Four publishers, four instances, `0` counter-examples found so far. ⚠️ Stated as a heuristic on
`4` cases, not a law; check the payload every time (`P188`, `P189`).

## T328 — 🔴 `WebFetch` to arbitrary hosts is dead in this environment, which bounds every regulatory claim this base can make

`T246` records that "the primary-law hosts remain unreachable from this environment", and several
passes have repeated it as a property of those hosts. **`p737` establishes that it is a property of
the environment and that it is total.**

`WebFetch` failed at **DNS resolution** — `getaddrinfo ENOTFOUND`, not a `403`, not a timeout — for
**`2 / 2`** hosts attempted: `www.i-scoop.eu` and `digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu`. The failure mode
is this session's **network allow-list**: hosts off the list do not resolve at all.

🔴 **Consequences, stated plainly because they are permanent until the environment changes:**

1. **No pass running here can verify a regulatory claim against primary text.** EUR-Lex, the
   Official Journal, state legislature sites and ministry portals are all off-list. Every date in
   `T318`, `T321`, `T324` and `T325` rests on **corroborated secondary sources**, and that
   limitation belongs in any client-facing use of them.
2. **The surviving channels are narrow and should be used deliberately:** `WebSearch` (summaries
   with citations, but not the cited text), `gh api -X GET search/repositories` (metadata) and
   `raw.githubusercontent.com` (bytes, for anything in a public repository).
3. 🟢 **The mitigation `p737` actually used, and it works: corroborate across independent
   secondary readings and publish the disagreement.** The EU date is now confirmed from three
   readings; the Article 50 date is published **as a conflict** rather than resolved; the Illinois
   mandate is **refused** for want of a second source (`T324`). 🔵 **A declared conflict is a usable
   finding. A single-sourced date presented as settled is not.**

# 🆕 Trends new at `p736` (researched 2026-11-10) — `T310`–`T320`

**Added above `p735`'s `T298`–`T309`.** Four are instrument findings, four are supply findings and
three are demand findings — and **one retracts a prior pass's published instrument verdict with
controls**, which this base has not had to do before.

## T310 — 🟢 `T298` RETRACTED: the supply channel was never dead, and a validation error about query contents was read as an outage

`p735` published that `gh api -X GET search/repositories` *"returns `422 Validation Failed` for
every query… because `GH_TOKEN` is invalid"*, and moved the base onto an unauthenticated
replacement. 🔬 **`p736` re-ran the channel and it carried all `41` legs of this pass:**
`topic:education-ai` → `200`/`69`; `topic:ai-education` → `581`; `topic:ai-tutor` → `891`;
`topic:learning-analytics` → `403`; `user:mitodl` → `186`; `org:apereo` → `30`;
`org:openedx stars:>100` → `4`. ⚠️ **Exactly one query shape still returns `422`, and it is the one
`p735` tested with: `repo:{owner}/{name}`.** 🔵 **The cause is not the credential: `repo:` is not a
valid qualifier for the repository-search endpoint** — it belongs to code and issue search — so the
endpoint is correctly rejecting a malformed query and would have done so on a healthy token.
🟢 **`gh auth status` *does* still report `GH_TOKEN` invalid, and the channel works anyway.** Two
rules follow, and they generalise past GitHub entirely: **a credential warning is not a
channel-health signal**, and **an error about the *contents* of a request is not evidence about the
*availability* of the service**. Probe a channel with a request the endpoint supports before
declaring it dead — and when a prior pass's instrument verdict is load-bearing, re-run its control
rather than inheriting it. Cost of not doing so: one pass of migration work and four passes'
exposure to a wrong rule. Controls: `evidence/channel-controls.2026-11-10-p736.tsv`.
🔵 **Secondary result, with the cause finally named from the error body:** `gh api
repos/{owner}/{repo}` returns `403` *"GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this
session. Use add_repo to request access."* — so `T289`'s dead `repos/` namespace is **session
repository-scoping**, an environment property, not a GitHub or network fact. `T302` stands: tree
enumeration is unavailable here, so no pass running in this environment may issue a compliant
`grant-absent` verdict.

## T311 — 🔴 A whole-payload licence match calls every GPL-3.0 repository AGPL-3.0, because GPL-3.0 §13 names the AGPL

The canonical GPL-3.0 text contains the string *"GNU Affero General Public License"* **three
times**, because **§13 is titled "Use with the GNU Affero General Public License"**. Any gate that
searches the whole payload for `GNU AFFERO` before `GNU GENERAL` therefore classifies **every
GPL-3.0 repository as AGPL-3.0**. 🔬 Measured `2 / 2` on the payloads that triggered it:
`h5p/h5p-php-library` (`LICENSE.txt`, `35,146 B`) and `ging/escapp` (`LICENSE`, `35,149 B`) — both
**GPL-3.0**, both initially reported AGPL. 🔴 **This is not a cosmetic misfile. AGPL-3.0's network
clause forbids offering a derivative as a service and GPL-3.0's does not**, so the defect
systematically converts usable platforms into rejected ones — the single most expensive direction
for this base's errors to run. 🟢 **The repair is to anchor on the first line that *names a
family*, skipping decoration, and it is published runnable as `P188`.** 🔵 Byte constants measured
today as *corroboration only*, never as the test: **GPL-3.0 `35,146`–`35,149 B`, AGPL-3.0
`34,520`–`34,523 B`, canonical Apache-2.0 `11,357`–`11,358 B`.** This is the seventh consecutive
pass to repair this gate; `T313` explains why the repairs keep being needed.

## T312 — 🔴 A missing `LICENSE` file is not evidence of a missing grant: three grants this pass live only in a manifest

| Repository | Stars | Licence file at `HEAD` | Where the grant actually is | Grant |
|---|--:|---|---|---|
| `h5p/h5p-interactive-video` | 267 | **none** (5 names probed) | `library.json`, `package.json` | **MIT** |
| `h5p/h5p-course-presentation` | 57 | **none** | `library.json` | **MIT** |
| `kstateome/canvas-api` | 78 | **none** (6 names probed) | `pom.xml` `<licenses>` | **LGPL-3.0** |

🔴 **In all three cases the GitHub index was right and a LICENSE-file-only probe was wrong** — the
opposite direction from the index errors in `T313`, which is exactly why neither channel can be
trusted alone. 🟢 **Standing rule: read the manifest — `package.json`, `library.json`, `pom.xml`,
`Cargo.toml`, `pyproject.toml`, `composer.json`, `*.gemspec` — before recording an absence.** Whole
ecosystems (npm, Maven, Cargo) conventionally declare the grant *only* there. 🔵 **This points the
same way as `T302` from a different direction:** this base cannot enumerate a repository tree here,
and it now also knows that the paths it *can* probe do not exhaust where grants live — so the
honest verdict is always **"no grant found at the probed paths"**, never *"grant-absent"*.

## T313 — 🔴 For MIT and Apache, byte size and canonical-text digests cannot decide a licence, and one valid Apache grant proves it alone

The `11` MIT payloads read this pass span **`1,060 B` to `2,285 B`** raw, and **not one** sits at
this base's published `1,020 B` stock constant: `1,060`, `1,063`, `1,070`, `1,070`, `1,071`,
`1,074`, `1,081`, `1,090`, `1,097`, `1,129`, `1,175`, `2,285`. The variance is the copyright-holder
line, the year, and — in two measured cases — **YAML frontmatter** (`instructure/instructure-ui`)
and **appended third-party notices** (`lenguaje-latino/latino`).

🔴 **The decisive case is Apache, and it is not a variance argument at all.**
`apereo/java-cas-client` carries a **`2,321 B`** `LICENSE` whose operative sentence is *"Apereo
licenses this file to you under the Apache License, Version 2.0"* — **a short-form notice that is
not the canonical Apache text in any part.** It matches no size band and no digest of the canonical
text, and **GitHub's own `licensee` cannot classify it either, which is precisely why the index
reports `NOASSERTION`.** The grant is nonetheless unambiguous and fully permissive. 🟢 **Conclusion,
and it should end seven passes of constant-chasing: a licence is a legal instrument identified by
its operative clause, not a file identified by its length.** Classify on the clause; record bytes
as corroboration. `P188`, `25 / 25`.

## T314 — 🟢 Higher education's identity layer has a permissive first-party implementation with 11.4k stars, and this base did not hold it

[`apereo/cas`](https://github.com/apereo/cas) — **`11,393★`, Apache-2.0, pushed `2026-11-10`** — is
the CAS/SAML2/OpenID-Connect single-sign-on server that higher education actually runs, from the
foundation that publishes Sakai and Opencast. 🔴 **It was absent from this base's `3,343`-address
ledger, together with `phpCAS` (`800★`), `java-cas-client` (`948★`) and `cas-initializr` (`22★`) —
and `org:apereo`, a single query, returned `30` repositories of which `28` were novel.** Meanwhile
`P169`, `P183` and `P186` had each already concluded that an engagement begins at the identity
integration.

🔵 **The diagnosis is the generalisable finding, and it is about method rather than about CAS.**
This base's discovery has been **phrase-led** — `tutoring agent`, `grading rubric LLM`,
`lesson plan generator` — and **a phrase leg finds applications and never infrastructure, because
infrastructure is not described in the vertical's vocabulary.** `apereo/cas`'s description does not
contain the word *education*; neither would Postgres's, or Keycloak's. 🟢 **Remedy, cheap and
immediately actionable: enumerate the known institutional publishers by `org:`/`user:` instead of
describing what you want.** This pass's `org:` legs produced **all `14`** foundations rows while the
`4` mandated prose legs produced **`0`** — the `40`th consecutive nil. 🔵 **Why it matters
commercially:** every LMS this base holds is copyleft (Moodle GPL-3.0, Open edX / Canvas / Frappe
AGPL-3.0, Sakai ECL-2.0) — **identity is the one layer of the institution's existing stack that is
already Apache-2.0**, so it is where a studio can build with no licence argument at all. And under
`T306`'s Annex III obligations, *who did what* is an identity question before it is a model
question: an agent that marks, advises or admits must act as an authenticated principal.

## T315 — 🟢 H5P's licence split makes the interactive-content layer permissively extensible, and that is a lighter route into an LMS than LTI

The H5P **core** (`h5p/h5p-php-library`, `154★`) is **GPL-3.0** (`T311`). The **content types** are
**MIT**: `h5p-interactive-video` (`267★`), `h5p-course-presentation` (`57★`),
`h5p-boilerplate` (`11★` — the official scaffold), `h5p-math-display`, `h5p-audio-recorder`,
`h5p-speak-the-words`, `h5p-three-image`, `h5p-multi-media-choice`, `h5p-drag-text`.
🟢 **Consequence: a studio can ship a new AI-driven interactive content type, under MIT, into an
institution's existing H5P installation — and H5P is already embedded in Moodle, Canvas, Open edX,
WordPress and Drupal.** No fork of the GPL core, and **no LTI registration either**, which makes it
strictly lighter than `P186`'s route. 🔵 **Why this is the cheapest reach-the-student path this
base holds:** the institution has already done the integration, the accessibility work and the
procurement; a content type is a drop-in. Published as **`P190`**. ⚠️ The limit is real: you inherit
H5P's authoring and runtime model, so this fits content-shaped interventions and not workflow-shaped
ones. ⚠️ And `h5p-interactive-video`'s grant is declared in `library.json` with **no licence file**
(`T312`), so confirm each content type's manifest rather than assuming the estate is uniform.

## T316 — 🔴 The recency head of a saturated topic is worthless, measured: 20/20 of the freshest `ai-tutor` repositories carry ≤7 stars

`topic:ai-tutor` (`891` repositories) and `topic:ai-education` (`581`) are the **cleanest** legs of
this pass — sorted by stars they return this base's own held rows, which is correct behaviour for a
saturated namespace. 🔴 **Sorted by `updated`, the top `20` `topic:ai-tutor` rows carry `≤ 7★`,
`17 / 20` carry `≤ 2★`, and all were pushed `2026-11-09` or `2026-11-10`.** The namespace absorbs a
continuous stream of one-person first commits — personal study apps, kanji tutors, single-course
helpers — of which essentially none survives to a second pass. 🟢 **Standing instruction, and it is
a cost finding rather than a quality one: do not spend a leg on the recency head of a saturated
topic. Rank on stars and `pushed_at` jointly.** All three fresh rows this pass filed
(`selfsemester`, `vistep`, `teacher-to-skills`) were found that way. 🔵 **The corollary matters for
reading this base's own history:** a pass that reports many new low-star agent rows has probably
sampled churn, not supply.

| Repository | Stars | Licence | Last push |
|---|--:|---|---|
| `instructure/canvas-lms` | 6,908 | **AGPL-3.0** | 2026-04-30 |
| `instructure/instructure-ui` | 486 | **MIT** (payload; index `NOASSERTION`) | **2026-11-10** |
| `instructure/ims-lti` | 203 | **MIT** | 2026-10-02 |
| `instructure/common-cartridge-viewer` | 95 | **MIT** | 2026-11-04 |
| `instructure/canvas-ios` | 925 | **no grant found** at 5 probed paths | 2026-05-19 |
| `instructure/canvas-android` | 155 | **no grant found** | 2026-08-27 |

🟢 **Read as a whole this is a deliberate and genuinely useful posture: the platform is copyleft and
the integration surface is permissive.** `instructure-ui` (accessible React components Canvas itself
is built from), `ims-lti` and `common-cartridge-viewer` are exactly the three capabilities an
outside developer needs — **look native, speak LTI, read course exports** — and all three are MIT
and current. 🔵 **The accessibility inheritance is the commercial edge:** with the **April 2026** ADA
web-accessibility deadline now past for large US public institutions (`T318`), "our tool is
accessible because it is built from the LMS vendor's own audited components" is a procurement answer
rather than a promise. 🔴 **Two warnings.** The mobile apps show **no grant at the probed paths** —
so do not plan to fork them; reach mobile through LTI and the web view. And **`canvas-lms` has not
been pushed in six months** because Canvas is developed on an internal mirror and GitHub receives
release drops — **any plan built on its apparent commit activity will be wrong.**

## T318 — 🟢 Regulation crossed from guidance into binding instruments in all four regions, and the binding clause is different in each

The 2026 position, with the instrument named per region so a proposal can cite it:

- **North America — statute, at state level, and the operative clause is policy adoption plus
  teacher training.** Roughly **`134` AI-in-education bills across `31` states** in the 2026
  session. **Ohio** was first to require **every** K-12 district to adopt a formal AI-use policy,
  deadline **`1 July 2026`**. **North Carolina** (Session Law 2026-41) mandates AI-literacy
  standards, a state model policy by **`31 December 2026`**, district policies by
  **`30 June 2027`** and **teacher professional development by June 2028**. **Maryland, Idaho,
  Oklahoma and Virginia** carry 2026 laws requiring both state guidance and mandatory
  district-level adoption. Federally, the **K-12 AI Literacy and Readiness Act of 2026** has
  advanced out of House committee; there are still **no binding federal AI curriculum standards**.
  🔵 Also binding and often missed: the **April 2026** ADA deadline for large public institutions
  to meet updated web-accessibility guidance **including vendor apps**.
- **EMEA — the EU AI Act, with education in Annex III and the date now `2 December 2027`.**
  Admissions, student evaluation and exam scoring are **high-risk**. The Digital Omnibus
  amendments were **adopted June 2026** and **entered into force `27 July 2026`**, moving
  stand-alone Annex III obligations from `2 August 2026` to **`2 December 2027`**, with AI embedded
  in regulated products at **`2 August 2028`**. National layers are already live: the **UK DfE's
  January 2026 generative-AI product safety standards for education** and **Ofqual's March 2026
  resources on AI and coursework integrity**. In the Gulf, **Dubai's KHDA** has issued explicit
  responsible-AI guidance to private schools. 🔵 This confirms `T306`'s `2 December 2027` date from
  a second independent reading.
- **APAC — three divergent regimes, and the buyer is the ministry or the regulator.**
  **South Korea's AI Basic Act entered into force `22 January 2026`**, with enforcement decrees
  still being finalised and a guidance-first grace period through 2026. **Vietnam** names
  **education — specifically automated assessment and behavioural analysis — as a high-risk
  sector**. **Australia's TEQSA** requires **all** higher-education providers to file institutional
  action plans addressing generative-AI risk. **China** regulates by targeted instrument; **Japan
  and Singapore** remain light-touch.
- **LATAM — volume without an education-specific instrument.** A 2026 Universidad de los Andes
  study counts **`716` AI-related regulatory instruments, rules and legislative proposals across
  `23` countries and territories**. **Brazil's PL 2.338/2023** is risk-based and still the main
  bill; **Colombia** chose a budgeted government-wide programme through 2030 rather than horizontal
  obligations. **Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Mexico and Peru** have adopted the
  OECD AI Principles. 🔴 **No education-specific AI law was found in any of them.**

🟢 **What this means for a proposal, and it is the same shape everywhere with a different noun:
the deliverable the statute names is an artefact, not a model.** North America wants a **policy and
a training record**; EMEA wants **traceability, human oversight and residency**; APAC wants an
**institutional action plan**; LATAM wants a **register and a data boundary**. `P185`, `P187`,
`P181` and `P191` each sell one of those. ⚠️ **Secondary sources only** — `725-F` holds, the
primary-law hosts remain unreachable from this environment (`T246`), and every date above should be
settled by a reader with access before it is quoted to a client.

`1,104` repositories. 🔵 **The generalisable point: prefer the channel with no credential for
public metadata.** An authenticated channel buys rate limit and costs availability; this base lost
four passes' worth of instrument continuity to that trade and did not notice until the token died.

## T301 — `NOASSERTION` means "read the bytes", and a Markdown `#` was defeating the gate

[`FitzyCodesThings/core-lms`](https://github.com/FitzyCodesThings/core-lms) is indexed
`NOASSERTION` by GitHub and gated `1049 B`/`a8494dc0f02d` under `P180` — `29 B` over the MIT
constant, which reads as a non-stock grant. **Both channels were wrong for one cause.** The payload
titles itself **`# Released Under MIT License`**; `P180`'s title-line strip matches only a bare
`MIT License`-shaped line, so the heading survived canonicalisation.
`printf '%s' '# Released Under MIT License' | wc -c` = **`28`**, plus the separator space that
`tr '\n' ' '` introduces = **the `29 B` residue exactly**. Widening the strip to allow an optional
Markdown heading marker and a `Released Under` preamble makes the payload **byte-identical to stock
MIT**. 🟢 **Published as `P184`; regression-tested on `18` payloads with `14 / 14` MIT and `3 / 3`
Apache at constants and `0` regressions on `p734`'s controls.** 🔵 **The rule worth more than the
repair: an index value of `NOASSERTION` is an instruction to read the payload, not grounds to
discard a repository** — this base's own `p727` entry already recorded three index fields wrong
against four correct payload-derived cells, and this is the fourth instance.

## T306 — 🟢 `719-D` CLOSED: the EU AI Act Annex III date for education is `2 December 2027`

`p719` found sources split between `2 August 2026` and `2 December 2027`, adopted neither, and

`24 July 2026`**, **in force `27 July 2026`**, moving stand-alone **Annex III** high-risk

`2 August 2030`. 🔴 **Three things were NOT delayed:** **Article 50 transparency duties have applied

client-facing compliance commitment should be confirmed against it. 🔵 **What it means
commercially: `2027` is a planning window, not a reprieve.** An EU institution procuring an
admissions or assessment system today is procuring an Annex III high-risk system; the compliant
architecture is explainability, traceability and human oversight, and it is demonstrable now.

### 🟢 T286 — The licence gate was never irreproducible or unnamed; it was missing a trailing space

`p733` named the digest (`sha256`, first `12` hex) and published `1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f`, and
`P176` states the rule as a runnable shell function. **Run exactly as published, it lands one byte
over on every payload tested** — `1021 B` / `783d6159681f`, itself a perfectly stable constant
across `6` MIT payloads. The cause is the last step: `tr '\n' ' '` converts the payload's **final**
newline into a **trailing space**, which the published rule never removes. Adding `sed 's/ *$//'`
reproduces `1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f` **exactly**.
🔬 **Controlled against `p733`'s own evidence, which is why this is a repair and not a disagreement:**
the control payload is [`popcodeorg/popcode`](https://github.com/popcodeorg/popcode) — the row
`p733` cited for its `T279` repair. As-written `1021 B` / `783d6159681f`; trailing-space-stripped
`1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f`. 🔵 **Why it matters beyond one byte:** a gate whose published form
disagrees with its published constant refuses *every* correct grant, so a later pass either
abandons the constant (as `p729` did) or silently re-derives it (as `p731` did). Both have now
happened. Published complete as **`P180`**.

### 🟢 T287 — The Apache constant `p733` declared unreproducible is reproducible, and it is not the published number

`T280` recorded that the rule reproducing the MIT constant does not reproduce the Apache one, and
published `9130 B` / `6e1ffb7fc4e2` as unverified. With `T286`'s trailing-space step the Apache
family **does** resolve to a single constant: **`9942 B` / `3fda30957805`**.
🔬 **Reproduced on `5` independent payloads, across `5` publishers, `3` filenames and a `56`-byte
spread of raw sizes** — [`didi/xiaoju-survey`](https://github.com/didi/xiaoju-survey) (`LICENSE`,
`11,412 B`), [`zhangjiarui530/OpenEduECNU`](https://github.com/zhangjiarui530/OpenEduECNU)
(`LICENSE`, `11,357 B`), [`openedx/edx-cookiecutters`](https://github.com/openedx/edx-cookiecutters)
(`LICENSE.txt`, `11,358 B`), [`openedx/edx-bootstrap`](https://github.com/openedx/edx-bootstrap)
(`LICENSE`, `11,356 B`) and [`google/moodle-on-gcp`](https://github.com/google/moodle-on-gcp)
(`LICENSE.md`, `11,357 B`) — corporate APAC, academic APAC, two foundation repos and a hyperscaler.
🔴 **`9130 B` / `6e1ffb7fc4e2` is retired.** No normalisation tested here produces it, including on
`xiaoju-survey`, the payload `p733` computed it from. ⚠️ **And `p733`'s raw byte counts are
systematically `+1`:** it reported `11,413 B` where this pass measures `11,412`, `1,514` where this
pass measures `1,513`, and `1,088` where this pass measures `1,087` — **`3 / 3`, exactly one over.**
Two opposite off-by-ones in one pass, which is the signature of a measurement harness that adds a
byte on read and a gate that strips one on write.

### 🔴 T288 — The gate cannot certify BSD at all, and the cause is formatting rather than the holder name

A hash gate works on MIT and Apache because their stock terms are **holder-invariant**: strip the
title and the copyright line and every publisher's bytes agree. **BSD does not behave this way.**
Three BSD payloads read this pass produced **three different values**:
[`freeCodeCamp/classroom`](https://github.com/freeCodeCamp/classroom) `1451 B`/`99f846c132c0`,
[`SURFnet/pea-poc`](https://github.com/SURFnet/pea-poc) `1480 B`/`96fabc6ac22e`, and
[`opencast/helper-scripts`](https://github.com/opencast/helper-scripts) `1278 B`/`ab132540e375`.
🔬 **Diffed at word level rather than guessed at.** `helper-scripts` is the **2-clause** text
(`0` numbered clauses) — a different licence, correctly a different constant. The two **3-clause**
payloads differ by `29 B` for three reasons, none of them the holder: `classroom` renders its
clauses as `-` bullets where `pea-poc` numbers them `1.` `2.` `3.`; `classroom` omits
*"All rights reserved."*; and `classroom` omits the word *"contributors"* from clause 3. Both carry
the stock holder-invariant *"Neither the name of the copyright holder"* wording.
🔵 **Consequence, and it is a scope correction to a gate this base made mandatory:** BSD terms are
reformatted freely by publishers while remaining semantically stock, so **any** byte-exact BSD gate
refuses correct grants. `P180` restricts certification to MIT and Apache and requires BSD rows to
be filed with measured bytes and **no stock claim**. ⚠️ `p733` published `1441 B`/`8cb6ec54329a` for
`classroom`; this pass measures `1451`/`1452 B` and cannot reproduce it under either rule.

### 🔴 T289 — The whole `repos/` API namespace is dead in this environment, not just `repos/.../license`

`p731`'s `731-J` recorded `repos/{owner}/{repo}/license` returning `403` outside this session's
GitHub scope. **It is the entire namespace.** `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}` returns `403` with
*"GitHub access to this repository is not enabled for this session"* for every out-of-scope
repository — including ones this pass then verified as alive and filed —

### 🟢 T277 — The licence gate was reproducible all along; what was missing was the name of its digest

`p732` published `1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f` and described its rule but **named no hash algorithm
anywhere in this KB**. Reconstructed and confirmed this pass: **`sha256`, first `12` hex, over the
terms-only form with newlines collapsed to single spaces.** 🔵 **The collapse step is load-bearing
and was never stated** — the newline-joined form is *also* `1020 B` but hashes to `ee796286d939`,
so a later pass verifying only the length would believe it had reproduced the gate when it had not.
**Transferable lesson: a published constant without its algorithm is a number, not a check.** Any
instrument this base publishes from here should state rule *and* digest, as `P176` now does.

### 🔴 T278 — The gate silently refused stock MIT payloads with Windows line endings, and that bias points at the publisher class this base keeps declaring regions empty of

[`sizwinz/SkillWise`](https://github.com/sizwinz/SkillWise) is stock MIT and gated to `1034 B` —
a refusal — because its payload carries **`20` CR bytes** that the canonicalisation retained.
`tr -d '\r'` moves it to `1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f` exactly. 🔵 **The direction of the bias is the
finding, not the byte count.** `729-B` already established that a prior instrument selected against
*institutional* publishers and that the bias produced a **published regional nil**; CRLF correlates
with Windows authoring, and Windows authoring correlates with schools, districts, ministries and
non-specialist academic publishers. **The same failure mode has now arrived twice through two
unrelated mechanisms**, which makes it a property of this pipeline rather than an accident.

### 🔴 T279 — Two unrelated publishers hit the same wrong constant, which is how you tell a rule defect from a tampered payload

[`popcodeorg/popcode`](https://github.com/popcodeorg/popcode) and
[`makebrainwaves/BrainWaves`](https://github.com/makebrainwaves/BrainWaves) both gated to
**`1042 B` / `dcdd5bec314a`** — identical to each other. Cause: both open `The MIT License (MIT)`,
which a `^(MIT )?Licen[cs]e$` title rule does not match, so the title survives canonicalisation;
`The MIT License (MIT) ` is exactly **`22` bytes** and `1042 − 1020 = 22`. 🔵 **The transferable
method lesson is diagnostic, not cosmetic:** a *tampered* payload is tampered uniquely and will not
collide with another publisher's, so **a shared wrong constant is near-conclusive evidence that the
rule is wrong rather than the grant.** A gate that reports only pass/fail cannot produce this
evidence — which is the argument for publishing the computed value on every row, as this base does.

and certifies no row against a number it could not compute.

## T272 — This base's MIT licence gate has been certifying a text with two of MIT's terms deleted 🔴 new at p732

The gate published at `p728` and made mandatory since drops **every line containing the string
`copyright`**. In a stock MIT payload that is not one line, it is **three**:

| Line | Content | Is it a term? |
|---|---|---|
| 3 | `Copyright (c) 2026 Jason Tangen` | No — attribution metadata. Correct to drop. |
| 12 | `The above copyright notice and this permission notice shall be included in all` | 🔴 **Yes — the attribution obligation, MIT's only condition.** |
| 18 | `AUTHORS OR COPYRIGHT HOLDERS BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM, DAMAGES OR OTHER` | 🔴 **Yes — part of the liability disclaimer.** |

So the `870 B` / `3d87852cf34a` constant this base certifies MIT rows against is computed over a
text **missing MIT's single condition and part of its disclaimer**. It is holder-invariant
*because* it deletes the holder line — and it buys that invariance by also deleting two things
that bind.

**What this does and does not mean, measured rather than asserted.** `p732` built seven controls.
Channel L **correctly flags** tampering that disturbs neighbouring retained lines: deleting the
attribution clause outright moves it to `822 B`, gutting the disclaimer to `938 B`. But a tamper
that **stays inside a dropped line** is invisible:

| Control | Change | Channel L | Channel H |
|---|---|---|---|
| `stock` | none | `870`/`3d87852cf34a` ✅ pass | `1020`/`fe2a9817987f` ✅ pass |
| `attr_negated` | `shall be included` → **`need NOT be included`** | `870`/`3d87852cf34a` 🔴 **passes** | `1023`/`8487e8205c74` ✅ flags |
| `liable2` | `BE LIABLE FOR ANY CLAIM` → **`ARE FULLY LIABLE FOR EVERY CLAIM`** | `870`/`3d87852cf34a` 🔴 **passes** | `1027`/`01eb22566b08` ✅ flags |
| `noncommercial` | holder line + **`NONCOMMERCIAL USE ONLY.`** | `870` 🔴 passes | `1020` 🔴 **passes** |

The first two are the defect: **a payload that revokes MIT's only condition, or inverts its
disclaimer, is certified by this base's current gate at the exact stock constant.** Both are
realistic shapes for a licence altered to look permissive.

🟢 **Repair, implemented and published as `P172`.** Drop only the holder-attribution line, matched
on its *shape* (`^copyright\s*(\(c\)|©)?\s*\d{4}…`) rather than on the word appearing anywhere.
New constant **`1020 B` / `fe2a9817987f`**, measured identical across **`18 / 18`** MIT payloads
read this pass, with holder lines spanning `24`–`53` bytes and one containing CJK. Invariance
preserved; nothing that binds is deleted.

⚠️ **The limit is real and is published with the repair.** The `noncommercial` control passes
*both* channels, because both discard the holder line and the restriction was appended to it. One
hash cannot be both holder-invariant and holder-line-sensitive. `P172` therefore pairs the hash
with a **separate shape assertion** on the holder line, which flags that control. `7 / 7` controls
then behave as specified and `18 / 18` real payloads pass.

🔵 **Consequence for this base, stated plainly.** Every MIT row certified before `p732` was
certified by an instrument that could not see two classes of tamper. Nothing found this pass
suggests any existing row *is* tampered — all `15` re-read payloads are stock under the stricter
rule — but the earlier certifications are weaker than they were recorded as being. Re-reading the
standing MIT rows under `P172` is cheap and is the recommended first leg of `p733`.

## T273 — Retention tooling is now shipped as a plugin for the learner's existing tool, not as an app to migrate to 🟢 new at p732

`p731` opened `T265` on spaced repetition becoming a component. `p732` sharpens it: the
*distribution channel* is the change, and it is now measured across two consecutive passes.

- [`ctrlaltwill/learnkit`](https://github.com/ctrlaltwill/learnkit) (`183★`, MIT) — FSRS, cloze and
  image-occlusion cards, TTS and retention analytics **inside Obsidian**.
- `pieralukasz/true-recall` (`66★`, MIT, filed `p731`) — FSRS v6 and image occlusion, also **inside
  Obsidian**, by a different author.
- [`kubk/memo-card`](https://github.com/kubk/memo-card) (`147★`, MIT) — delivered as a **Telegram
  mini-app** with a stated ~1k MAU.
- [`chrichuang218/ai-learning-coach`](https://github.com/chrichuang218/ai-learning-coach) (`228★`,
  MIT) — installed with `claude plugin install` / `codex plugin marketplace add`; the pedagogy is a
  **plugin for the learner's coding agent**.
- [`eudoxia0/hashcards`](https://github.com/eudoxia0/hashcards) (`1,188★`, Apache-2.0) — the corpus
  is **plain text in a repository**; the host is the learner's editor and version control.

**Two independent Obsidian-native FSRS plugins in two passes is the hard signal.** The consistent
shape is that the scheduler goes to where the learner's material already lives — notes, a chat
client, a git repository, a coding agent — and the material never moves.

🔵 **Engagement consequence.** The standard proposal for a retention programme assumes a platform
the client adopts and populates, which is where these programmes die: the content migration is the
cost and the behaviour change is the risk. The cheaper shape, now with five permissive precedents,
is **to schedule against the document estate the client already has**. For a client that cannot be
moved off its existing tooling, this is not a compromise — it is the only version that ships.

## T274 — The Apache-2.0 APPENDIX is not part of the terms, and hashing it produces both false passes and false refusals 🔴 new at p732

Apache-2.0 payloads in this base are canonicalised **whole-file**, APPENDIX included. The APPENDIX
is headed *"How to apply the Apache License to your work"* and is boilerplate *instructions*; the
licence text itself places it outside the terms. Hashing it has now produced errors in both
directions, found in the same pass.

**False refusal.** [`evalle/dca`](https://github.com/evalle/dca) (`1,413★`) canonicalises whole-file
to **exactly `9,478 B`** — the stock length — with hash **`8a8071588bc2`** instead of
`399d47608b81`. A diff against a known-stock payload returns a single opcode: `"[]"` → `"{}"`,
**two characters, inside the APPENDIX instruction text**. The grant is stock Apache-2.0. The
whole-file hash refuses it.

**False pass.** That same row is a genuine **length collision**: a check on canonical *length*
alone — which this base has used in prose as shorthand for the constant — passes a payload whose
canonical bytes differ. Length and hash disagree here for the first time on record.

🟢 **Repair, implemented and published as `P173`: canonicalise the terms only**, truncating at
`^APPENDIX:`. Measured across four Apache payloads:

| Repo | Whole-file | **Terms-only (`P173`)** |
|---|---|---|
| `eudoxia0/hashcards` | `9478`/`399d47608b81` | **`8484`/`c7396247b0c2`** |
| `viktoruj/cks` | `9478`/`399d47608b81` | **`8484`/`c7396247b0c2`** |
| `evalle/dca` | `9478`/**`8a8071588bc2`** ← refused | **`8484`/`c7396247b0c2`** |
| `uw-it-aca/myuw` | `8484`/`c7396247b0c2` ← "anomaly" | **`8484`/`c7396247b0c2`** |

🟢 **The fourth row is the result that matters, and it recovers a finding this base mis-read.**
`p731` recorded `uw-it-aca/myuw` as an **Apache-2.0 anomaly** — *"Apache-2.0 without the APPENDIX,
`10,173 B` raw → `8,484 B` canonical against the `9,478 B` constant, the `1,049 B` deficit is the
boilerplate-instruction appendix"* — and gave it a named exception (`T269`). Under `P173` **MyUW is
not anomalous at all: it is byte-identical to stock on the terms.** `p731` computed the right
number (`8,484 B`) and interpreted it as a deficit requiring an exception, when it is the
**correct canonical form**.

🔵 **Net effect: one constant replaces a constant plus a growing exception list.** `P173` yields a
single Apache-2.0 value, **`8484 B` / `c7396247b0c2`**, that accepts stock payloads, `{}`-variant
appendices, and appendix-free payloads alike — because none of those differ in anything that binds.
Two recorded "anomalies" of this base dissolve into it.

## T275 — The academic-integrity threat is now courseware-specific automation, not generic chatbot use 🔴 new at p732

Institutional AI policy — and most vendor integrity tooling — is written against a model of the
student pasting an essay prompt into a general chatbot. The supply side has moved past that.

[`googlyblox/auto-mcgraw`](https://github.com/googlyblox/auto-mcgraw) (`89★`, MIT, pushed
`2026-09-30`) is a maintained, permissively licensed tool that **automates McGraw Hill Smartbook
homework** with LLM integration. It does not target "assessment" in the abstract; it targets a
**named commercial courseware platform** that thousands of institutions license by name.

This is a different problem from the one policy addresses:

- **Detection is irrelevant.** The work is submitted through the platform's own flow, as the
  student, on time. There is no text whose provenance a classifier could judge.
- **It scales per-platform, not per-student.** One tool, written once, serves everyone enrolled in
  any course using that courseware.
- **Permissive licensing makes removal meaningless.** `MIT` means every fork is lawful and the
  artefact cannot be withdrawn.

🔵 **Engagement consequence, and it is a commercial opening rather than only a risk.** When this
studio is asked to advise on assessment design, the honest answer is that **completion-based and
auto-graded coursework in a major platform is no longer evidence of learning**, and the client
should be told so in those words. What survives is assessment of *state and process* rather than of
submitted answers — exactly the shape of `p731`'s `dsoxlab` (grade the container),
`viktoruj/cks` (grade the cluster), `sebastianhaba/book-to-course-skill` (exercises checked by
**unit tests**), and `ArnaudGuiovanna/tutor-mcp` (mastery against a **frozen rubric**, with probes
*refused* below threshold). `P174` and `P175` are written to that constraint. The base holds the
components; the client's current assessment estate is the thing that has stopped working.

## T276 — The AI-in-education market's 2026 base is agreed; the disagreement is entirely in the growth rate, and one published figure fails its own arithmetic 🟢 new at p732

This base has carried the market question as "roughly `$10B`, high-30s-to-low-40s CAGR, and no
agreement beyond that". `p732` tightened it by **checking each vendor's figures against each
other** — which costs nothing and is possible even where primary sources are unreachable
(`725-F`, re-confirmed this pass at `6 / 6` hosts).

| Source | 2026 base | Endpoint | Claimed CAGR | Implied by its own endpoints | Consistent? |
|---|---|---|---|--:|---|
| Research and Markets | `$10.6B` | `$42.48B` (2030) | 41.5% | 41.5% | ✅ |
| Precedence Research | `$9.58B` | `$136.79B` (2035) | 34.52% | 34.4% | ✅ |
| Grand View Research | `$11.4B` | `$57.2B` (2033) | 25.9% | 25.9% | ✅ |
| The Business Research Co (higher-ed only) | `$4.09B` | `$13.46B` (2030) | 34.7% | 34.7% | ✅ |
| **Coherent Market Insights** | `$11.40B` | `$57.25B` (2033) | **16.8%** | **25.9%** | 🔴 **No** |

**Two readings, both useful:**

1. 🟢 **The base year is not in dispute.** Four independent houses put 2026 between **`$9.58B` and
   `$11.4B`** — a `±9%` spread around `~$10.5B`. This base can now quote a 2026 figure with a
   stated range instead of hedging.
2. 🔴 **One widely cited CAGR is arithmetically impossible.** Coherent Market Insights publishes
   `16.8%` from `$11.40B` (2026) to `$57.25B` (2033); `16.8%` compounded over seven years gives
   **`$33.8B`**, not `$57.25B`, while its own endpoints imply `25.9%`. The figure set is internally
   contradictory, so **at least one of its three published numbers is wrong** and none of them
   should be cited.

🔵 **Consequence: the honest CAGR range narrows from `16.8%–45%` to `~26%–45%`** once the
self-inconsistent entry is dropped, and the remaining spread is explained by scope (whether
embedded AI features and corporate training are counted) rather than by disagreement about
trajectory. 🟢 **And the transferable method is the point:** vendor market figures can be
**falsified without access to the vendor**, by compounding their own base against their own
endpoint. `1 of 5` failed here. Run this check before quoting any market number in a deck —
it is three lines of arithmetic and it caught a number this base might otherwise have carried.
