## T265 — Spaced repetition stopped being a product category and became a component, and FSRS is the component 🟢 new at p731

`p731`'s supply sweep returned **six novel permissive retention implementations in one pass**, and
not one of them is a flashcard app you migrate to:

| Repo | Stars | Grant (byte-read) | What it actually is |
|---|--:|---|---|
| [`pieralukasz/true-recall`](https://github.com/pieralukasz/true-recall) | 66 | MIT `870 B` | An **Obsidian plugin**. FSRS v6, AI-generated cards, image occlusion. |
| [`dralkh/spaceforge`](https://github.com/dralkh/spaceforge) | 15 | MIT (unwrapped) | FSRS **and** SM-2 side by side, plus MCQ generation. |
| [`dorianspitz23/booksum`](https://github.com/dorianspitz23/booksum) | 12 | MIT `870 B` | A **book summariser** whose last stage happens to be a review schedule. |
| [`cert-pepper/cert-pepper`](https://github.com/cert-pepper/cert-pepper) | 6 | MIT `870 B` | A **CLI** for certification exams. |
| [`Chain-Tang/AnnotationTutor`](https://github.com/Chain-Tang/AnnotationTutor) | 5 | MIT `870 B` | A **reading-annotation** tool that emits review items. |
| [`harrystaley/Pre-Calculus_Anki`](https://github.com/harrystaley/Pre-Calculus_Anki) | 6 | MIT | **Content only** — decks, no scheduler, because the scheduler is assumed. |

**The scheduler is no longer the differentiator; the capture surface is.** Five of the six attach
to something the learner was already doing — their notes, their book, their terminal, their
annotations — and inherit FSRS from a library. `p667` recorded that "retention is a layer, not an
algorithm"; this pass gives that a second, sharper reading: **the layer has been commoditised and
the contested ground moved to where the items come from.**

🔵 **What this means for an engagement.** Do not build a scheduler and do not propose migrating a
client's learners into a new review app — both are now undifferentiated and both lose. Build the
*capture*: the integration that turns the client's existing material and the learner's existing
behaviour into review items, and let FSRS do the scheduling. `AnnotationTutor` is the clearest
reference and `true-recall` the clearest proof that the plugin route is viable.

⚠️ **Honest limit:** all six are `≤66★` and five are single-author. This trend is a statement about
*where new supply is arriving*, not a recommendation to take a production dependency on any one of them.

## T266 — A licence gate needs two normalisations, because they fail on disjoint inputs — and disagreement between them diagnoses formatting, never a modified grant 🔴 new at p731

This base published a mandatory licence normalisation at `p728` and corrected its specification at
`p729`. `p731` ran it against **`33` payloads read first-hand**, alongside a repaired variant, and
the two rules **disagree on `3 of 33` (`9.1 %`)** — every disagreement a formatting artefact, every
underlying grant correct and permissive.

**The published rule (drop every *line* containing `copyright`) fails on unwrapped payloads.**
`2 of 33` payloads (`6.1 %`) are unwrapped — one paragraph per physical line:

| Payload | Lines | Longest line | Line rule | Truth |
|---|--:|--:|--:|---|
| [`mitodl/mitx-grading-library`](https://github.com/mitodl/mitx-grading-library) | 5 | `755` cols | **`142 B`** | Complete `BSD-3-Clause`. Clauses 1, 2, 3 and the disclaimer each contain the word *copyright*, so the rule deleted **the grant** and left `142 B` of residue. |
| [`dralkh/spaceforge`](https://github.com/dralkh/spaceforge) | 5 | `460` cols | **`436 B`** | Stock `MIT`, plus four curly quotation marks. |

**The repaired rule — unwrap to paragraphs, then drop copyright *sentences* — fails on exactly one
other shape.** `1 of 33`: [`The-Purple-Movement/Beyond-Syllabus`](https://github.com/The-Purple-Movement/Beyond-Syllabus)
writes `Copyright (c) 2021 The Purple Movement` **with no terminal period, on the line immediately
above the grant with no blank line between**. Sentence-splitting therefore treats the notice and the
whole permission paragraph as one sentence and deletes both: `587 B` against a `1,020 B` constant.
The *line* rule handles it perfectly (`870 B`, stock).

🟢 **And the repaired rule recovers a constant this base gave up on.** `p729` recorded that
`P163` had mandated a stock-`MIT` body of **`1,020 B` / sha256₁₂ `fe2a9817987f`** and that
*"seven procedures reproduce none of it"*, so `p729` replaced it with the line rule. **`p731`
reproduces it exactly, on `17` payloads across `14` independent publishers.** The procedure is:
*unwrap to paragraphs → drop the title paragraph → drop copyright **sentences** → collapse
whitespace → measure*. `P163`'s constant was never wrong; only its procedure was missing. `729-A`
closes by recovery rather than by replacement.

**Neither rule is safe alone. Run both. The constants, measured on `40` payloads this pass:**

| Family | Line-rule canonical | Pubs | Span-rule canonical | Pubs |
|---|---|--:|---|--:|
| `MIT` | `870 B` / `3d87852cf34a` | `15` | **`1,020 B`** / **`fe2a9817987f`** | `14` |
| `Apache-2.0` | `9,478 B` / `399d47608b81` | `8` | `10,178 B` / `0649bc87ac07` | `7` |
| `Apache-2.0` *(second accepted body, `T269`)* | `9,478 B` / `8a8071588bc2` | `3` | `10,178 B` / `037c3ea46e3f` | `3` |
| `BSD-3-Clause` | `1,091 B` / `90bd78b45663` | **`1`** — not a constant | `1,441 B` / `6a1dee59e06b` | **`1`** |
| *control:* `404` body | `14 B` / `d5558cd419c8` | — | `14 B` / `d5558cd419c8` | — |

The `17`-payload counts on the two `MIT` rows are **different sets**, which is the whole point:
`Beyond-Syllabus` passes the line rule and fails the span rule, `spaceforge` does the reverse.
The `BSD` rows remain single-publisher (all `mitodl`) and must not be used as gates.

🔵 **The operative rule, stated so a later pass can run it mechanically:** compute both bodies.
**Agreement with a constant on either channel is a pass.** Disagreement between the two channels is
an instruction to **read the payload by hand**, not a refusal — on `3 of 3` specimens this pass the
disagreement was wrap state or punctuation and the grant was sound. A single-channel gate would have
refused three correct permissive grants, one of them the most reusable row of the pass.

This base has recorded the North American school-district and university publisher tier as absent or
empty across several passes. `p731` enumerated four publishers in one pass:

|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| [`mitodl`](https://github.com/mitodl) — MIT Open Learning | 186 | 112 | `60.2 %` | 183 | 36 |

| [`Unicon`](https://github.com/Unicon) | 31 | 23 | `74.2 %` | 29 | 5 |
| [`ucfopen`](https://github.com/ucfopen) — U. Central Florida | 65 | 14 | `21.5 %` | 60 | 3 |

**`268` novel permissive repositories from four `user:` queries**, against a channel this base

## T268 — Inside one publisher the grant tracks the architectural layer; across publishers it tracks the publisher — so neither is a screening heuristic 🔴 new at p731

Two measurements from the same pass, pointing opposite ways.

**Within `ucfopen` the split is total and it follows the layer:**

| Layer | Repos | Grant |
|---|--:|---|
| `*-materia-widget` — content/authoring | **30** | `AGPL-3.0`, **`30 / 30`**, no exceptions |
| LTI tools and templates — integration | 7 | `MIT` **`6 / 7`** |

The estate's most-adopted artefact, [`ucfopen/canvasapi`](https://github.com/ucfopen/canvasapi)
(`681★`), sits on the permissive side. The platform it protects — `Materia` (`52★`), `Obojobo`
(`72★`) — sits on the copyleft side. **A studio can build Canvas integrations on this estate and
cannot embed its learning objects.** This replicates `p634`'s Open edX reading on an independent
publisher: permissive at the edges, copyleft at the core.

🔴 **And then the same pass falsifies the generalisation `p634` drew from it.** `p634` measured
`15 / 15` Open edX XBlocks `AGPL-3.0` and concluded the extension point carries the licence.
[`mitodl/open-edx-plugins`](https://github.com/mitodl/open-edx-plugins) is a maintained set of Open
edX plugins under **`BSD-3-Clause`**, pushed `2026-11-09`. Same platform, same extension point,
opposite grant.

🔵 **The rule that survives both:** *the grant is a property of the publisher's policy, and within a
publisher, of the layer.* There is no inference from the extension point, the file type or the
platform. **Read the payload, every time, per repository.** Both halves of this trend exist because
a screening heuristic would have produced a wrong answer in one direction or the other.

## T269 — `Apache-2.0` has two accepted canonical bodies at identical length, and a complete Apache grant can be `1,049 B` short of the constant 🔴 new at p731

Three facts, all byte-read at `p731`, each of which defeats one of this base's licence instruments.

**1. Two hashes, one length.** `10` Apache-2.0 payloads normalise to exactly `9,478 B`. They carry
**two distinct `sha256₁₂` values**, and the divergence is a single character at position `8,662`, in
the APPENDIX boilerplate instruction:

| Body | sha256₁₂ | Appendix text | Publishers observed |
|---|---|---|--:|
| A | `399d47608b81` | `fields enclosed by brackets "[]"` | `mitodl`, `Unicon`, `stephrobert`, `MiniriceAI`, `uw-it-aca`, `tuc-urz`, `Open-Education-AI` |
| B | **`8a8071588bc2`** | `fields enclosed by brackets "{}"` | `uw-it-aca`, `ucfopen`, `elixirschool` |

Both are published Apache Foundation revisions. The difference is in the *instructions for applying*
the licence, not in the terms. 🔴 **A hash gate admitting only `399d47608b81` refuses body B — and
body B is what the University of Washington estate ships, `123` Apache-2.0 repositories.** Both
hashes are hereby recorded as **accepted constants**.

🔴 **2. `T151` is falsified.** `p731` registered that the licence-payload hash *"identifies the
OWNER, not the repository"*. `uw-it-aca` publishes **both** bodies — `django-blti` and
`uw-restclients-canvas` give `8a8071588bc2`, `pathways` gives `399d47608b81` — and body B appears
across **three unrelated owners**. The hash identifies the **text revision the publisher copied**,
which correlates with owner and is not determined by it.

🟢 **3. A short Apache payload can be complete.** [`uw-it-aca/myuw`](https://github.com/uw-it-aca/myuw)
normalises to `8,484 B`, `994 B` under the constant, and is **not truncated**: it ends at
`END OF TERMS AND CONDITIONS` and omits the APPENDIX entirely (`1,049 B` on the span channel). The
appendix is guidance, not terms; the grant is whole. Second instance of this shape after `p619`'s
`597 B` case, and the first where the missing span is named rather than merely observed.

🔵 **Consequence for the gate:** for `Apache-2.0`, *length alone* cannot detect a one-character
appendix variant, and *hash alone* refuses two legitimate publishers. The gate must accept
`{399d47608b81, 8a8071588bc2}` at `9,478 B`, and treat `~8,484 B` as "appendix absent — inspect the
tail" rather than as tampering.

`p730` re-scoped the long-running leg nil as *"market figures saturated, regulatory instruments and
capital series were not"*. `p731` ran the mandated global and four regional legs and probed

`Florida`, `Ohio State`, `Utrecht`, `Estado de México`, `Ley Nahui`, `Article 61`, `2026-12-02`,
`Digital Omnibus`, `Class 3`, `Beijing class-hours`, `Kenya`, `Nigeria`, `Rwanda`, `Singapore`,
`Indonesia`, `Philippines` — every one of them present. The two that were not held are
sub-details of an instrument this base already holds: China's April 2026 *AI + Education* plan
requiring universities to run AI as **a basic public course**, issued by **five central departments**.

🔴 **So the regulatory-instrument channel is now saturated as well, and the honest reading is that
the leg's *phrasing* has been exhausted in all three of its halves** — supply, market figures and
instruments.

🟢 **What did pay were the two regions this base had written off.** Both were declared gaps, both
were addressed with one targeted leg each, and both returned named instruments:

- **Africa** — absent from the EMEA sweep for four consecutive passes. One leg returned four
  jurisdictions with named instruments (`T271`, and the EMEA block of `intel/market.md`).
- **Canada** — *"returned almost nothing"*, the North America limb recorded as US-only. One leg
  returned **four provinces with formal AI guidance for educators** (British Columbia, New
  Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, Quebec), **Manitoba in progress**, Ontario's `2026–27`
  guidance, and a named board policy (Vancouver School Board, 2026).

🔵 **The transferable lesson, and it is the same one `p730` learned on the supply side:** a nil from
a broad leg measures the leg. **A declared gap is a query specification** — spend the leg on the gap
by name, not on the general phrasing that produced the gap.

⚠️ **One correction to this base's own record while doing so.** `intel/open-gaps.md` says Africa is
*absent* across four passes. Measured against the files: `Kenya` appears `79` times, `Nigeria` `69`,
`Rwanda` `24`. **Africa was never absent from this base — it was absent from the leg, and never
shelved.** That is `p610`'s *"mentioned and never shelved"* defect recurring in the regional axis,
and the gap text should say "unshelved", not "absent".

**South Africa**, 2026, in sequence:

| Date | Event |
|---|---|
| `2026-04-10` | Final draft **National AI Policy** published in the Government Gazette — **Notice 3880 of 2026**, Gazette **54477**. |
| `2026-04` | At least **`6` of its `67` academic references are found not to exist.** Journal editors confirm the attributed articles were never published. |
| `2026-06-12` | Minister **Solly Malatsi** withdraws Notice 3880 **in its entirety**, effective on publication. |
| `2026-11` → `2027-01` | Revised documents targeted for Cabinet (November 2026) and public comment (January 2027). South Africa has **no national AI policy** in the interim. |

🔵 **Why this belongs in an education knowledge base rather than a governance one.** It is the single
most usable argument a studio has in this sector, and it is not hypothetical: **a ministry published
an AI policy containing fabricated sources, and had to retract the whole instrument.** Every
education engagement that generates content — curriculum, assessment items, reading lists, policy
drafts — is one step from the same failure, and the remedy is the provenance discipline this base
already specifies (`P87`'s diligence gate, `P90`'s primary-source corpus, `P91`'s auditable judge).
Lead with this fact when selling verification, grounding or citation-audit work into a public-sector
education client. It ends the argument about whether the control is worth paying for.

⚠️ **Source grade, stated because this base's rule is to state it.** The gazette PDF was not reached
(`eur-lex.europa.eu` and peers fail DNS in this session per `725-F`; `artificialintelligenceact.eu`
fails the same way and is added to that list). The sequence above is corroborated across independent
outlets including ITWeb and African Business, and **one discrepancy is left open rather than
smoothed:** the withdrawing instrument is called *General Notice 3978* by one source and a
*Government Notice* by others. Check `gov.za` Gazette `54477` and the June withdrawal notice before
quoting the instrument number in a deliverable. The withdrawal itself, the date and the cause are
not in dispute.

## 🆕 T258–T261 — added at p729 (2026-11-09)

## T262 — In education, the bigger the repository, the likelier its grant is one Globant cannot build on — and the index field will not tell you 🟢 new at p730

`p730` verified `20` subjects. **Six of the seven largest by stars cannot be used in client work**,
and the licences are each a different flavour of almost-open:

| Repo | Stars | Grant, read from the bytes | Why it fails |
|---|--:|---|---|
| [`xiaoyang111222/cn-math-taxonomy`](https://github.com/xiaoyang111222/cn-math-taxonomy) | **7,244** | CC BY-**NC** 4.0 | Non-commercial. The restriction is on *use*, so no API boundary cures it. |
| [`chadyi/StudyOnTV`](https://github.com/chadyi/StudyOnTV) | 1,159 | *"Source Available License — Personal Use Only"*, © all rights reserved | Source-available ≠ open source. No commercial use, no fork. |
| [`GarethManning/education-agent-skills`](https://github.com/GarethManning/education-agent-skills) | 969 | CC BY-**SA** 4.0 | Commercial use allowed; **adaptations must be released under the same licence**. |
| [`canyongbs/advisingapp`](https://github.com/canyongbs/advisingapp) | 340 | **Elastic License 2.0** | Not OSI. Forbids providing the software as a hosted/managed service — the usual studio delivery model. |
| [`learning-commons-org/knowledge-graph`](https://github.com/learning-commons-org/knowledge-graph) | 167 | **resolved per dataset** | `LICENSE.md` grants nothing; each dataset carries its own terms in a separate catalogue. |
| [`bigdata-ustc/Agent4Edu`](https://github.com/bigdata-ustc/Agent4Edu) | 102 | **none** | `LICENSE`, `.md`, `.txt`, `LICENCE`, `COPYING`, `UNLICENSE` → all `404`. |

**The instrument finding is the useful half.** `search/repositories` reported **`NOASSERTION` for
five of the six** and `NONE` for the sixth. `NOASSERTION` does not mean *unusual licence*; it means
**the classifier could not identify the file**, which happens precisely when the file is a bespoke
licence, a Creative Commons text, a vendor licence or a pointer to somewhere else. 🔴 **So in this
domain `NOASSERTION` is not a soft warning to resolve later — it is the single highest-yield
signal that a payload read will end in a refusal.**

**Why education specifically.** The pattern is not random. The six are curriculum graphs, teacher
skill libraries, children's software and institutional platforms — **artefacts whose authors are
educators, publishers or institutions rather than software vendors**, and that author class reaches
for Creative Commons (where `NC` and `SA` are the defaults offered first) or for a protective
custom licence. The more pedagogically valuable the artefact, the more likely its author thought
about commercial use and said no.

**What to do with it.**
1. **Treat `NOASSERTION` as a stop, not a flag.** Read the payload before the repo enters a proposal.
2. **Separate the two failure modes when advising a client.** `NC` and personal-use are *refusals*;
   `SA` and `MPL` are *constraints you can design around*; per-dataset licensing is a *lookup task*.
3. **Budget for licensing the good ones.** `cn-math-taxonomy` is the prerequisite graph every tutor
   on these shelves lacks. `NC` is a licence, not a wall: the author can be asked.

## T263 — Four jurisdictions put school AI curriculum into force in the same school year, and every one of them names its delivery channel 🟢 new at p730

Not four pilots. Four instruments, each with a named implementing body and a named training channel:

| Jurisdiction | Instrument | Scale named | Delivery channel named in the instrument |
|---|---|---|---|
| **China** | AI + Education Action Plan, Ministry of Education + 4 departments, April 2026; Beijing floor **≥ 8 class-hours/year** | national, 2030 integration target | local curriculum authorities |
| **India** | CBSE **Computational Thinking & AI**, Classes 3–8, launched `2026-04-01` for `2026-27`, circular `Acad-15/2026` | **~500,000 teachers** | **NISHTHA** platform; framework by an **IIT Madras**-chaired committee |
| **Saudi Arabia** | **50 AI learning units** across **22 updated subjects** | **6M+** students | **SDAIA** + MoE + **National Centre for Curriculum** + MCIT |
| **UAE** | Cabinet-approved AI curriculum, **all public and private schools**, plus a mechanism to offer it to other countries' ministries | **22,000 teachers** | **MBZUAI** + Emirates College for Advanced Education; **Code.org** advising on content |

🟢 **The commercial reading is the inversion of what an AI studio instinctively proposes.** None of
these four jurisdictions is buying a tutor. All four are buying **teacher capability and localised
curriculum artefacts**, on a deadline, at a scale their own institutions cannot staff. The
deliverables are lesson sequences, assessment rubrics, teacher-training content and the localisation
of all of it — and the UAE instrument makes localisation a *recurring* product by committing to hand
the curriculum to other ministries.

🔵 **It also explains which open-source supply is actually relevant.** `p730`'s `esp-labs-web`
(MIT, ESP32-S3 labs, **`11` languages shipped**) and `get-it` (Apache-2.0, comprehension
accessibility) are worth more against this demand than any tutoring agent on these shelves, because
the hard part of a national rollout is *material a teacher can deliver in the local language*, not
inference.

🔴 **Two things this trend must not be read as saying.** China's national plan reads as direction and
guidance, **not** as a compulsory statute, whatever secondary coverage says; and CBSE's own documents
disagree with each other on whether its curriculum is advised or directed. Both conflicts are
recorded in `intel/market.md` § *Declared gaps*.

## T264 — Forecast CAGR and actual capital are moving in opposite directions, and the gap names the buyer 🟢 new at p730

**The forecasts have stopped converging.** Three `2026` base-year estimates: **`$9.58B`** at
`34.52%` (Precedence), **`$10.6B`** at `41.5%` to `$42.48B` by 2030 (Research and Markets),
**`$11.40B`** at `16.8%` to `$57.25B` by 2033 (Coherent). 🔴 **A `2.5×` spread in CAGR on the same
base year means the three are not measuring the same market.** Quote a range with its source
attached, never one number.

**Actual capital went the other way.** HolonIQ: **`$1.0B` of edtech venture capital in H1 2026,
`−26%` year on year**, after `$2.6B` in 2025 and `$2.4B` in full-year 2024 — **`−89%` below the
`$20.8B` 2021 peak**. Inside the decline, **East Asia deal volume rose `37%`** and early-childhood
deal count more than tripled.

🟢 **These are not contradictory, and reconciling them is the actionable part: the forecasts are
describing institutional budget, and the funding series is describing venture appetite.** Every
large, dated, named AI-in-education commitment this base holds is public procurement — Ohio's
district mandate (`2026-07-01`), India's `500,000` teachers, Saudi's `6M` students, the UAE's
`22,000` teachers, UNESCO's `8` CONALEP/DGETI campuses. **None of it is venture-funded, and all of
it is budget-funded.**

**What follows for a studio.**
1. **Sell to the procurement motion, not the product motion**: longer cycles, named institutional
   buyers, compliance artefacts as first-class deliverables (`T262`'s licence posture is one).
2. **Expect reference transfer across jurisdictions** — a UAE curriculum built for export, a UNESCO
   model built to be copied, an Ohio model policy built to be adapted. One delivered reference is
   worth more here than in any venture-funded market.
3. 🔴 **Stop pricing against the `41.5%` CAGR.** The capital series says the available money this
   year is institutional, and institutional budgets do not compound at `41.5%`.

## T258 — A published constant without its normalisation procedure is not a measurement, and two correct procedures can agree on the byte count while disagreeing on the hash

`p728` replaced a byte *band* for stock-`MIT` licence payloads with an exact *constant* — the right
move, and this base's instrument history is better for it. It published **`1,020 B` / sha256₁₂
`fe2a9817987f`** and mandated a standing gate (`P163`) to run it. **It did not publish the
normalisation.**

`p729` tried seven normalisations against publishers `p728` itself names as stock `MIT`
(`zzllrr/mather`, `132465798a/zx-study`, `parz0val0/scan-to-practice`,
`CommitHu502Craft/professor-skill`): keep newlines with blank lines, drop blank lines, rstrip each
line, add a trailing newline, strip the ends, add a trailing newline to that, and collapse all
whitespace. **Every one lands between `870` and `874 B`. None reaches `1,020 B`.**

The finding is not that `p728` was `150` bytes out. It is this:

| Normalisation | Bytes | sha256₁₂ | Stable across publishers? |
|---|--:|---|---|
| Strip title + copyright lines, **collapse all whitespace** | **870** | **`3d87852cf34a`** | ✅ `n=17`, spread `0` |
| Strip title + copyright lines, **join with `\n`, drop blanks** | **870** | `a7a3589acf19` | ✅ `n=4`, spread `0` |
| Strip title + copyright lines, keep blank lines | 874 | `37744877e46c` | ✅ |
| `p728` as published | `1,020` | `fe2a9817987f` | ❓ **not reproduced by any of the seven** |

**Two of them are each perfectly stable and they disagree.** Same byte count, different hash. So a
gate that records only the length *cannot detect that it is running a different procedure from the
one that calibrated it* — it will pass, silently, on the wrong normalisation. The pair
(`procedure`, `constant`) is the unit; neither half travels alone.

**The generalisation, which is what makes this a trend and not a bug report.** This base's standing
practice is to publish a measured number so a later pass can re-derive it. A number is re-derivable
only if the *operation* that produced it is recorded at the same time. `729-A` is the third defect of
this exact shape in this base's own instruments — `700-B` (a probe not exhaustive in *case*), `703-D`
(a hash that identified the owner rather than the repository), and now a constant without its
procedure — and in all three the number looked fine and the method was unstated.

🟢 **Measured consequence, not hypothetical:** one *published* cell on
[`../repos/foundations.md`](../repos/foundations.md) (`BennettSchwartz/membrane`) cited
`1,020 B` / `fe2a9817987f` as its verification evidence. Re-measured at `p729`: `870 B` /
`3d87852cf34a`. The row's verdict was right and its evidence was not re-derivable. Corrected in place.

🔵 **The gate also generalises past `MIT`, which `p728` asserted without measuring.** Under the
canonical procedure, `Apache-2.0` is **`9,478 B` / `399d47608b81`** across **`8` independent
publishers, spread `0 B`**, against a raw spread of `34 B`. First data points recorded for
`BSD-3-Clause` (`1,091 B` / `90bd78b45663`) and `Unlicense` (`1,042 B` / `fe0829b13da5`) at `n=1`
each — **recorded as single observations, explicitly not yet constants.**

→ Operationalised as `P164` in [`../compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md), which publishes the
procedure, the constants, and the negative controls together.

## T259 — A byte-length tolerance on a licence payload selects against institutional publishers, and in this base it suppressed the region it then declared empty

The retired band for stock `MIT` was **`1,056`–`1,097 B`**. Three payloads have now overshot it, and
**every one of the three names an institution in the copyright line**:

| Repository | Raw | Copyright holder | Canonical body |
|---|--:|---|--:|
| `SirhanMacx/gnps-civic-readiness` | **`1,112 B`** | *Great Neck Public Schools — Social Studies Department* | `870 B` ✅ |
| `ilios/frontend` | **`1,105 B`** | *The Regents of the University of California* | `870 B` ✅ |
| `opencast/studio` (`p726`) | **`1,164 B`** | *Opencast Studio Developers* + a second holder | `870 B` ✅ |

**Zero individual-author payloads have overshot in any pass.** All three are plain stock `MIT`; the
band was wrong about all three.

The mechanism is mundane and that is the point. A band on raw bytes measures the *copyright line*,
because that is the only variable content in a stock grant. An individual writes `© 2026 Jane Smith`.
A school district writes `© 2026 Great Neck Public Schools — Social Studies Department`, and the
em-dash costs three bytes rather than one. A university system writes `© The Regents of the
University of California`. A consortium writes two holder lines. **The longer the institution's
name, the further outside the tolerance its licence falls** — and `p728` had already identified the
non-ASCII half of this effect as a bias against non-Latin-script publishers without noticing that the
same arithmetic penalises *institutions in any script*.

🔴 **Why this is a market finding and not only an instrument one.** `703-G` registered that North
America's repeated nil on these shelves had a known cause — US authors tag no country and write in
English, so neither of this base's working region discriminators reaches them — and named the
remedy: **sweep district and university GitHub organisations.** That is precisely the publisher class
the byte band was rejecting. The first row produced by that sweep
(`gnps-civic-readiness`, a working **New York State Seal of Civic Readiness** portal, forkable by any
district in the state) is also the **largest overshoot on record**. The instrument was selecting
against the supply tier whose absence the base was reporting as a fact about the region.

🔵 **The derived region tally on the agents shelf after this pass: `APAC 27` · `Global 15` · `EMEA 4`
· `North America 1` · `LATAM 1`.** North America is at one row out of forty-eight, and part of the
cause is now known to have been ours.

## T260 — A permissive licence can be substantively valid and textually non-canonical at the same time, and the two gates that could catch it fail in opposite directions

[`HKUDS/DeepTutor`](https://github.com/HKUDS/DeepTutor) is the largest education-native repository on
these shelves at **`57,571★`**. Its `Apache-2.0` payload is the **single outlier** against `T258`'s
`n=8` constant: **`9,494 B` / `fe1d4bc9501f`**, `+16 B`.

Diffed line-for-line against `apache.org/licenses/LICENSE-2.0.txt`, fetched this pass:

1. **The APPENDIX instructions are rewritten, with *"Apache"* replaced by *"Alarm"***. Canonical:
   *"We also recommend that a file or class name and description of purpose be included on the same
   'printed page' as the copyright notice for easier identification within third-party archives."*
   DeepTutor: *"Please also get an \"Alarm or alarm\" copyright header and make that the reference to
   the Apache License and the Disclaimer of Warranty (Alarm is the umbrella trademark for a
   collection of Open Source projects)."*
2. **§1, `Contribution` definition:** *"received by **the** Licensor"* (canonical: *"received by
   Licensor"*).
3. **§4(d), NOTICE handling:** *"excluding **any** notices"* (canonical: *"excluding **those**
   notices"*).

🟢 **The verdict is to keep the row.** The grant (§2), patent grant (§3), redistribution conditions
(§4 beyond the wording change) and warranty disclaimer (§7–§8) are byte-intact. The APPENDIX is
instructions for *applying* the licence, not licence terms. The two §-level edits are an article and
a synonym with no operative effect. **It is Apache-2.0 and it stays on the shelf.**

🔴 **What fails is both available instruments, in opposite directions.**

- **An exact-payload gate rejects it.** Had `P163` been executable as published and keyed on whole-
  payload equality, it would have refused a correctly-licensed `57,571★` repository — the base's own
  headline row.
- **`spdx_id` never notices.** GitHub reports a clean `Apache-2.0`; its classifier is tolerant of
  paraphrase, so the field cannot tell an intact grant from an edited one.

→ Hence `P164`'s rule: **verify by section, not by whole-payload equality.** A payload that differs
from the constant is a flag to *diff*, never a verdict. The practical shape: compare the canonical
body; if it differs, diff against the upstream text and classify the deltas as operative or
non-operative before deciding. 🔵 **And a procurement note that follows directly:** a client's own
dependency scanner is almost certainly in the tolerant class, so "the scanner says Apache-2.0" does
not establish that the text was not altered. For anything that must survive legal review, the diff
is the evidence, not the badge.

## T261 — `spdx_id` has three provenances and only one is a grant; and the regional search legs have now saturated as a market instrument, which was the last job they still did

**Two saturation readings, filed together because both are about an instrument reaching the end of
what it can tell this base.**

**1. The licence field's third provenance.**
[`kitschpatrol/yanki-connect`](https://github.com/kitschpatrol/yanki-connect) (`59★`, a fully-typed
AnkiConnect client — a genuinely useful interoperability component this base would otherwise want) is
reported `MIT` by `gh api search/repositories`. **Seven root grant paths were probed and all seven
return `404`**: `LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, `LICENSE.txt`, `license`, `license.md`, `LICENSE-MIT`,
`licenses/LICENSE`. The field's actual source, read this pass, is `package.json`'s
`"license": "MIT"`.

So `spdx_id` is now known to arise three ways:

| Provenance | Example | Admissible here? |
|---|---|---|
| A grant document in the repository | the other `19` rows filed this pass | ✅ yes |
| A **package-manifest field** | `yanki-connect` (`package.json`) | ❌ no — a declaration, not a grant |
| Absent, or defeated by a prepended notice | `tcexam` → `NOASSERTION` (`p728`) | ❌ no |

**A manifest field is the author stating an intention; a grant is a document conveying rights.** The
row was found, verified alive, verified useful — and **deliberately not filed**, with the reason
recorded rather than the row quietly dropped. 🔵 This matters beyond one row: a dependency scanner
reading manifests will report a licence for every package in a tree, and some fraction of those
packages carry **no grant at all**. The number is unknown here and is a declared gap.

**2. The regional legs have saturated.**
`703-H` re-scoped the four mandated regional legs from a *supply* instrument (which had nilled 31
consecutive times) to a *market* instrument, on the evidence that they returned no repository
addresses but substantial demand intelligence. **That second job has now also run out.** This pass
the four legs returned roughly `35` distinct figures, and **exactly one was not already held in
[`market.md`](market.md)** — the Pearson/Workera acquisition, which this base held only in
`agents/trending.md`.

Everything else they produced was already on the page: UNESCO IESALC's `87 %` adoption / `26 %`
formal framework / `55 %` no AI budget, the Digital Education Council's `92 %` students / `79 %`
faculty, Uruguay's `75 %` of public-school teachers, Brazil's `53 %` of administrators against `22 %`
with guidelines, Europe at `$2.64B` → `$8.0B` (`31.9 %` CAGR), the `10 %` of `450+` institutions with
formal guidelines, the `716` LATAM regulatory instruments across `23` countries, Korea's AI Basic Act
in force `22 Jan 2026`, Vietnam's July 2026 listing of education among six high-risk sectors, and the
Digital Omnibus deferral of stand-alone Annex III obligations to `2 Dec 2027`.

🔵 **This is a saturation reading, not a failure, and the response is a budget change rather than a
retirement.** The legs are still returning correct intelligence; they are no longer returning *new*
intelligence, because this base has been running them for dozens of passes against a market whose
headline numbers are published annually. **Run them as confirmation — cheap, and they would catch a
reversal — and stop costing them as discovery.** The regional *supply* question has a better
instrument already measured and in use: owner expansion (`T134`, `T150`), which produced all `19`
rows filed this pass and `0` came from the mandate.

## 🆕 T255–T257 — added at p728 (2026-11-09)

## T255 — A licence payload is verified by an exact constant, not by a byte-length tolerance; the tolerance form has a built-in bias against non-Latin-script publishers

**Status: measured this pass on 12 publishers with 4 negative controls. This supersedes the raw-byte band for stock MIT.**

This base has verified licences by payload rather than by GitHub's index field for many passes,
and the practice has repeatedly paid — `727-D` found the blog channel wrong on three licences the
payload method had right, and `728-G` adds `tcexam` (index `NOASSERTION`, payload `AGPL-3.0`).
But the *test applied to the payload* was a **raw byte-length band**, `1,056`–`1,097 B` for stock
`MIT`, measured at `p616`. That band had two documented false-positive modes (`726-A`):

1. a second copyright line, or a decorative underline under the title — the normal shape of a
   long-lived or forked project;
2. **multi-byte UTF-8 in the copyright holder's own name**, which means *any publisher whose name
   is not ASCII pays bytes for it.* That mode is **systematically biased against exactly the
   Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Arabic and Cyrillic publishers** that supply most of this industry's
   new permissive code.

**Measured this pass.** Strip the title block and every `Copyright` line, normalise whitespace
(which removes the hard-wrap-versus-reflow variable a raw count cannot see), and the stock `MIT`
grant body is **`1,020 B`, with spread `0 B` and one identical sha256₁₂ `fe2a9817987f`, across
`12` independent publishers** whose raw payloads span `1,063`–`1,164 B`. The twelve include both
of mode 1's false positives (two copyright lines each) and two non-ASCII holders. **Both modes
disappear.** Negative controls: `Apache-2.0` → `10,056 B`; `AGPL-3.0` → `33,449 B`; `MIT` with a
non-commercial clause **added** → `1,098 B`; `MIT` with the warranty disclaimer **deleted** →
`559 B`. All four rejected, both tamper directions caught.

🔵 **Why it matters beyond this base's bookkeeping, and it is a client-facing fact.** The question
*"is this really the MIT licence, or MIT with something added?"* is the one that decides whether a
repository can ship inside a deliverable, and it is asked about hundreds of dependencies per
engagement. **A tolerance band answers it with a maybe and mis-flags foreign-language publishers;
an equality test against one constant answers it yes or no and is trivially automatable** — one
normalisation and one hash comparison, no legal review for the ones that match. The residual cost
is bounded and known: only payloads that *fail* the hash need reading, and a failure is
informative rather than suspicious (a second copyright line is not a defect).

⚠️ **Limits, stated so this is not over-read.** The constant is established for `MIT` only; the
equivalent constants for `Apache-2.0` and the GNU family are not measured here, and Apache
additionally resists byte tests for a reason `726-G` already named (its `APPENDIX` is optional and
its wrapping is not normative, so section-counting is the right test there, not length). Twelve
publishers is enough to establish a constant and not enough to bound the rate of benign variants
this base has never seen.

## T256 — Vocational and technical training is a separate, permissively-licensed supply tier, and its product shape is a simulator of a rig too expensive to put in front of a learner

**Status: new category, 2 repositories this pass, 0 in the preceding 727 passes.**

Every curated row this base held before this pass served academic education — K-12 or higher
education, a tutor or a study tool attached to a curriculum. This pass filed two repositories that
serve neither: [`malgaroshy-maker/factoryforge`](https://github.com/malgaroshy-maker/factoryforge)
(`41★`, MIT) teaches **PLC programming** by having the learner write ladder logic or SCL in the
real industrial toolchains — TIA Portal, OpenPLC, Node-RED, Ignition — and drive a Godot 4.7
physics factory with it; [`DNiev/ecu-lab`](https://github.com/DNiev/ecu-lab) (`67★`, MIT) teaches
**engine calibration** by having them edit the same tables a working tuner edits and read a
simulated dyno pull.

🔵 **Both implement one shape, and naming it is the useful part: a high-fidelity simulator of
equipment too expensive, too dangerous or too scarce to give a learner.** The pedagogy is not
explanation and not conversation — it is *consequence*. The learner acts on a realistic control
surface and the simulated system responds as the real one would. Note what is absent from both:
no LLM is required for the core loop, and neither project has one. **The AI opportunity is the
layer above** — diagnosing *why* a calibration failed, or marking a ladder-logic solution against
intent rather than output.

🔵 **Why this is a distinct market and not a sub-segment of the academic one.** It is a different
buyer (an industrial training or workforce budget, often an employer rather than an institution),
a different success measure (**certification pass rate**, which is auditable and which the buyer
already reports), a different procurement cycle, and **no LMS to sit beside** — which removes the
integration constraint that shapes most of this base's academic patterns (`P138`). It also
connects directly to the demand-side reading this base already holds: `T233`'s finding that new
budget is at the workforce and credentialing end, and the `2026` microcredential and
skills-first-LMS movement recorded on `intel/market.md`.

⚠️ **Thin evidence, stated plainly: two repositories, `41★` and `67★`, both single-maintainer, one
of them unplaced by region.** This is a category observation, not a measured market. The claim
being made is that the *shape* is coherent and recurs — not that there is mature open-source
supply here. There is not; the gap is recorded on `repos/foundations.md` as such.

## T257 — Open-source discovery in this sector is now polluted by two adversarial signal classes, and both survive a stars-and-licence filter

**Status: measured this pass — 185 distinct repositories across 8 legs.**

`726-F` and `728-J` established that discovery in this industry fails mostly through *homonymy*:
`topic:adaptive-learning` returns concept-drift ML, `topic:xapi` returns Cisco Webex code,
`aprendizaje` returns reinforcement learning. Those are accidents of vocabulary. **This pass
measured two classes that are not accidents.**

**1. Integrity-defeat software ranks inside education topics, at the top.**
[`UseInterstellar/Interstellar`](https://github.com/UseInterstellar/Interstellar) — **`2,200★`,
AGPL-3.0, actively maintained** — is a school-network-filter-evasion web proxy bundled with games,
and it ranks under education topics alongside `55gms/55GMS` (`164★`), `nautilus-os/GUST` (`140★`)
and `PeteZah-Games/PeteZahGames` (`118★`). **By stars, `Interstellar` would be the fourth-largest
row on this base's agent shelf.** This is `T251`'s integrity-defeat layer arriving through the
*discovery instrument* rather than through assessment design — and it ranks highly precisely
because its users are students, who are numerous and who star things.

**2. An SEO/astroturf cluster.** Roughly `15` repositories in the novel set share four properties:
licence **`NONE`**, **every one pushed on the same day**, titles written for a search engine
(*"Best Open-Source X for 2026"*, *"X 2026: Interactive Y"*), and star counts in a **narrow
`50`–`70` band**. Individually each property is innocuous; **the conjunction is the signal**, and a
narrow star band across unrelated projects pushed on one day is not organic.

🔵 **Why this is a trend rather than a nuisance.** The default method for assessing an open-source
option — rank by stars, check the licence is permissive, check it is recently pushed — **passes
both classes.** Class 1 passes it comfortably and is actively maintained. Class 2 fails only on the
licence check, and that check is the one most often deferred. 🟢 **The usable consequence is that
fitness has to be assessed on the artefact and never on its metrics**, which is what this base's
payload-first practice already does for licences and now has to do for *purpose*: read what the
repository is for. For a studio the stake is concrete — proposing class 1 to an education client
is not a weak recommendation but an actively damaging one, since the client's own integrity policy
is what that software exists to defeat.

## 🆕 T253–T254 — added at p727 (2026-11-09)

## T253 — A `topic:` head has the same ambiguity defect a single search term has, and conjunction is the fix

`p726` measured the `topic:` discovery channel and filed the result as `726-F`: **18 heads, 1,013
distinct repositories, 600 novel (59.2 %), zero filed.** The cause was homonymy —
`topic:adaptive-learning` returns concept-drift detection, adaptive sampling and gradient
boosting, and `topic:xapi` returns Cisco Webex device code rather than the Experience API this
industry's conformance tier is built on. **That measurement is sound and is not withdrawn.**

**What `p727` withdraws is the generalisation.** Run conjunctively, the same channel produced
every one of this pass's three rows:

| Leg | Shape | Novel rows filed |
|---|---|--:|
| `topic:education topic:llm pushed:>2026-09-01 stars:>100` | domain head **AND** technique head | **3** |
| `topic:ai-tutor pushed:>2026-09-01` | single domain-bearing head | 0 — all 12 already held |
| `topic:intelligent-tutoring-system pushed:>2026-06-01` | single domain-bearing head | 0 — all already held |
| `grading agent LLM rubric pushed:>2026-09-01 stars:>50` | phrase leg | 0 rows returned at all |

🔵 **Mechanism — and this is `T252` arriving on a second channel rather than a new law.** `T252`
established that *a single-term leg needs a domain-bearing term*, because `maestro` is a
conductor and an orchestrator and `guru` is a teacher and a brand suffix. **A topic head is a
term, and it carries the identical defect**: `adaptive-learning` is a pedagogy *and* a sampling
strategy. Conjunction fixes it because it supplies the domain-bearing term as a **second filter
the repository's author had to opt into**. `topic:education topic:llm` cannot return a
gradient-boosting library — nobody tags one `education`.

🟢 **Rule: run the `topic:` channel as a domain head ANDed with a technique head.** The
single-head form is what `726-F` measured at `0 / 600` and there is no reason to run it again.
⚠️ **Limit, measured not assumed:** the conjunctive leg returned only `12` rows. It is a
*precision* instrument, not a volume one — it will not substitute for the publisher-estate
enumeration that paid `8` rows at `p726`.

## T254 — Licence follows the business model one tier further down: the local-first learner application is converging on AGPL while the skill tier stays MIT

`T250` established that **the licence follows the business model of the publisher, not the
maturity of the software** — a government mandating a framework must license it permissively
because its suppliers are commercial, while an open-core vendor selling hosting chooses `AGPL`
precisely to tax the hosting competitor. `p727` finds the same law operating *inside* the
application tier, which `T250` did not reach.

**The measurement.** Both of this pass's application-class finds are copyleft, and both are
local-first desktop products:

- [`sitor-ai/frametell`](https://github.com/sitor-ai/frametell) — **490★, AGPL-3.0** (`LICENSE`,
  `34,523 B`, read this pass), explainer-video generation under an AI director agent,
  local-first, 96 forks in the month since creation.
- [`helixnow/deep-student`](https://github.com/helixnow/deep-student) — **309★, AGPL-3.0**
  (`34,532 B`), a local-first AI learning workbench whose agent acts across every application
  on a "Study Desktop", 60 forks.

Against that, every **skill**-shaped artefact this base has filed recently is permissive:
`universal-examprep-skill`, `teacher-to-skills`, `universal-diagnostic-tutor-skill`,
`Good Learning` and `learn-anything-with-AI` — **all MIT**.

🔵 **Why this is a trend and not two rows.** A local-first desktop application's only
competitor is somebody who takes the code and runs it as a hosted service; **the network clause
is the only defence that reaches that competitor**, so the application tier reaches for `AGPL`.
A skill is a prompt artefact — there is no hosting to protect and nothing to tax — so it stays
`MIT`. The licence is predicted by *what the publisher is defending*, which is exactly `T250`'s
claim at a smaller scale.

🟢 **Consequence for a studio, and it is a scoping fact rather than a licence opinion: the
local-first application tier cannot be forked closed, and the skill tier can.** An engagement
that wants a client-branded, closed derivative should compose skills over a permissive platform
(`OpenOLAT` Apache-2.0, `oppia` Apache-2.0, `egovframe-msa-edu` Apache-2.0) rather than fork a
desktop application — and should price an `AGPL` application as *deploy-and-contribute*, not as
*fork-and-own*.

⚠️ **The limit, stated so the next pass tests it rather than inheriting it.** This rests on
**two** AGPL applications against five MIT skills. It is a consistent reading of `T250`'s
mechanism, not an established base rate: `course2md` and `ClassCue` are both local-first
desktop learner applications on this base's own shelf and both are **MIT**, which is a
counterexample inside the same category. 🔵 The distinction that may matter — and that a later
pass should measure rather than assume — is **whether the application has a hosted commercial
version to protect**, not whether it runs locally.

## 🆕 T250–T252 — added at p726 (2026-11-09)

## T250 — The permissive learner platform is arriving from public-sector reference stacks, not from the LMS market

For twenty-eight passes this base recorded the platform tier as structurally copyleft: Moodle `GPL-3.0`,
Open edX and Canvas and LearnHouse `AGPL-3.0`, Sakai `ECL-2.0`, Chamilo `GPL-3.0`. `p723` half-closed that
with `Selleo/mentingo` (`MIT`) and called it *vendor-steered*, correctly. **`p726` closes the other half, and
the publisher is a government.**

- [`eGovFramework/egovframe-msa-edu`](https://github.com/eGovFramework/egovframe-msa-edu) — `166★`,
  **Apache-2.0** (payload `11,357 B`, byte-exact stock), pushed `2026-11-08`. A **cloud-native microservice
  reference implementation of an online-education service**, published by Korea's Ministry of the Interior
  and Safety as part of the eGovFrame standard framework that Korean public institutions are required to

- It does not arrive alone. [`egovframe-common-components`](https://github.com/eGovFramework/egovframe-common-components)

  [`egovframe-runtime`](https://github.com/eGovFramework/egovframe-runtime) (`49★`, Apache-2.0) the runtime.

🔵 **Why this is a trend and not a repository.** A government that mandates a framework has to license it
permissively, because its suppliers are commercial. The LMS market has the opposite incentive: an open-core
vendor selling hosting chooses `AGPL` precisely to tax the hosting competitor. **So the licence follows the
business model of the publisher, not the maturity of the software** — and that predicts where to look next.
⚠️ The limit, stated because it decides staffing: a reference implementation is built to be *forked and
certified*, not deployed, and eGovFrame's documentation is Korean-first. Budget translation and
architecture review, not installation.

🔴 **And the counter-measurement, so this is not read as a rule.** Nine other national public-sector
estates were enumerated this pass — `project-sunbird` (India/DIKSHA), `DFE-Digital` (UK),
`GovTechSG` (Singapore), `ctt-gob-es` (Spain), `govbr` (Brazil), `Samagra-Development`, `kemdikbud`
(Indonesia), `MinEduc`, `educacionchile`. **Eight were already swept by earlier passes, and the novel
rows in them are digital signatures, accessibility crawlers and open-data catalogues — not education.**
Korea is `1 of 10`. The channel is real and it is thin; see `726-L`.

## T251 — The integrity-defeat layer is large, permissively licensed and actively maintained, and no assessment design can ignore it

This base has filed the detection and governance side of academic integrity for many passes. It has never
filed the other side, which turns out to be bigger than most of the shelf:

- [`ocsjs/ocsjs`](https://github.com/ocsjs/ocsjs) — **`4,246★`, MIT**, pushed `2026-11-08`. An
  "online-course assistant" that automates completion of courses on **超星学习通 (Chaoxing)** and
  **知道智慧树 (Zhihuishu)** — the two platforms most Chinese universities run their mandatory online
  coursework on. It is larger than every curated education row on this base's shelves except `DeepTutor`,
  `OpenMAIC` and the general frameworks.

🔵 **The point is not that cheating exists. It is that the defeat tooling is `MIT`, maintained, and
platform-specific** — which means it is cheaper to deploy than the assessment it defeats, and that any
engagement selling "AI-assisted online coursework" into APAC is selling into a market where completion
telemetry is already adversarial. 🟢 **Design consequence, concrete:** completion and time-on-task are
not assessment evidence in this market. Use artefacts that are expensive to automate — an online judge's
test-case results ([`glowxq/glowxq-oj`](https://github.com/glowxq/glowxq-oj), new at `p726`), oral or
viva components, or a proctored exam harness (`SafeExamBrowser/seb-server`, already on the roster).
⚠️ **Filed as intelligence, never as a component.** It is on no shelf and must not reach a client repository.

## T252 — The binding constraint on measuring this sector's open-source supply is now instrument homonymy, not language

`T234`, `T215`, `T249` and `725-D` traced a five-pass sequence in which this base's regional supply nils
turned out to be query artefacts: first the language, then the term count. **`p726` measures the next layer,
and it is the one that produces false *positives* rather than false nils.**

| Channel | Measured this pass | The collision |
|---|---|---|
| Language, single-term (`T249`'s own remedy) | `30` legs run at `stars:>=15` | `maestro` → mobile E2E test runners and workflow orchestrators; `guru` → iOS device libraries; `aula` → a database course's notes. **Zero education rows between them.** |
| `topic:` heads | `18` heads, `1,013` distinct repositories, **`600` novel (`59.2 %`)** | `topic:adaptive-learning` returns ML concept-drift and adaptive-sampling work; **`topic:xapi` returns Cisco Webex device-API code, not the Experience API** — a collision on this base's own standards vocabulary. |

🔵 **Both failure modes are the same defect: novelty is measured on the address and fitness is measured on
nothing.** A `59.2 %` novelty rate reads as abundant supply and resolves, on inspection, to student
coursework and homonyms — which is `p667`'s *"the novelty filter over-reports by `44.2 %`"* with a second
and larger cause. 🟢 **Operative rules for later passes, both cheap:** (1) a single-term leg must use a
**domain-bearing** term (`skola`, `escola`, `sekolah`, `教学` qualify; `maestro`, `guru`, `aula` do not);
(2) a `topic:` head that names a method rather than a sector must be read as unranked.
🟢 **And the positive finding that follows from it:** everything of platform scale filed this pass — all
`10` rows across three shelves — came from **enumerating an education-native publisher's estate**, a channel
with no homonymy at all because the owner *is* the discriminator. See `726-B`, `726-C`, `726-L`.

## 🆕 T247–T249 — added at p725 (2026-11-09)

## T247 — The jurisdictional standards layer is becoming open, machine-readable infrastructure, and it is EMEA-authored

For eight passes this base recorded the standards layer as the gap (`T203`: *the standards layer, not
the model, is the chokepoint between a demo and a delivery*). At p725 it has supply, and the supply has
a consistent shape: **small, single-author, EMEA, and built as access or vocabulary rather than as a
platform.**

- [`isakskogstad/Skolverket-MCP`](https://github.com/isakskogstad/Skolverket-MCP) — `13★`, **MIT**,
  Sweden — serves all three Skolverket open APIs (national curriculum, school-unit register, planned
  educations) as MCP tools, published in the MCP registry.
- [`YannHY/scenarisation`](https://github.com/YannHY/scenarisation) — `7★`, CC-BY-SA-4.0,
  France/Switzerland — encodes eight competency frameworks, Bloom, the AIAS scale and referentials for
  twelve-plus school systems plus ISCED 2011.

Read alongside the three read-only LMS bridges this base already holds — `Faixiang/Moodle-MCP`
(`204★`, MIT), `boyuchengz/canvas-mcp` (`119★`, MIT), `RohanMuppa/brightspace-mcp-server` (`64★`,
MIT) — the pattern is that **the integration surface for education AI is being published as MCP, by
individuals, ahead of any vendor roadmap.** Four of the five are MIT.

**Why it matters commercially.** "Aligned to the national curriculum" has been a claim a client had to
take on trust, backed by a scraped PDF. Where a ministry publishes an API and someone has wrapped it,
alignment becomes a *query against the ministry's own data* — auditable, and cheap to re-run when the
curriculum changes. That is a defensible deliverable in exactly the regions where `T217` and `T221`
say governance has overtaken capability as the buying constraint.

**What complicates it.** Every one of these is `7–204★` with one maintainer and no institutional
backing; two are months past their last push. **This is infrastructure with a bus factor of one.**
Treat them as reference implementations to pin and adopt, and price the maintenance — not as
dependencies to assume. Recipe and limits: `P157`.

## T248 — The "when is AI allowed" control has moved from policy prose into a data field

`T209` recorded detection being abandoned as a control and `T213` recorded that every region's 2026
regulation converges on one control that open tooling did not have. The control is **the permitted
level of AI use, per task**, and at p725 it exists as code: `scenarisation` carries the **AIAS AI
Assessment Scale** as a first-class field on every activity in a learning design, next to the
competency framework and the Bloom level.

That is a different object from an AI policy document. A policy says what is allowed; **a field says
it per activity, travels with the artefact, and can be reported on.** It is the difference between a
district having a policy and a district being able to answer *"which assessments in this course permit
generative AI, and at what level"* — the question an accreditor or a parent actually asks, and the one
`T221` says accreditation is becoming the enforcement channel for.

**Counter-signal, stated plainly.** One `7★` repository is an existence proof, not a standard. AIAS
itself is a published scale with uptake in the literature, but nothing here shows an LMS writing or
reading that field. **The honest claim is that the control is now specifiable and demonstrable, not
that it is adopted.** The commercial read: a client's assessment redesign programme — where `T209`
says the detection spend is moving — can now ship with a machine-readable permitted-use field instead
of a PDF appendix, and that is a differentiator available today.

## T249 — Regional supply measurement in this industry is query-syntax-bound, not supply-bound

This base has declared regional nils repeatedly, has twice corrected itself about them (`T215`: the
search language was the ceiling; `T234`: a declared nil is more often a fact about the base than about
the region), and at p725 the mechanism is finally measured rather than inferred.

**Five multi-term non-English legs returned zero rows each.** The same languages as **single terms**
with a `stars:` floor returned real repositories by the dozen — including both of this pass's new
finds and both of the base's best-known LATAM rows. The cause is not the language and not the supply:
`search/repositories` **ANDs** every term and matches **name, description and topics only, never the
README**, so a three- or four-word non-English query requires all of those words inside one short
description. That essentially never happens.

**The generalisable lesson, and it is not about GitHub.** A research leg that returns categorical zero
is reporting on *itself* at least as often as on the world, and a pipeline that writes nils into a
knowledge base without a positive control will accumulate confident absences that are artefacts. The
control is cheap: **run the same leg in a form you know should return something.** If the known-good
form is also nil, the instrument is broken; if it returns, the nil was syntax. Filed operationally as
`P158`.

**Direct consequence for engagement scoping.** Any claim of the form *"there is no open-source X in
region Y"* in this base that predates p725 and rests on a phrase-shaped leg should be treated as
**unmeasured, not as false and not as true** — `725-H` closed one such gap that had been re-asserted
across five passes, and the artefacts that closed it had been sitting in the index the whole time.

## 🆕 T245–T246 — added at p724 (2026-11-09)

## T245 — The institutional recording archive, not the curriculum, is where AI entry costs are lowest

Two permissive implementations of **lecture-capture-to-notes** appeared independently within three weeks of
each other, in different languages, with no shared lineage: [`mizorewww/course2md`](https://github.com/mizorewww/course2md)
(**`508★`**, MIT, Rust, created `2026-08-31`, pushed `2026-11-09`) and
[`drpwchen/lecture-to-notes`](https://github.com/drpwchen/lecture-to-notes) (**`117★`**, MIT, Python, created
`2026-08-02`, pushed `2026-11-03`). Convergent independent implementation is the strongest available signal
that a category is real rather than a single author's preoccupation.

**Why this is a trend and not a tool.** Every other entry point into an institution has a prerequisite:
a tutoring agent needs curriculum alignment, an LMS sidecar needs LTI credentials and an administrator's
consent, an assessment tool needs a rubric and a policy decision about integrity. **The recording archive has
no prerequisite** — it already exists, it is already owned by the institution, it is already unsearchable, and
nobody has to agree on pedagogy before it can be indexed. It is the shortest path from a signed engagement to
something a faculty member can see working.

**The evidence that complicates it.** Neither project is an institutional product. `course2md` is a
single-user desktop binary with no multi-tenancy, no SSO and no retention policy; `lecture-to-notes` is a
pipeline, not a service. **Both are components, and the gap between a working component and an institutional
deployment is exactly the gap a studio bills for** — but that gap should be quoted, not assumed away. And the
category inherits the one unresolved question of the whole field: a recording of a lecture is also a recording
of the students in it, which makes retention and consent a design input rather than a compliance afterthought.

🔵 **The sub-signal worth more than the category.** `lecture-to-notes` inverts the usual ordering: Whisper
ASR, frame extraction, OCR and slide-semantics vision **all run locally**, and the LLM is used **only at the
end, to write prose from evidence the pipeline already assembled**. That is `T228` (pedagogy-in-control)
arriving as an *architecture* rather than a stated intention — and it is what makes the pattern deployable at
all under the data-boundary constraints of `T229`.

## T246 — A knowledge base's remaining gaps are increasingly environmental rather than epistemic, and the two require opposite responses

This base has carried *"the Digital Omnibus education deadline cannot be asserted because the Official Journal
text has not been read"* for several passes, phrased as a diligence gap — the kind a later pass closes by
trying harder. **p724 establishes that no pass in this environment can close it.** `eur-lex.europa.eu`,
`ec.europa.eu`, `digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu` and `artificialintelligenceact.eu` **all fail DNS resolution
— `4` of `4`** — being outside the session's allowed network domains. The gap is a property of the
instrument, not of the effort.

**Why the distinction changes behaviour.** An *epistemic* gap is an instruction to a later pass: search again,
search differently, read the primary source. An *environmental* gap is an instruction to **stop searching and
record the blocker**, because every later pass will spend a leg reproducing the same failure. The two look
identical when written down as *"not verified"*, which is why they must not be written down the same way.

**The generalisation, which this base can now evidence against its own instrument history.** The same pattern
has already consumed legs here repeatedly: `curl -sI github.com/...` returning `403` for live and invented
addresses alike (five consecutive passes), `gh api repos/{owner}/{repo}` returning `403` under repository
scoping, `gh api users/{owner}` returning `403` and costing the base its region-attribution instrument
(`723-R`), and `search/repositories` having **no index entry at all** for `openedx/edx-platform` — the
second-most-deployed LMS in the industry. **In each case the environment, not the world, produced the absence.**
🔴 **The operational rule this yields:** before recording a nil, establish whether the instrument could have
returned a non-nil, and write *which* it was. A nil with a named cause is reusable; a bare nil is
indistinguishable from coverage, and this base has mistaken one for the other at least four times
(`722-E` EMEA supply, `722-N` North America, and the two withdrawn at `723-E`/`723-M2`).

🟢 **What this pass did with the rule.** The Omnibus finding is recorded with its **article-level citations**
(amended Article 113(c), recital 40, OJ publication `2026-07-24`, entry into force `2026-07-27`, Annex III
`2027-12-02`, Annex I `2028-08-02`, Article 5 NCII/CSAM `2026-12-02`) **and** with the explicit note that this
base still asserts no date of its own — so a reader who *does* have EUR-Lex access settles it in one lookup
instead of repeating the research.

## T235 — Secondary-source policy claims fail at roughly the rate the repository claims do, and nobody checks them

**Evidence.** p722 established that four of this base's published star counts were overstated
by 3.6× to 31× because nobody had re-read the index. p723 applies the same scepticism to
*policy* claims from industry roundups, and **two of the four checked do not survive**:

| Claim, as published by a secondary source | Verdict at p723 |
|---|---|
| "Illinois **Act 964** requires AI literacy for grades 6–12, effective 2026-08-01" | 🔴 **No such enacted Act found.** The real instruments are **PA 104-0399** (ISBE *guidance* mandate, effective 2026-01-01, guidance published 2026-07-09) and **PA 104-0565/SB 2909** (bans AI-assigned scores in **teacher evaluation**). A proposed AI-literacy bill, **HB4625**, was introduced only. |
| Philippines CHED "**Memorandum Order 21**, a national framework for AI in teaching, research and operations" | 🔴 **No such issuance found.** CHED is *"eyeing"* a national AI policy (Mar 2026); RAISE 2026 produced a *commitment* to a proposed framework (Feb 2026). The real 2026 CMOs: **18** = student affairs, **05** = health. |
| Estonia **AI Leap** national programme | 🟢 **Verified and far richer than the roundup stated** — 154 schools, ~20,000 students, ~4,900 teachers, €3.2M→€6M, Sept 2026 expansion to 38,000 students, graduating cohort spring 2027. |
| Ireland **HEA** *National Policy Framework on Generative AI in Teaching and Learning* | 🟢 **Verified**, published 2025-12-22. |

**What complicates it.** The two failures are not random: both are **over-specific**
— a named instrument with a number and a date, which is exactly the shape that reads as
authoritative and gets copied without checking. The two that verified were *under*-reported
by their sources.

🔵 **Implication for this base:** policy facts need the same two-channel discipline as
repository facts (`722-F`). An instrument number is a claim, not a citation. **A named statute
that cannot be located in the legislature's own record is filed as unverified, not as
pending** — the KB's convention of recording delisted repositories now extends to delisted
policy claims.

## T239 — Institutional AI *policy* is abandoning detection while institutional *purchasing* accelerates into it

**Evidence.** `T209` (p717) records detection being abandoned as a control, with spend moving
to assessment redesign — well-sourced, policy-side. p723 finds the purchasing-side counter:
**AI-detection tool use in higher education rose 38% → 68% in one year.** Alongside it, the
adoption–governance gap holds everywhere it is measured (~two-thirds of institutions without a
formal AI policy; LATAM at 87% using / 26% with a strategy).

**What complicates it.** The 68% figure is from a vendor-adjacent roundup citing an
unidentified primary survey; it is a direction, not a rate. The two readings are also not
strictly contradictory — policy leadership and procurement are different functions on
different clocks.

🔵 **Why it is a trend rather than a discrepancy:** it predicts the *shape of the room* in
an integrity engagement. The pedagogy lead has written detection off; the administrator has
just bought it. An assessment-redesign proposal is therefore a **replacement for a live
purchase**, not a greenfield improvement, and must be positioned against sunk cost. Pitching
it as new capability is how these engagements stall.

## T244 — Where a national programme includes its own research arm, the evidence buyers demand becomes a procurable deliverable

**Evidence.** `T226` establishes that evidence is now the buying criterion and that ~55% of
tools lack efficacy studies. Estonia's **AI Leap** is built in three parts, and the third is
**a research study measuring effectiveness** — a government-funded comparative evidence base
covering 154 schools, ~20,000 students and a cohort graduating spring 2027. Ireland's HEA
framework and North Carolina's **Session Law 2026-41** (staged deadlines through 2028) are the
same instinct expressed as policy rather than measurement.

**What complicates it.** It is one country, and a small one; the vendor relationships
(OpenAI, Anthropic) are reported as unsettled, so the programme's instrumentation may not be
independent of its suppliers.

🔵 **Implication:** Estonia is the most *instrumented* education system in this file, which
makes it the natural reference site — for comparative measurement work, and as the citation an
EMEA or North American proposal uses when the client asks "where has this been shown to
work?" **The scarce asset in this industry is not a tutor, it is a control group.**

## T226 — Evidence has become the buying criterion

Adoption is near-saturated (86% of education organisations use generative AI per Microsoft,
2025) but **only 45% of the most-used tools have published research meeting an ESSA evidence
tier**. The market now rewards products that solve a specific problem *and can prove it*.

*Implication:* efficacy study design is no longer academic overhead — it is part of the
product, and in US public procurement it is the gate.

## T227 — Agent-native tutoring has displaced chatbot tutoring

The chatbot-as-tutor pitch is explicitly named as **fading** in 2026 analyses. What replaced
it is architecturally different: persistent learner memory, multi-agent role separation and
explicit mastery models. The two largest projects in the industry demonstrate it — DeepTutor
(57,348★, Apache-2.0) is built on *lifelong* personalised tutoring with memory across
sessions, and OpenMAIC (43,112★, MIT) assigns separate agents to teacher, peer and assistant
roles rather than running one model in a loop.

*Implication:* a single-prompt tutor is now a 2023-shaped product. The defensible unit is the
learner model, not the conversation.

## T228 — Pedagogy-in-control is becoming the stated design constraint

The OECD's *Digital Education Outlook 2026* (January 2026) holds that AI helps learning
**only when pedagogy stays in control**. This is converging with the EU AI Act's human
oversight requirements for high-risk systems, and with the reappearance of Bayesian
Knowledge Tracing (OATutor, MIT) as the auditable mastery model of choice.

*Implication:* interpretable learner models are gaining ground over end-to-end LLM judgement
— partly for pedagogy, partly because high-risk classification demands explainability.

## T229 — Regulatory divergence is now the dominant integration cost

Four regimes, four shapes, same year:

- **EU** — education is high-risk under the AI Act; emotion recognition banned in schools
  since Feb 2025; high-risk obligations reported delayed to **2 Dec 2027**.
- **US** — a federal framework and K–12 task force, plus **~100 state bills** tracked this
  year and **15+ states** legislating. Guidance outpaces binding rules.
- **UAE** — **25 specific generative-AI prohibitions** for schools (Feb 2026).
- **LATAM** — **no binding national law found in force**; governance arriving via UNESCO,
  CENIA, IADB and ECLAC instead.

*Implication:* multi-region EdTech products need compliance as an architectural axis.
Building to EU high-risk standards yields a product sellable everywhere; the reverse does not hold.

## T230 — The adoption–governance gap is widest where adoption is highest

LATAM is the clearest case: **92% of students and 79% of faculty** actively using AI against
**only 30% of universities having published an AI policy**. UNESCO IESALC found the same
asymmetry across 200 institutions in 19 countries. EMEA shows a milder version — teachers in
six countries adopted AI *autonomously, without a regulatory framework*, with >90% usage in Spain.

*Implication:* the near-term buyer in both regions is an institution needing governance,
not a classroom needing another tool. Faster to deliver and reaches a defined decision-maker.

## T231 — Teacher enablement is the explicitly requested product

Across EMEA studies the educators' own stated priority is **structured training**. Surveys
also find teachers worried AI is entering classrooms faster than schools can manage. UNESCO
maintains a teacher AI competency framework; the European Commission updated AI ethics
guidance for teachers through the Digital Education Hub.

*Implication:* the demand signal points at enablement programmes, and the market is
oversupplied with tools relative to training.

## T232 — AI on top of incumbent LMSs beats LMS replacement

Moodle (~200k active sites, GPL-3.0), Canvas (AGPL-3.0) and Open edX (AGPL-3.0) are not
being displaced; they are being extended. The evidence is in the repositories: the most
relevant new education project this pass is a **Moodle plugin**
(`moodle-ai-skill-navigator`, 279★, GPL-3.0 — tutoring, quiz generation, mind maps, RAG over
course materials), and H5P remains the rendering surface inside all three.

*Implication:* propose LTI/plugin sidecars. It avoids AGPL entanglement, inherits the
install base, and survives the client's next LMS upgrade.

## T233 — Workforce and skills-first credentialing is where new budget is

Governments and employers are expanding early-career pathways, industry-aligned
microcredentials and in-flow-of-work learning. Instructure launched **Canvas Career**, a
skills-first AI LMS aimed at workforce learning. Skill-gap-to-learning-path generation is
the matching research direction (`gen-mentor`, CC0-1.0, WWW '25 oral).

Meanwhile the old consumer model is contracting: **Chegg cut 45% of staff (388 roles)** as AI
eroded homework-help traffic.

*Implication:* budget is rotating from consumer study aids to employer- and government-funded
skills infrastructure. Different buyer, larger contract, longer cycle.

## Counter-signals worth holding

Honest caveats on the above, so this file is not read as uniformly bullish:

- **Market sizing is unreliable.** Estimates for 2026–2027 span **$10–23B** — a >2× spread
  within a single year. Most sources are vendor-commissioned. Treat all CAGR figures as
  directional only.
- **Adoption figures measure usage, not value.** "86% use generative AI" and "95% of UK
  undergraduates" count touches, not learning outcomes. Trend 1 exists precisely because
  outcome evidence is scarce.
- **APAC adoption is patchier than its supply suggests.** The region produces the best
  open-source agents *and* reported only 30% virtual-tutor adoption with connectivity as a
  barrier. Supply leadership is not demand leadership.
- **EU timelines have already slipped once.** High-risk education obligations moved to
  Dec 2027; a compliance practice built on an assumed date should assume it can move again.
