# Accumulated registry — T1–T225 (preserved from p721)

Carried forward verbatim from prior passes. Figures inside were read at the pass that filed
each trend, **not today**.


## 🆕 T220–T225 — added at p720 (2026-11-09)

## T220 — The verified-solver tutor is now a convergent pattern, and one repository has MEASURED why it works

Three repositories found on three different legs, in three countries, independently forbid the model from computing the graded quantity: [`Divyakush2006/OS-Tutor`](https://github.com/Divyakush2006/OS-Tutor) (India), [`turtlelnc/MES-Homework`](https://github.com/turtlelnc/MES-Homework) (China), [`kunbo928/k-teach`](https://github.com/kunbo928/k-teach). `p719` saw the first instance of this shape in a `28★` phonics app and recorded it as `T219`, a deterministic **gate**. 🟢 **T220 upgrades it from a gate to an ARCHITECTURE, because `OS-Tutor` supplies the ablation: the solver adds `+23 / 57` problems with `0` lost (`p < 10⁻⁶`), while the fine-tune alone moves `30 → 34` and is NOT significant (`p = 0.557`).**

🔵 **The failure mode it names is the one that matters pedagogically: the model "states the rule correctly and then executes it wrongly" — `7 / 7` of its scheduling errors were correct arithmetic on a wrong schedule.** A learner cannot detect that error, which is precisely why a confident wrong trace is worse in education than in most domains. **Trend: through 2026 the credible education builds stop trying to make the model compute and start making it narrate.**

## T221 — Governance is now the stated constraint on five independent sources, and accreditation is emerging as the enforcement channel

`T217` recorded governance overtaking capability at `p719`. p720 adds the enforcement mechanism. UNESCO IESALC's asks for LATAM name **accreditation and quality assurance** as where AI literacy and governance should be embedded; Australia's higher-education regulator already **requires providers to submit plans** addressing generative-AI risks; Korea's AI Basic Act imposes human-oversight duties with a 2026 grace period.

🟢 **The trend is that AI governance in education is migrating from advisory guidance into the accreditation and licensing apparatus — the one layer an institution cannot decline.** 🔵 **Commercially this converts governance work from discretionary to mandatory spend, and it is the single most reliable education budget line visible in 2026.**

## T222 — Adoption has decoupled from governance almost everywhere, and the size of the gap is now measurable in four regions

| Region | Adoption | Governance |
|---|--:|--:|
| LATAM higher ed (UNESCO IESALC, `200` institutions / `19` countries) | **`87%`** use AI somewhere | 🔴 **`26%`** have any formal framework |
| Brazil schools (Cetic.br) | **`53%`** of administrators | 🔴 **`22%`** have guidelines |
| Europe (azumo aggregation) | — | 🔴 **~`10%`** have formal AI-use guidelines |
| US K-12 (relayed) | ~**`60%`** of teachers | 🔴 most districts have **no** student AI policy |

🔴 **Four regions, four different data sources, the same shape: deployment is two to four times ahead of policy.** 🟡 **The US and Europe figures are secondhand in the sources read this pass and need primary re-sourcing before client use.** 🟢 **The trend to record is that this gap stopped being a LATAM story in 2026 and became a global one — `p719`'s shelves treated the governance lag as a regional characteristic, and the numbers no longer support that reading.**

## T223 — Education-labelled permissive supply is being mass-produced, and discovery has stopped being the bottleneck

Measured this pass: **`1,917`** repositories match `agentic-star in:name` — MIT-licensed single-purpose agent templates over one proprietary vendor runtime. A second owner, `jinlize-tech`, holds **`102`** repositories against a declared *"planned 100-repository education-sector Skill and Agent ecosystem"*. A third pattern: one owner publishing **seven** near-identical `Sistema*Escolar` repositories, all `6★`, all MIT, within eleven days.

🔴 **A shelf that counts rows cannot tell `1,917` templates from `1,917` projects.** 🟢 **The trend: through 2026 the scarce input in open-source education intelligence is no longer finding permissively licensed artefacts — it is distinguishing an artefact from a generated catalogue entry.** 🔵 **The screen that works is not the licence and not the star count; it is whether the repository RUNS WITHOUT A NAMED VENDOR PLATFORM, which is `719-P`'s question asked at scale.**

## T224 — The permissive school-administration layer was built once and abandoned, and nothing has replaced it

Of ten permissive school-management, SIS, attendance and library systems at or above `48★`, **nine were last pushed between January 2020 and August 2024** and exactly one is live. 🔴 **None of the nine is `archived`, so none of them carries a warning flag.**

🟢 **The trend, stated against the grain of the market forecasts: while AI-in-education spend grows at a reported `34%` CAGR, the permissive open-source ADMINISTRATIVE substrate underneath it has been static-to-dead for two to six years.** The live options are copyleft incumbents (Moodle, OpenEduCat, Frappe Education, openSIS) or a build. 🔵 **The consequence for 2026–27 engagements: the AI layer has abundant permissive starting points and the record layer has effectively none, so "adopt open source" is a viable strategy for the tutor and a false economy for the SIS.**

## T225 — Licence laundering by fork: a permissive grant that is not the project's grant, and every scanner passes it

Measured this pass on a subject the mandated vertical leg recommended as MIT. Upstream [`idurar/idurar-erp-crm`](https://github.com/idurar/idurar-erp-crm) (`8,943★`) is **AGPL-3.0** — `34,230 B`, sha256₁₂ `7800536d5087`. A `3★` third-party fork, [`u4078974/idurar-erp-crm`](https://github.com/u4078974/idurar-erp-crm) on a `demo` branch, carries **MIT** — `1,063 B`, sha256₁₂ `105269960eb9` — **and the MIT text still names the upstream author.**

🔴 **A downstream fork cannot relicense AGPL-3.0 code as MIT.** The grant file is genuine MIT text; the SPDX detector is right about what the file says; the file has no authority over the code beneath it. **An automated licence scan reports `MIT` and passes.**

🟢 **The trend: as permissive-looking education supply is mass-produced (`T223`), the reliability of the licence FIELD falls while the reliability of the licence FILE stays flat.** This KB has now recorded three distinct ways a green licence cell can be wrong — `NOASSERTION` over a real grant, a permissive grant over a proprietary runtime (`719-P`), and a permissive grant with no authority over the code (`720-D3`). 🔵 **The screen that survives all three: read the payload, read the README's requirements, and compare against the fork network's upstream. Whenever a low-star repository carries a MORE permissive grant than a high-star repository of the same name, that is the signal.**

## 🆕 T215–T219 — added at p719 (2026-11-09)

## T215 — The search language, not the supply, was the regional ceiling

🟢 **The strongest trend p719 can evidence is methodological, and it is worth more than any market figure in this file.** Three consecutive passes recorded `LATAM` frozen at `25` rows and honestly stated the freeze. p719 ran the mandated English-language LATAM leg and got **policy literature and zero repositories**; it then ran six queries in **Spanish and Portuguese** and got **`25` repositories**, `5` with resolvable grants, `2` filable and new. The freeze broke to `27`.

🔴 **And the diagnostic detail that matters: the two BEST Spanish/Portuguese subjects were already held** ([`LabSirius/TutorIA`](https://github.com/LabSirius/TutorIA), Colombia; [`tcheld0n/CorrijAI`](https://github.com/tcheld0n/CorrijAI), ENEM). So the ceiling was never "LATAM builds nothing" and never "this base has missed LATAM's good work" — **it was that an English-language query cannot reach a non-English long tail, and the head had already been absorbed.** The same leg, run in Turkish-adjacent terms, surfaced [`Asperant/ExamEcho`](https://github.com/Asperant/ExamEcho) for `EMEA`.

🟢 **Implication for anyone reading this base as market intelligence: regional "AI maturity" rankings built from English-language sources systematically understate non-anglophone markets, and the error is in the instrument, not the market.** Treat every such ranking — including the ones quoted in [`market.md`](market.md) — as a measurement of English-language visibility until proven otherwise.

## T216 — The licence trap moved from the grant into the runtime

🔴 **New trap class, first recorded this pass as `719-P`.** Two education agent templates filed to [`../repos/foundations.md`](../repos/foundations.md) carry byte-verified canonical **MIT** grants and **both state that they "do not run standalone"** — each requires SoftBank's proprietary **AGENTIC STAR** platform plus the `agenticstar-agentcore` framework, and start-up fails immediately without it.

🔴 **Every licence instrument this base has built — SPDX reading, byte counts, `sha256₁₂` fingerprints, clause-presence diffs — returns GREEN on these two, correctly, and tells you nothing about the dependency.** The grant is genuinely permissive; the runtime is genuinely closed.

🟢 **The trend to expect, and to screen for: as vendor platforms court agent developers, "MIT template, proprietary host" becomes the default distribution shape, because it gives the vendor an open-source adoption story at zero licensing cost.** The screening question `is the grant permissive?` is now necessary and insufficient; **`what must exist for this to start?`** has to be asked beside it, and only the README answers it.

## T217 — Governance overtook capability as the stated 2026 constraint, and five independent sources now say it the same way

🟢 **This converged in this pass in a way it had not before.** 1EdTech frames AI in education as moving **from experimentation to governance**, with policies, data boundaries and oversight as the gating items. HolonIQ expects 2026 emphasis on ethics, transparency, agentic use cases and **proven instructional benefit**. Campus Technology's panel expects AI to become **embedded infrastructure** across admissions, advising and administration rather than a standalone product. TutorFlow calls **disciplined, bounded, measured** adoption the only credible trend. The **OECD 2026 Digital Education Outlook** and one trade source independently name the move **from general-purpose tools to purpose-built educational platforms** as the defining shift.

🔵 **That last one is the reading that most directly justifies an inventory like this base:** when a general-purpose assistant stops being the default answer, a curated per-industry map of open-source starting points becomes the scarce asset rather than a convenience.

## T218 — Provisioning is solved; value evidence is not — and four independent numbers say so from four directions

🔴 **The four readings, from unrelated sources, all pointing at the same hole:**
- **`86%`** of students across 16 countries already use AI in their studies.
- 🔴 **`~15%`** of students *with Khanmigo access* actually use it — the availability-versus-engagement gap in one figure.
- **~two-thirds** of higher-education institutions still have no formal AI policy.
- 🔴 **UNESCO IESALC: ten times more universities USING AI than MEASURING what it delivers** (`87%` adoption against `26%` with any formal framework, and `55%` with no AI budget at all, across `200` institutions in `19` countries).

🟢 **So the durable 2026 engagement is the measurement layer, and this base acquired both of its halves this pass** (`719-E`): [`JacobFV/formal-language-cirriculum`](https://github.com/JacobFV/formal-language-cirriculum) for evaluation items drawn from a **procedural generator**, which therefore **cannot have been trained on**, and [`Grvrajput/llm-eval-rubric-kit`](https://github.com/Grvrajput/llm-eval-rubric-kit) for **judge-agnostic, deterministic** weighting and rating with mandatory rationales. Unbiasable items plus auditable scoring is the whole rig.

## T219 — The reliable pattern for generated learning content is a DETERMINISTIC GATE, and the clearest example of it is a 28★ phonics app

🟢 **Found at [`finereli/yarareads`](https://github.com/finereli/yarareads) and generalised as `P-719-A`.** `npm run check` compares every word of every story against the sounds the individual learner has been marked as knowing — **by pronunciation, not spelling**, so "cake" fails if the split `a` has not been taught — and **fails the build**. An MCP-connected agent writes new stories; **the checker, not the model, decides whether they ship.**

🟢 **Three independent subjects filed this pass converge on the same arrangement, which is what makes it a trend rather than one repo's good idea:** `yarareads` gates on decodability; [`aloktripathi1/GyanKosh`](https://github.com/aloktripathi1/GyanKosh) traces every claim to an **exact quote and character offset** and **re-validates that independently on every run, not only at generation time**; [`Asperant/ExamEcho`](https://github.com/Asperant/ExamEcho) reduces loose model output to **strict domain rules** with fallback-and-retry and exposes quality as SSE metadata.

🟢 **The shared shape: leave the generator unconstrained, make the constraint deterministic, put it in CI, and give the gate the authority.** 🔴 **The inverse — a well-prompted generator with human spot-checking — is what every stalled education pilot in this file has in common.**

## 🆕 T210–T214 — added at p718 (2026-11-09)

### 🔴 T210 — The open TTS layer has NO maintained permissive engine, and the roundups all still say "Piper, MIT"
Measured from the payloads at p718. [`rhasspy/piper`](https://github.com/rhasspy/piper) is **MIT** (`LICENSE.md` `1,070 B`, sha256₁₂ `7fdf45feb790`) and **archived**, its README reduced to one line: *“Development has moved.”* The destination, [`OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl`](https://github.com/OHF-Voice/piper1-gpl), is **GPL-3.0** (`COPYING` `35,146 B`) and says so in its own name. The alternative, [`coqui-ai/TTS`](https://github.com/coqui-ai/TTS), is **MPL-2.0** with upstream dead since `2024-08-16`; the live fork `idiap/coqui-ai-TTS` is MPL-2.0 with a payload **one byte** off upstream's.

🟢 **The trend, not the datum: permissive-to-copyleft migration on the MAINTAINED path is now a recognisable pattern in voice and it is invisible to every licence table that keys on the best-known repository.** The star count stays attached to the archived MIT repo, so the layer *looks* permissive in aggregate and is not. **Generalised rule: when a project is archived, the licence of its successor is a separate fact that must be read separately.** `p707` saw the same shape in a live relicensing (`klyro`, MIT → AGPL-3.0 in seven days); this is its archival form.

### 🔴 T211 — Source-available with production FORBIDDEN is now sitting on the highest-starred repo in a layer education needs
[`tldraw/tldraw`](https://github.com/tldraw/tldraw), **`51,426★`**, `spdx_id` **`NOASSERTION`**, `LICENSE.md` `4,608 B` sha256₁₂ `777f0637ce8b`, under **Conditions**: *“Not to use the Software in Production Environments.”* Development use is granted, production is not, and a commercial key is sold separately.

🟢 **Why it is a trend and not one repository's choice:** this is the third distinct *non-OSI* grant shape this KB has had to type in recent passes — `NOASSERTION`-because-modified (`MinerU`, Apache + additional terms), `NOASSERTION`-because-split (`litellm`, MIT outside named directories), and now `NOASSERTION`-because-bespoke-and-production-gated. 🔴 **All three sit on repositories a roundup would call open source, and all three carry five-figure star counts.** The defensive practice is now settled and cheap: `spdx_id == NOASSERTION` → read the payload bytes before the repository enters a proposal.

### 🟢 T212 — Digital credentials are the one 2026 trend that arrived through two unrelated channels in the same pass
1EdTech names **digital credentials and digital competencies** among its three trends to watch, driven by **employer expectations** rather than institutional demand — and independently, a `user:1EdTech` enumeration found this KB held `4` of the body's `46` repositories, with the mint-and-verify pair (`OpenCASE` for CASE competency frameworks, the Open Badges **public validator**, `cert-schema` for Blockcerts) entirely unheld until p718.

🟢 **The composable consequence is the part worth keeping:** *align this learner's measured gap to an official curriculum outcome, then issue a credential an employer can verify* is a complete, demand-backed product arc — and **the join key is a machine-readable standards framework, which almost no institution has.** That is why `OpenCASE` is filed as a platform row and not a library: the gap between a tutor's diagnosis and a recognised outcome is a standards-publishing problem, not a model problem.

### 🔴 T213 — Every region's 2026 regulation converges on ONE control, and it is the control open education tooling was missing entirely
Independently, in four regional legs: **California AB 1159** bars student data from training AI models; **NYC DOE** guidance states the same; the **EU AI Act** makes education access and assessment Annex III high-risk with duties binding `2027-12-02` (and an NCII/CSAM prohibition from `2026-12-02`); **Vietnam's** July 2026 decision names automated educational assessment as high-risk; **Australia's** higher-education regulator already requires universities to file generative-AI risk plans; **UNESCO IESALC** measures only **`26%`** of LAC universities with any formal framework against **`87%`** adoption.

🔴 **Against that, p718's presence check found `0` de-identification tools across `309` agent rows, `325` foundation rows and `125` platform rows.** The remedy is filed as a **three-rung ladder**, and the rungs are not substitutes: [`microsoft/presidio`](https://github.com/microsoft/presidio) (MIT) redacts identifiers from free text; [`arx-deidentifier/arx`](https://github.com/arx-deidentifier/arx) (Apache-2.0) handles the re-identifying *combination* in a table with no names in it; [`opendp/opendp`](https://github.com/opendp/opendp) (MIT) produces a bound an institution can publish and defend. 🟢 **The failure mode to name in any proposal: implementing rung one and reporting rung three.**

### 🟢 T214 — The pedagogical argument has flipped from "give students AI access" to "gate it", and there is now a cited literature and shipped code for it
[`epequeno/mathmate`](https://github.com/epequeno/mathmate) (MIT) is built around a finding it cites in its own README — **Bastani et al. 2025 and Lehmann et al. 2024: students with unguarded model access finish faster and learn *worse*** — and ships the countermeasure as the product: a Socratic hint ladder, a tool loop capped at three rounds, and path-scoped memory. [`fcescob/understand`](https://github.com/fcescob/understand) (MIT) implements the same idea as **mastery gating with an explicit escape hatch** — *“just tell me”* drops the gate — and [`ProjectAJ14/eklavya`](https://github.com/ProjectAJ14/eklavya), already on this shelf, puts the gate on a **git commit**.

🟢 **This is the clearest convergence of pedagogy and architecture this KB has recorded: the differentiating feature of a 2026 education agent is what it REFUSES to do.** 🔵 **And it is what separates a real education agent from the dominant false positive — p718's keyword sweep returned `102` novel repositories of which the great majority were curricula *teaching AI engineering*; none of them gate anything, because a curriculum has no learner model to gate against.**

## 🆕 T205–T209 — added at p717 (2026-11-09)

### 🔴 T205 — The EU education AI deadline MOVED to `2027-12-02`, and the guidance still being published says `2026-08-02`
The Digital Omnibus deferred the AI Act's Annex III high-risk obligations for education — admissions, student evaluation, exam scoring, proctoring — from **`2026-08-02` to `2027-12-02`** (one source names the amendment **Regulation (EU) 2026/1744**). 🔴 **Compliance-vendor guides dated into 2026 still assert the August 2026 date**, so the market is currently being sold urgency against a deadline that no longer exists. 🟢 **What did not move:** **Article 50 transparency/disclosure duties stay on `2026-08-02`** — the only education AI obligation with a live 2026 date — and the **emotion-recognition prohibition has been in force since `2025-02-02`**, which makes any affect-inferring proctoring or engagement-monitoring feature a present exposure rather than a future one. **Consequence for a studio:** sell the Article 50 disclosure work and the emotion-recognition audit *now*; scope conformity assessment as an 18-month programme, not an emergency.

### 🟢 T206 — The three-market split in APAC, and South Korea's reversal is the most instructive half of it
**China mandates, South Korea retreated, Japan watches.** China's MoE guidelines make AI instruction compulsory from ~age six across all grades (reported `6` hours/year lower grades, one hour/fortnight higher, named *"Artificial Intelligence and Technology"* for 2026–27) **while barring primary pupils from independent generative-AI use and barring teachers from substituting AI for core instruction** — so the demand is curriculum, teacher training and AI-literacy assessment, *not* a student chatbot. South Korea **stripped "textbook" status from its AI textbooks, reclassifying them as supplementary materials** and pushing the decision to principals, after uptake of **under `30%` of `6,339` elementary schools**. Japan's MEXT is **neutral**, steering generative AI to lesson prep and administrative drafting with teacher judgement required. 🟢 **The transferable trend: a national mandate that lands ahead of teacher capability converts into thousands of school-level decisions, not a programme.** That is a channel cost, and it should be priced in before any ministry engagement.

### 🔴 T207 — GitHub-only discovery systematically under-reports EMEA, and this pass has a clean instance
`AlekSIS` — a real German school information system with timetables, digital class records and person/group management — **has no GitHub address at all**; `git ls-remote https://github.com/AlekSIS/AlekSIS-Core` returns the credential prompt GitHub issues for a non-existent path, while every other subject in the pass resolved. The project lives on the **Teckids `edugit.org` GitLab**. Combined with the standing `Opetushallitus` EUPL block (real grants no scanner will classify, recorded at `p690`), the pattern is consistent: **European public-sector education software is disproportionately hosted off GitHub and under EUPL**, so a GitHub-search-plus-`spdx_id` instrument reports it as *absent* or *unknown licence*. 🟢 **Read every `EMEA` count in this KB as a floor set by the instrument, not a measurement of the region** — and add a non-GitHub forge leg (`edugit.org`, institutional GitLab, public forges) before claiming EMEA coverage.

### 🔴 T208 — `NOASSERTION` is a payload-read instruction, and four of the most-starred "open source" building blocks fail the gate
Four subjects this pass probed carry a grant that is not what the roundups call it: **[`opendatalab/MinerU`](https://github.com/opendatalab/MinerU)** (`83,333★`) is **Apache-2.0 *plus additional terms*** on a `3,300 B` `LICENSE.md`; **[`BerriAI/litellm`](https://github.com/BerriAI/litellm)** (`62,934★`) is a **split grant** on a `1,418 B` payload with named directories carved out of MIT; **[`microsoft/autogen`](https://github.com/microsoft/autogen)** (`61,752★`) ships **`CC-BY-4.0`** — a *content* licence — as its root `LICENSE`; **[`FlowiseAI/Flowise`](https://github.com/FlowiseAI/Flowise)** (`55,568★`) is **`archived: true`**, read-only since `2026-08-13`. 🟢 **In all four, `spdx_id == NOASSERTION` was the detector correctly refusing to classify a modified grant** — the opposite of noise. **The cheap tell costs one `wc -c`: an Apache-2.0 claim on a payload that is not ~`11,350 B` is a modified Apache grant.** Canonical cross-check from this pass: `ragflow` and `smolagents` both read `11,356 B` / sha256₁₂ `43070e2d4e53`.

### 🟢 T209 — Detection is being abandoned as a control, and the spend is moving to assessment redesign
**Curtin University will disable Turnitin's AI detection in 2026**, and US R1 practice is reported as course-by-course discretion rather than detection mandates. At the same time **`86%` of education organisations report using generative AI while most lack a policy**, and teacher use roughly doubled year-on-year (`60%` in 2024-25). 🟢 **The trend is a substitution, not a retreat:** institutions that stop trying to detect AI have to redesign what they assess — oral defence, process evidence, versioned drafts, in-class work — which is a curriculum and workflow engagement, and a larger one than a detector licence. ⚠️ All figures here are secondary; confirm before they reach a client deck.

# 📡 Trends — Education

> What is actually changing in AI + education as of November 2026. Each trend names its evidence and its confidence.

🔴 **Read this before citing any `T` number: four identifiers on this page resolve to two different trends each, and `156` references across the shelves point at them.** Re-measured at p685 by counting headings rather than trusting the last figure: **`87` `## T` headings, `83` distinct numbers, `0` gaps** — 🔄 **re-derived at p687: `93` headings, `89` distinct numbers, `max = T93`, and now `4` gaps at `T84`–`T87`.** 🟢 **Those four gaps are the reservation this banner's own repair plan created, not a defect — do NOT close them.** p685 set aside `T84`–`T87` to receive the renumbered second occurrences of `T31`/`T32`/`T39`/`T40`; p686 then filed `T88`–`T90` and p687 `T91`–`T93`, both correctly numbering from `max(## T)` and stepping over the reserved block. 🔴 **A future pass that re-derives this census will see `4` gaps and may read them as a numbering error. Reusing `T84`–`T87` for new trends would consume the only free identifiers the collision repair can land in, and the repair would then have nowhere to go.** The reserved block is load-bearing; the next `T` number is `T125` — so the heading count is *not* the trend count (the `distinct` vs `total` distinction this page records as **T62**). The collisions are **`T31`, `T32`, `T39` and `T40`**, each used once by `p657`/`p658` and again by `p661`/`p664`:

🔴 **p685 deliberately did not repair it, and the reason is a data-integrity one rather than a scheduling one.** Renumbering the second of each pair to free identifiers (`T84`–`T87`) is mechanical, but **rewriting the `156` citations is not**: each site meant one specific trend, that intent is not recoverable from the token `T39`, and a bulk reassignment would silently point a documented claim at the wrong evidence. **A wrong citation is worse than an ambiguous one, because it reads as resolved.** The repair is therefore: renumber the four second-occurrence headings, then disambiguate references **one at a time, by reading each site**, and leave `T31`/`T32`/`T39`/`T40` permanently retired rather than reused. 🔵 **Until that is done, every `T31`/`T32`/`T39`/`T40` citation on these shelves should be read as naming a *pair*, not a trend.** New trends are numbered from `max(## T)`, never from the last heading in file order — `p685` filed **T82** and **T83** that way and both are unique.

## 🆕 T200–T204 — added at p716 (2026-11-09)

### T200 — 🔵 **When the tooling floor drops, institutional demand fragments from PLATFORMS into disposable per-classroom tools — and the supply side now shows it at n=1 school** 🟢 new

Owner expansion on a single account ([`cagoooo`](https://github.com/cagoooo), 石門國小 / Shimen Elementary, Taoyuan 🇹🇼) returns **more than forty MIT-licensed repositories**, nearly all `0★`, built by one teacher: real-time polling and word clouds, a canteen ordering system, automatic timetabling, a repair-request system, portrait-release consent forms, zhuyin and English typing games, a lantern-riddle game (`716-I`).

🟢 **This is not a curation finding, it is a demand-shape finding.** The output of an AI-enabled teacher is not one platform; it is **forty small, locally-owned, disposable tools**, each solving one school's one problem — and almost none of them would ever be bought, because each has a single-classroom addressable market.

🔵 **What follows for a public-sector K-12 engagement is a change of deliverable.** The thing to sell is **not** a product and **not** forty products. It is a **generator plus a governance wrapper**: a sanctioned way for staff to produce these tools, with the review, accessibility, data-protection and retirement policy already attached. 🔴 **And the risk is the mirror image:** forty unreviewed staff-built tools handling children's data is the shadow-IT problem of the next few years, which is precisely the capacity gap `T187` and the p716 LATAM/EMEA legs both measure. **The governance wrapper is the billable part**, and it is mandated reading against the EMEA teacher-training and AI-Act obligations rather than discretionary.

### T201 — 🔴 **The business generative AI has actually destroyed is ANSWER DELIVERY, and it is now a documented casualty rather than a prediction** 🟢 new

**Chegg cut `45 %` of its staff — `388` roles — and recalled its former CEO**, after generative AI and Google AI Overviews gutted homework-help traffic (North America leg, p716). Set that beside the global market discipline measured in the same pass: **rising revenue, falling investment, and a market that now rewards products which can prove results.**

🔵 **The strategic consequence is a positioning test that can be applied to any education product in one question: does it deliver the answer, or does it deliver the learner's capability to produce the answer?** The first is the business that just shed `45 %` of its staff. The second is what every Socratic / hint-only / refuses-to-do-the-work row on this base's agents shelf is built to do — a cohort that has grown steadily and now includes rows whose README explicitly states the refusal (`dylanj7/scholara`, `ThinkStepOfficial/thinkstep-tutor`, `relleturner/agora`, `baney75/myelinate`).

**What changes for an engagement:** the refusal to answer stops being a pedagogical preference to defend and becomes **the commercially defensible architecture**, with a named casualty as the evidence. 🔴 **And the corollary is a disqualifier:** any client proposal whose core value is faster answer retrieval is being proposed into the one segment with a proven collapse.

### T202 — 🟢 **“Verify the human after the agent” has become its own product category, and p716 is the first pass to see independent implementations converge** 🟢 new

Two unrelated projects, filed in the same pass, implement the same previously-unnamed thing: **after the coding agent writes the code, quiz the human on it before the work is allowed to proceed.**

| subject | licence | mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| [`ProjectAJ14/eklavya`](https://github.com/ProjectAJ14/eklavya) | MIT, `29★` | local knowledge graph + spaced repetition + **an optional commit gate** |
| [`SunflowersLwtech/covate`](https://github.com/SunflowersLwtech/covate) | MIT, `8★` | MCP server + a hosted **learning ledger** |

Related and already shelved: `mcp-tool-shop-org`-style skill packs, `baney75/myelinate`, `Noam-Marom/academic-students`.

🟢 **Why this is a trend and not two repositories.** `T192` established that education agent supply had shifted from applications to **skills/specifications**. T202 is the next step: the *subject* of the specification has moved from the learner to **the developer who just used an agent**, and the enforcement point has moved into the **engineering workflow** — a commit gate, not a lesson. That is a corporate-learning product with a technical enforcement surface, which is a materially different sale from an LMS course.

🔵 **Why Globant should care specifically:** this is the one education pattern whose buyer is an **engineering organisation** rather than an education institution — the same buyer the studio already sells delivery work to. The commit gate is the smallest credible pilot in this whole base: one repository, one plugin, measurable in a sprint.

### T203 — 🔴 **The standards layer, not the model, is the chokepoint between a demo and a delivery — and this base had declared the gap before it found the fix** 🟢 new

This base's foundations shelf carried a declared gap reading *“LMS interoperability — nothing standards-shaped — every tutor row hand-rolls launch and grade-return”* and *“assessment delivery — item generation that terminates in a JSON blob.”* With `302` agent rows on the shelf, a large share of them content generators, **the generation problem is solved and the delivery problem is not.**

p716 closed part of it with [`jcputney/elearning-module-parser`](https://github.com/jcputney/elearning-module-parser) (Apache-2.0) — **SCORM 1.2, SCORM 2004, AICC, xAPI, cmi5**.

🟢 **The trend claim is about where value is moving, not about one library.** When adoption is near-universal (`86 %`, `T198`) and investors demand proof (`T201`), the scarce capability stops being *can you generate a lesson* and becomes **can you get it into the gradebook the institution already runs, in a format its auditors accept**. That is standards work: unglamorous, permissively licensed, and now the actual differentiator.

🔵 **Corroborating vendor signal:** **Instructure launched `Canvas Career`**, a skills-first AI LMS for workforce learning — the incumbent moving to skills-first delivery, which only works if skills attainment is **recorded in a portable format**. Micro-credentials appear on every momentum list in the p716 global leg; **blockchain credentialing appears on every fading list.** The durable layer is the boring standard (`cmi5`, `xAPI`), not the novel ledger.

### T204 — 🟢 **Offline-first and a stated RAM floor are becoming procurement REQUIREMENTS in APAC and LATAM, not accessibility extras** 🟢 new

The p716 APAC leg produced one hard adoption figure — **virtual-tutor adoption at `30 %`** — against uptake described as **patchy, with limited connectivity named as the probable barrier.** The region is simultaneously described as the fastest-growing. **Appetite is not the constraint; bandwidth is.**

Supply has started answering in the specific terms a procurement officer can test:

| subject | stated constraint |
|---|---|
| [`danilo-labs/Sagavar`](https://github.com/danilo-labs/Sagavar) | runs in **`4 GB` RAM, zero internet** (Ollama / KoboldCpp) |
| [`georgekimaninjoroge/Meridian`](https://github.com/georgekimaninjoroge/Meridian) | **offline-first** LMS as an architectural default |
| `Kolibri` *(already shelved)* | offline-first distribution |
| `abdalluh17777/personal-local-ai-tutor` *(logged)* | `100 %` local on one consumer GPU |

🟢 **The trend is that the claim has become QUANTIFIED.** *“Works offline”* is a marketing phrase; **“`4 GB` of RAM and no internet” is a specification a buyer can verify on the hardware they already own** — and once one vendor states a number, the others must. Combined with `T195` (sovereignty converging from two directions, making self-hosted inference the education default), the result is that **a cloud-only architecture is becoming disqualifying in two of four regions**, not merely disfavoured.

🔵 **Design rule for an engagement:** state the RAM floor and the offline behaviour in the proposal, as numbers, before being asked. In LATAM it also sidesteps the `62`-point governance gap (`p716` LATAM leg), because data that never leaves the building is a much shorter policy conversation at institutions where **only ≈`30 %` have a published AI policy at all.**

## 🆕 T196–T199 — added at p715 (2026-11-09)

### T196 — 🔴 "Open source" in a licence's NAME is now a thing to verify, because a major public funder has taken the phrase

The **"IDB Open-Source Software License" (effective December 2025)** is published by the Inter-American Development Bank, is called open source, and is not: §11 permits termination *"in its sole discretion"*, §12 then obliges the user to destroy or return the code, §4 binds derivatives and their future releases to the same terms, §10 has the user indemnify the bank for exercising the rights granted, and §15 forces AAA arbitration seated in Washington DC. It governs **`79` repositories**, `0` of them permissively licensed.

🔵 **The trend this instances, and it is the one to watch:** large public and multilateral funders are publishing **bespoke, named, source-available licences** rather than adopting OSI ones — close enough to open source to be catalogued as such by downstream tooling, and revocable in ways no OSI licence is. 🔴 **For a studio the practical consequence is that "it's on GitHub under an open-source licence" has stopped being a usable clearance statement.** The clause to grep for is termination-at-discretion.

### T197 — 🔴 `NOASSERTION` is a weak NEGATIVE predictor of a buildable grant, measured across four independent causes

This base has now recovered the real grant behind a `NOASSERTION` licence field on four structurally different causes: a family the detector cannot name (**EUPL**, `99/100` on one Finnish national agency), a **bespoke licence under a language-suffixed filename** (`LICENSE-ENG.md`, IDB), a **content licence rather than a software one** (**CC BY-SA 4.0**, `education-agent-skills`, `965★`), and a **`19`-byte assertion in place of a licence text** (`frappe/education`: `License: GNU GPL V3`, `703★`).

🟢 **`4 / 4` recovered. `0 / 4` permissive.** 🔴 So the correct prior when the field reads `NOASSERTION` is **not** *"probably fine, the detector is just blind"* — it is *"probably not buildable, read the clauses."* The blindness is real and the recovered grants are real; **none of them has yet been MIT or Apache-2.0.**

### T198 — 🟢 Adoption is near-universal and governance is the lagging variable in all four regions — but the REGULATORY gradient is now steep, and it runs opposite to the adoption one

The four mandated regional legs agree on shape: adoption ahead of policy everywhere, roughly two-thirds of higher-education institutions still without a formal AI policy. 🔵 **What is new at p715 is how far apart the binding instruments have moved.**

| region | binding instruments naming education | measured adoption |
|---|---|---|
| **EMEA** | 🔴 strongest — EU AI Act **Annex III high-risk** (date contradictory: `2027-12-02` vs stale August 2026); UK DfE product safety standards (Jan 2026); Ofqual coursework-integrity resources (Mar 2026) | 🔴 **no regional figure returned** |
| **APAC** | 🟢 **Vietnam** names education in a binding high-risk list (extra duties for systems live before `2026-08-15`); **Australia TEQSA** mandates a generative-AI action plan from every provider; **Korea** AI Basic Act in force `2026-01-22`, penalties deferred | 🔴 none returned |
| **North America** | 🟡 no federal statute — executive only (EO 14277); `134` bills in `31` states; **NC SL 2026-41** dates: `2026-12-31` / `2027-06-30` / `2028-06-30` | `60%` of teachers; `55%` of principals have not restricted access |
| **LATAM** | 🔴 **none — no current binding national AI-in-education law anywhere in the region**; `85%` of countries have a strategy, **only Brazil and Colombia fund one** | 🟢 **highest measured: `92%` students / `79%` faculty (DEC/Tec de Monterrey); `87%` of institutions (UNESCO IESALC)** |

🔴 **The inversion is the finding: the region with the highest measured adoption has the least binding regulation, and the region with the strictest regime returned no adoption data at all.** A studio should price LATAM engagements as **adoption-led, governance-greenfield** and EMEA engagements as **compliance-led**, and they are not the same deliverable.

### T199 — 🟢 Endangered- and indigenous-language education is a real, funded, almost-unsupplied niche

Chile's national AI centre publishes a **Spanish ↔ Rapa Nui** translation stack under **Apache-2.0**, with a fine-tuned NLLB-200-3.3B checkpoint and a self-hostable PyTriton server ([`CENIA-DEV/multilingual-translator-app`](https://github.com/CENIA-DEV/multilingual-translator-app)). 🔵 **Chile, Peru, Bolivia, Paraguay and Mexico all operate intercultural bilingual education mandates**, which makes this a *procurement* category rather than a research interest — and this is the only permissively licensed substrate addressing one that this base has found in `715` passes. 🔴 **Bound on the claim:** one repository, `1★`, an applied MVP from a research centre, not a maintained product. The niche is evidenced; the supply is one row deep.

## 🆕 T191–T195 — added at p714 (2026-11-08)

### 🔴 T191 — A licence census over European public-sector education code is wrong by default, because the detector cannot name the EUPL 🟢 new

GitHub's `license.spdx_id` returns **`NOASSERTION` for `99` of the first `100`** repositories published by **Finland's national education agency**, [`Opetushallitus`](https://github.com/Opetushallitus) (`182` repositories in total). The payloads were read directly on `9` of them: **`9 / 9` are EUPL-1.1 or EUPL-1.2**, and four of the nine are byte-identical (`631 B`, sha256₁₂ `85088c175fdf`) to a payload this base had already classified on its own shelves.

🔴 **The trend is a measurement hazard with a direction: it under-reports European public-sector supply specifically.** The EUPL is the European Commission's own licence and the default for a large volume of ministry-funded education software — and it is precisely the family the detector declines to classify. **Any “share of permissive repositories by region” figure computed from the API is therefore biased against EMEA by construction.**

🔵 **Signal to act on:** when a European public body's estate is assessed, read the grant payload, and classify by **sha256 identity** against payloads already read — it is one `curl` per repository and it needs no prose parsing. 🔴 **And state the read convention**: see `T193`'s sibling finding `714-D`, where one byte of trailing newline produced two hashes for one file.

### 🟢 T192 — Education agent supply has shifted from APPLICATIONS to SKILLS, and the unit of reuse is now a specification 🟢 new

Of the `15` education agents filed at p714, **`9` are a `SKILL.md` plus a teaching protocol** — not a deployable service: [`hwl668/Scientific-learning-skills-`](https://github.com/hwl668/Scientific-learning-skills-), [`wildcat430524/Steps2Great-skill`](https://github.com/wildcat430524/Steps2Great-skill), [`rage/course-material-agent-skills`](https://github.com/rage/course-material-agent-skills), [`YJLi-new/undergraduate-coding-tutor`](https://github.com/YJLi-new/undergraduate-coding-tutor), [`klausners/course-builder`](https://github.com/klausners/course-builder), [`baney75/myelinate`](https://github.com/baney75/myelinate) and others. One states it outright: *“它不是软件、不是课程、不是网站”* — **it is not software, not a course, not a website.**

🟢 **Why this is a trend and not a fashion: a protocol is portable across model vendors and a deployable is not.** Several of these declare `Claude Code | Codex | OpenClaw | GPTs | Generic` compatibility in the README, which is a deliberate bet that the harness will change and the pedagogy will not.

🔵 **Signal to act on:** the studio's reusable asset in education is shifting from a codebase to a **specified teaching method** — cheaper to author, cheaper to localise, and far cheaper to keep current. 🔴 **The cost is that quality becomes unverifiable by inspection**: a `SKILL.md` has no test suite, so the diligence question moves from *“does it build?”* to *“is the pedagogy sound and who says so?”*

### 🔴 T193 — When the product is a document, the document's licence is the product's licence — and the two are increasingly different files 🟢 new

[`wildcat430524/Steps2Great-skill`](https://github.com/wildcat430524/Steps2Great-skill) ships `LICENSE` (**MIT**, code) and **`LICENSE-DOCS`** (**CC BY 4.0** — *“protocol, subject packs, templates, tutorials, examples, README”*). Its own README says the artefact is not software. **So MIT governs the part that barely exists and CC BY 4.0 governs the substance.**

🔴 **This is the direct consequence of `T192`.** As supply becomes skill-shaped, the grant that matters stops being the code grant — and every licence probe in common use, including this base's own until p714, reads `LICENSE` and stops. Swept across p714's filings: **`1 / 15`**, which is early rather than negligible.

🔵 **Signal to act on:** for any skill-shaped dependency, enumerate **every** `LICENSE*` file, not the first one. 🟢 **CC BY 4.0 is commercially usable — attribution only, not NonCommercial** — but attribution on *content* is a different obligation from an MIT code dependency and has to reach the rendered output, not just a `NOTICE` file. 🔴 **Contrast [`byoungd/English-level-up-tips`](https://github.com/byoungd/English-level-up-tips), refused at p714 as CC BY-**NC**-4.0**: the same licence family, one clause apart, and the other side of that clause is unusable.

### 🔴 T194 — In North America student adoption has outrun institutional permission, and that inversion is the sellable problem 🟢 new

A Gallup study reports **over `60%` of US college students use AI weekly for coursework**, while **roughly half of their institutions officially discourage or prohibit it**. 🔴 **This is the exact inverse of `T187`'s LATAM shape.** LATAM has `87%` use against `26%` with any formal framework — adoption outrunning *capacity*. North America has adoption outrunning *permission*: the policy exists and it says no, and usage proceeds regardless.

🔵 **The two call for opposite engagements.** LATAM needs framework and capacity built where none exists (`P110`). **North America needs existing prohibitions converted into workable, auditable permission** — acceptable-use boundaries, disclosure norms, assessment redesign that assumes AI availability — because a ban that `60%` of students ignore weekly is not a control, it is an unmanaged risk with an audit trail nobody is keeping.

🔵 **Signal to act on:** in North America, lead with assessment redesign and disclosure instrumentation rather than with a tutor. 🔴 **And note the regulatory direction of travel is unhelpful here**: UNC's 2026 analysis argues US AI regulation is **slowing**, naming *“the growing chasm between the U.S. and its allies”* — so institutional policy, not statute, will remain the binding instrument in this region for the near term.

### 🟢 T195 — Sovereignty is converging from two directions, which makes self-hosted inference the DEFAULT for education rather than a concession 🟢 new

**EMEA:** the European University Association's January 2026 report urges mindful adoption and **explicitly prioritising European LLMs**. **APAC:** `itnews.asia` frames *“AI sovereignty will set the pace for Asia Pacific in 2026”*, and Forrester describes APAC enterprises moving from pilots toward **sovereign, governed deployment**, with the region converging on shared principles implemented **per market**.

🟢 **Two regions, different motivations — regulatory in EMEA, strategic and data-residency in APAC — arriving at the same architectural requirement.** Together they cover `100` of this base's `274` agent rows by region placement.

🔵 **Signal to act on:** specify education products for **local or self-hosted inference first**, with a hosted frontier model as the optional accelerator. That inverts the usual default and it is why [`ollama/ollama`](https://github.com/ollama/ollama) and the local-first [`munimtechnologies/feedback-commons`](https://github.com/munimtechnologies/feedback-commons) filed at p714 carry more weight here than their star counts imply. 🔴 **The constraint compounds with LATAM's**: offline-first for connectivity (`kolibri`) and self-hosted for sovereignty are **the same engineering**, which means one architecture serves three regions and only North America tolerates the cloud-only default.


## 🆕 T186–T190 — added at p713 (2026-11-08)

### 🔴 T186 — The EU's high-risk deadline for education moved by ~16 months, and a deferred deadline defers the WRONG obligations 🟢 new

Education AI is high-risk under **Annex III** of the EU AI Act. The date those obligations bite moved from **`2026-08-02`** to **`2027-12-02`** for stand-alone Annex III systems, and to **`2028-08-02`** for AI embedded in regulated products, via the **Digital Omnibus** amendment against a May 2026 political agreement.

🔴 **The trend is not the postponement — it is what the postponement does to attention.** Two obligations did **not** move: the **Article 4 AI-literacy duty for staff has been in force since February 2025**, and the **NCII/CSAM prohibition lands `2026-12-02`**. An institution that deferred its whole AI programme to the old August 2026 date has deferred a duty that was already live and one arriving within the year.

🔵 **Signal to act on:** the near-term EMEA conversation is literacy and content-safety, not high-risk conformity — and the extra 16 months is **build time** for a dossier produced by a pipeline (`P114`) rather than written once. 🔴 **Provenance: two independent sources in this pass carry the new dates and one still publishes `August 2026`. Not primary-verified — `ACTION TN` registers checking the Official Journal before this date enters a client-facing document.**

### 🟢 T187 — Governance capacity is the binding constraint, not model capability, and LATAM is where it is actually MEASURED 🟢 new

UNESCO IESALC, `200` HEIs across `19` countries: **`87%` use AI in at least one area; `26%` have any formal framework; `55%` have no specific AI budget; under `10%` have both guidelines and the capacity to apply them.** Brazil reproduces the shape independently at school level (Cetic.br 2026: `53%` of administrators use AI, `22%` of schools have guidelines).

🟢 **A 61-point gap between use and governance means adoption ALREADY HAPPENED, ungoverned.** The sellable work is therefore policy, documentation and operating capacity — a services engagement — rather than a tool.

🔵 **And the trend generalises beyond LATAM:** `T186`'s EMEA deadlines, North America's `134` bills across `31` states, and Korea's and Vietnam's 2026 frameworks all describe the same movement — **from experimentation to governed use** — which the global leg found stated independently. LATAM is simply the only region where somebody instrumented it. 🔴 **EMEA's leg, by contrast, returned no hard adoption rate for European schools at all** — an informed gap, recorded as one.

### 🟢 T188 — A regulator's own test harness is open source and permissive, so conformance becomes a BUILD rather than a purchase 🟢 new

Singapore's **AI Verify**, stewarded by the AI Verify Foundation under IMDA, is **Apache-2.0** on GitHub ([`aiverify-foundation/aiverify`](https://github.com/aiverify-foundation/aiverify), `106★`), with a CI harness ([`moonshot-cicd`](https://github.com/aiverify-foundation/moonshot-cicd), Apache-2.0).

🟢 **The trend: compliance tooling is arriving from the regulator side under permissive licences, and its architecture is plug-in shaped.** *"Show the ministry how this tutor was evaluated"* becomes a plugin-authoring job on an Apache-2.0 base, not a bespoke build and not a consultancy report. 🔵 **Read with `T186`: an EMEA institution with 16 more months can build a dossier on the APAC regulator's harness** — the instruments are not jurisdiction-locked even though the obligations are. 🔴 **AI Verify 2.0 is announced as upcoming**, so both architecture and plugin API may move; re-read next pass.

🟢 **This trend is also how it was FOUND, which is `713-G`:** a mandated regional leg named the instrument in prose with no URL, and eleven passes of scoring those legs `0 / N repository addresses` had been measuring the wrong unit.

### 🔴 T189 — Accessibility is a DATED legal deadline rather than a quality goal, and the remedy is MIT-licensed and sits in the authoring flow 🟢 new

North America's **April 2026 ADA deadline for large public institutions** is in force. The obligation is content-shaped — every course page, document and video — which makes it unlike the policy obligations in `T186` and `T187`: there is no framework to write, only artefacts to fix, and there are a great many of them.

🟢 **The leverage point is the authoring surface, not the remediation backlog.** [`instructure/tinymce-a11y-checker`](https://github.com/instructure/tinymce-a11y-checker) (MIT) checks accessibility **inside TinyMCE**, the editor Canvas and much of the sector embed — catching a defect before the content exists in ten thousand copies rather than after. `P115` is the engagement shape.

🔴 **Filed with its defect: the checker was last pushed `2024-06-26`** and is the stalest artefact this base filed at p713. Verified ALIVE at `master` on `2026-11-08`. **A fork is likely, and that is the engagement rather than an obstacle to it** — but a pattern that silently assumes an actively maintained upstream here would be wrong.

### 🟢 T190 — The small-model tier is a COST architecture, and it is what makes more than half of LATAM's universities addressable at all 🟢 new

UNESCO IESALC measured **`55%` of LATAM universities with no specific AI budget**. Any engagement priced against per-token cloud inference is unsellable to more than half the region.

🟢 **Three artefacts filed at p713 are the answer to that constraint rather than capability rows:** [`HKUDS/MiniRAG`](https://github.com/HKUDS/MiniRAG) (MIT, ACL 2026 — RAG built for small and open-sourced models), [`HKUDS/LightReasoner`](https://github.com/HKUDS/LightReasoner) (MIT, ACL 2026 Oral — a small model generates the teaching signal that improves a larger one), and [`moodlehq/moodleapp`](https://github.com/moodlehq/moodleapp) (Apache-2.0) for delivery on phones the students already carry. **The expensive model is needed for less of the loop, or for none of it.**

🔵 **The generalisation: "small model" on these shelves should be read as a PROCUREMENT property, not a performance compromise.** It is what decides whether an institution with no AI line item can run the thing at all — and it is the same property that answers EMEA data-residency and APAC data-exposure concerns, because a model that runs on owned hardware does not egress. 🔴 **`MiniRAG` was last pushed `2025-10-16` and its grant names an individual rather than the lab; `LightReasoner` is research code with `10` open issues.** Both are filed for the architecture, with the staleness stated.

## 🆕 T182–T185 — added at p712 (2026-11-08)

### 🔧 T182 — A repository declares its own region in MACHINE-READABLE form, and `T170`'s "operate vs buy" key is the second-best channel, not the first 🟢 new

`T170` (p709) keyed regional placement on whether a region's institutions **operate** or **buy** their systems. That holds as an explanation of *why* supply clusters, but p712 found a channel that is strictly cheaper and strictly more reliable for the act of placing a row: **the artifact ships its own region key.**

- **`es-419`** — the UN M.49 code for Latin America — committed as an i18n catalogue file is an unambiguous `LATAM` declaration. [`JhostinAleck/brightspace-mcp`](https://github.com/JhostinAleck/brightspace-mcp) ships `src/shared-kernel/output/i18n/catalogs/es-419.json`.
- **An IANA timezone** in config, docs and tests places an artifact the same way: `Asia/Hong_Kong` in `37` files of [`wongcyrus/Google-AI-Classroom`](https://github.com/wongcyrus/Google-AI-Classroom).
- **The grant's copyright holder line** places a row whenever the holder is an institution: *"Copyright (c) 2024 Tufts Center for Engineering Education and Outreach"*.

🔧 **The guard: place on the catalogues a project ships, never on the locales its schema permits.** The same repository lists `pt-BR` and `fr-CA` as permitted values and ships no catalogue for either; matching on the option list files one artifact in three regions.

🔴 **And the channel the obvious approach reaches for is the worst of the four.** The owner's declared GitHub profile location answered for `7 / 27` owners; `20 / 27` declare nothing a probe can match. `gh api users/{login}` is refused outright in a repo-scoped session, and `search/users` does not return a `location` field at all — only a `location:` qualifier you must supply a guess for. **This is why `711-C` mistook a reading failure for a vocabulary failure.**

### 🔴 T183 — A university ACRONYM in a repository name is a continent-level trap, and resolving it needs a DOMAIN 🟢 new

`mcp-blackboard-ucsc` is **Università Cattolica del Sacro Cuore** in Italy, not UC Santa Cruz. Neither the repository name nor the README states the country; the only locator is the institution's own domain (`unicatt.it`) in the configuration, corroborated by Italian workflow terms and an Italian exam-registration template. 🔵 **The trend, not the instance: as institution-bound agents proliferate (`T168`), acronym collisions become systematic, and every collision a naive pipeline resolves to the English-speaking reading exports a European or Asian row to North America.** The rule is mechanical — resolve an acronym from an email or web domain in the payload, never from the acronym.

### 🔴 T184 — An MIT grant can have NO IDENTIFIABLE LICENSOR, and no licence detector can see it 🟢 new

Research repositories published under double-blind review are leaking review anonymity into their `LICENSE` files. [`Veteran-Zero/MERIT`](https://github.com/Veteran-Zero/MERIT) carries the canonical MIT text with the holder line **`Copyright (c) 2026 Anonymous Authors`**. MIT grants permission *by* the copyright holder, so **there is no traceable party granting anything** — and GitHub reports a clean `MIT`, because the payload *is* MIT. 🔵 **This is a new defect class for the licence-reading discipline this base has built** (`T167` payload-reads are dated facts; `T172` metadata absence is a signal): **the payload can be perfect and the GRANT still void of a licensor.** The check costs one `grep -i copyright` on a file this base already downloads. 🔵 Second-order trend in the same row: **a permissive licence on an orchestration pinned to closed models** (Gemini-2.5-Flash, Gemini-2.5-Pro, Qwen3-Embedding-8B) grants the wiring and none of the intelligence — which is becoming the normal shape of "open source" agentic research code.

### 🟢 T185 — Where an LMS issues no student API keys, a deep and permanently un-commercial integration field forms 🟢 new

`T179` (p711) recorded institutions switching **off** Canvas personal access tokens, invalidating most LMS agent integrations. Brightspace/D2L shows the complementary case and it is instructive: **D2L issues no student API keys at all**, so every one of the `51` MIT-licensed D2L repositories found this pass authenticates by borrowing the user's own browser session — Playwright profile, pasted cookie, Valence token or OS keychain.

**The consequences are symmetric and both are commercially decisive.** 🟢 A student-side D2L integration needs **no tenant admin, no procurement and no institutional decision**, which is why the field is `51` repositories deep with no vendor in it. 🔴 **And nothing requiring institutional authority can be built this way at all**: of `9` substantive artifacts, `0` are instructor-side and **none can write a grade.** Grading, gradebook and roster writes exist only on the Blackboard and Canvas families, where an administrator can issue credentials.

🔵 **The generalisable rule for scoping any LMS engagement: ask what credential the platform issues to a student before designing anything.** No student credential means a thriving free field and a hard ceiling at the point where authority is required — and the ceiling, not the field, determines what can be sold.

## 🆕 T177–T181 — added at p711 (2026-11-08)

### 🔧 T177 — `T173` is CORRECTED: a thin region measures **the query**, not the grants. Put `license:` IN the search and the same sweep returns `8 / 8` granted 🔧 corrects `T173` at p711

`T173` (p710) read: *“A thin region measures GRANTS, not supply: `10 / 11` long-tail education repositories outside the US/EU are alive and UNGRANTED.”* **The `10 / 11` measurement stands. The inference drawn from it does not.**

p710 swept Spanish and Portuguese, then fetched `LICENSE` on the hits — which samples the population as it is, overwhelmingly ungranted. p711 ran the **same language sweep with `license:mit` as a search qualifier**, so GitHub's index filtered on the grant *before returning results*, and got **`8 / 8` alive and MIT, every payload read from the bytes.**

🟢 **The corrected trend: in any region whose long tail is individual developers, the grant must be a QUERY TERM, not a post-filter.** The unqualified sweep tells you the shape of the field; the qualified sweep tells you what you may legally build on. **Run both.** ⚠ Bounded honestly: the granted subset is **small and term-sensitive** — `2`, `12`, `1`, `4` hits on four productive legs and `total_count: 0` on five others. It is findable, not abundant. 🔴 **Carry the correction to every other industry base**, because the inference *“thin region ⇒ ungranted supply”* has been propagating for roughly thirty passes and part of it was a method artefact.

### 🟢 T178 — Education AI's compliance clock has SPLIT: the high-risk deadline moved to **2027-12-02**, but the transparency duty landed **2026-08-02**. The gap is the engagement window 🟢 new at p711

The EU's **Digital Omnibus on AI** moved the AI Act deadline for stand-alone **Annex III high-risk** systems — which is where education sits when AI touches **admissions, assessment or proctoring** — from `2026-08-02` to **`2027-12-02`**. AI embedded in regulated products moves to `2028-08-02`.

🔴 **Two duties did NOT move, and they are the ones that bind today:** the **Article 50 transparency** obligations (chatbot disclosure, synthetic-content labelling) apply from **`2026-08-02`**, and the **Article 4 AI-literacy** duty has applied since **`2025-02-02`** to *every* organisation that uses AI — therefore to every school.

🟢 **What this means commercially, and it is the opposite of a pause:** a client has **~13 months** in which a high-risk education deployment is buildable without the full Annex III conformity burden, **while disclosure, labelling and staff AI literacy are already enforceable**. The deployer carries the duty even when the tool is third-party. 🟢 **Therefore: ship transparency and literacy now, and architect for Annex III conformity in the same engagement rather than as a later project** — the deadline moved, it did not disappear, and a system designed without it will be rebuilt. ⚠ Dates are from secondary legal commentary and conflict with pre-Omnibus sources; verify against the Official Journal before putting them in a client deliverable.

### 🔴 T179 — Institutions are switching OFF student personal access tokens, and that quietly invalidates most LMS agent integrations 🔴 new at p711

[`CorCvusRamboChen/canvas-session-mcp`](https://github.com/CorCvusRamboChen/canvas-session-mcp) (MIT) authenticates through the student's **ordinary browser login** — real Chrome/Edge window, SSO and MFA as usual — and states the reason plainly: **“many universities no longer let students do that”**, referring to creating a Canvas personal access token.

🔴 **This is a trend about procurement, not code.** This base holds a large Canvas-agent cohort and **the majority of it authenticates with a personal access token.** At an institution that has disabled student token creation, **every one of those integrations is dead on arrival**, and no amount of engineering changes it — it is an IT policy decision.

🟢 **Operationally: establish the client's token policy BEFORE selecting an LMS integration.** It eliminates most of the field in one question. The surviving architectures are browser-session auth (student-side) and an institutionally-issued service credential (admin-side), and those two paths have **different data-protection reviews**, so the choice is made early or made twice.

### 🟢 T180 — Rubric assessment is going VERIFICATION-FIRST: the model proposes, the code checks. It is displacing LLM-as-judge where a grade has consequences 🟢 new at p711

[`fborrasumh/planificaia-docente`](https://github.com/fborrasumh/planificaia-docente) (MIT, Universidad Miguel Hernández, Zenodo DOI `10.5281/zenodo.23091372`) marks student work against a rubric the model structures and **the code then validates deterministically**: rubric weights must sum to `100`, **every descriptor must appear literally in the source document**, submissions are grouped by e-mail, duplicate-flagged, **SHA-256 fingerprinted per file**, and checked for milestone chaining.

🟢 **The inversion is the trend.** LLM-as-judge asks the model to be trustworthy. This asks the model to be *checkable*, and spends the engineering on the checks — and the checks are cheap, deterministic and explainable to a student contesting a grade. 🟢 **Where a mark carries consequences — credit, progression, certification — the defensible architecture is a model proposal plus a deterministic validator plus a named human decision-maker**, and this base can now point at a permissive education-native implementation rather than at [`microsoft/LLM-Rubric`](https://github.com/microsoft/LLM-Rubric), which is permissive but **not education**. 🔴 **Remaining gap: this is a single-file app for one university subject. A verification-first rubric engine at INSTITUTIONAL scale does not exist permissively.**

### 🟢 T181 — The cheapest pedagogical safeguard found this year is an INTERACTION ORDERING, not a model capability 🟢 new at p711

[`EstebanBond/artematico`](https://github.com/EstebanBond/artematico) (MIT) is a children's illustration course where an AI vision mentor marks drawings against a rubric calibrated per technique and per course week. **Its safeguard is a disabled button: “Evaluar” does not enable until the child has recorded their own self-assessment first.** Feedback is then bounded to exactly three items — one success, one correction, one micro-exercise.

🟢 **No model, prompt or guardrail is doing the pedagogical work; the ordering of two UI events is.** Self-assessment before feedback is what separates a tool that builds metacognition from one that outsources it, and it costs one disabled attribute to implement. 🟢 **It also answers the objection this base hears most from educators** — *“the AI will do the thinking for them”* — with a mechanism rather than a policy, which is what makes it usable in a procurement conversation. 🔴 **No other row across `236` agents on this shelf does it**, which is the finding: the field is optimising model quality and leaving the cheapest intervention on the floor.

## 🆕 T173–T176 — added at p710 (2026-11-08)

### T173 — A thin region measures GRANTS, not supply: `10 / 11` long-tail education repositories outside the US/EU are alive and UNGRANTED 🔴 new at p710

For dozens of passes this base read a thin region column as a discovery failure and answered it with more sweeps. p710 asked a different question — *not “do repositories exist?” but “do the repositories that exist carry a grant?”* — and probed five licence filenames (`LICENSE`, `LICENSE.md`, `LICENSE.txt`, `COPYING`, `LICENCE`) against every regional candidate found.

**Result: `10 / 11` are alive (`git ls-remote`) and serve `404` for all five.** Five LATAM teacher-formation and tutoring projects (Mexico's Nueva Escuela Mexicana, Brazil's EPT, Brazilian educational games, a mobile virtual tutor), one South African CAPS-aligned study platform, and four Indian JEE/NEET tutors — including one with a student model trained on **16M practice attempts**, benchmarked LightGBM against BKT, DKT and SAKT. **The global tail, by contrast, is overwhelmingly MIT.**

**Signal**: the inference *“thin column ⇒ thin supply”* is false wherever a region's tail is individual developers rather than institutions. The blocker is a missing file, and a licence is one commit — so the cheapest intervention is **asking the author**, not sweeping again or forking. Proof that the class *can* be granted: a Spanish primary-teacher-formation unit found in the same pass carries MIT. **Transferable to every Globant industry base with a thin non-US region.**

### T174 — Statutory instruments are the most reliable region key there is, and they are how North America finally placed 🟢 new at p710

A repository places to a region when the thing it names exists in exactly one jurisdiction (`709-C`). p710's finding is that **education STATUTES are the densest source of such names, and they had never been used as a key on these shelves.** IDEA produces the IEP and the due-process complaint; Section 504 produces the 504 plan; FERPA produces the directory-information notice; Perkins V produces the CTE plan. Each exists nowhere else on earth.

This broke a two-pass North American supply nil with three rows in one sweep, and it works symmetrically abroad: Israel's *inclusion committee*, Spain's `DAM` FP qualification, Madrid's ESO/Bachillerato stages, Pakistan's MDCAT, India's JEE/NEET.

**Signal**: sweep for the *artefact a statute names*, not for the country. **And the corollary matters more than the key: the same client need decomposes into DIFFERENT software per legal system** — under IDEA the work is adversarial prose assembly with traced assertions and exposed arithmetic; under Israel's committee process it is structured extraction with PII redaction. A studio that scopes "AI for special education" from the US shape will mis-scope the EMEA engagement.

### T175 — Prerequisite auditing arrived twice in one week from unrelated authors — the long-missing CONSUMER for knowledge tracing 🟢 new at p710

Two projects with no connection to each other — a rural-Gujarat FLN system for Standards 1–8 and an advanced-STEM multi-agent tutor — independently implemented **prerequisite auditing**: traverse a curriculum prerequisite graph and refuse to teach a topic until its prerequisites clear, instead of reporting a mark.

This base has held knowledge tracing for hundreds of passes (`pyKT`, `pyBKT`, `EduKTM`, `EduCAT`): all of it **estimates** mastery and none of it **acts** on the estimate. Two independent implementations in one week is the point at which that stops being a research idea.

**Signal**: the diagnostic claim is also the commercial one — *“a child failing two-digit addition has usually not mastered place-value bundling”* is a root cause a parent, teacher and ministry all understand, where a score of 35% is not. Pair it with the FLN system's three deployment constraints, which are what decide whether a rural rollout survives: **physical manipulatives** so no second device is needed, **offline resilience as a premise**, and **no public ranking**. See `P106` in [`../compose/patterns.md`](../compose/patterns.md).

### T176 — "Adaptive learning" names two different fields, and the education sense is the MINORITY of search results 🔴 new at p710

In machine learning, *adaptive learning* means a model adapting during training. In education it means instruction adapting to a learner. Both senses are MIT-licensed, recent and well-starred, and p710's `adaptive learning` leg returned the ML sense at the top: a NeurIPS 2026 optimiser for LLM agents, and a multi-agent RL ecosystem testbed for the Baldwin effect.

**Signal**: the fix is not a better keyword but a **required co-occurrence** — a learner noun (`student`, `pupil`, `learner`, `docente`, `aluno`) or a named curriculum stage must appear, or the hit is presumed ML-sense and refused. This base has already filed two subjects it had to annotate as *not education*; the discriminator is cheap and should run before filing, not after. **Applies to every industry base whose vocabulary collides with a machine-learning term** — "agent", "reward", "policy" and "curriculum learning" all have this problem.
